title: Plasma and intra-abdominal drain fluid pharmacokinetics of linezolid in critically ill patients with complicated intra-abdominal infections: implications for pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics target attainment against Enterococcus spp.
authors: Benítez-Cano A; De Antonio-Cuscó M; Ramos I; Prim N; Adalia R; Juanes-Borrego AM; Sorlí L; Luque S
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Linezolid is widely used for severe intra-abdominal infections (IAIs) caused by Enterococcus spp.; however, data on its peritoneal penetration are limited. We aimed to characterize plasma and peritoneal fluid (PF) linezolid exposure and evaluate pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD) target attainment.

METHODS: In this prospective observational study, critically ill adults with confirmed or suspected IAIs received intravenous linezolid (600 mg every 12 h). Paired plasma and PF samples were collected at steady state (before dosing and, 1, 3, 5, 8 and 12 h after infusion). Linezolid concentrations were quantified by validated high-performance liquid chromatography. Area under the concentration-time curve from 0 to 12 h (AUC0-12h) was calculated by non-compartmental analysis and peritoneal penetration as the PF-to-plasma AUC0-12h ratio. PK/PD target attainment (AUC0-24h/MIC ≥80, ≥100 and ≥120) was evaluated assuming Enterococcus spp. MICs of 1 and 2 mg/L.

RESULTS: Thirteen patients were included. Median (IQR) linezolid AUC0-12h was 62.3 (39.2-81.2) mg·h/L in plasma and 54.3 (40.5-68.8) mg·h/L in PF, with a median penetration ratio of 0.9 (0.8-1.0). Plasma and PF exposures were strongly correlated despite marked interindividual variability. Assuming an MIC of 1 mg/L, 69.2% and 76.9% of patients achieved an AUC0-24h/MIC ≥80 in plasma and PF, respectively, decreasing to 30.8% and 15.4% at a MIC of 2 mg/L.

CONCLUSIONS: Linezolid achieved substantial peritoneal penetration with comparable cumulative plasma and PF exposure despite marked interindividual variability. Target attainment decreased markedly when a MIC of 2 mg/L was assumed.

title: Long-read sequencing of clinical multidrug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis reveals a novel ethA structural variant conferring ethionamide resistance.
authors: Wang Q; Geng Y; Wu L; Xia D; Li R; Hu B; Gao S; Lu J; Dai J; Xu F; Zheng X; Xiang G
abstract: Multidrug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MDR-MTB) poses a major obstacle to global tuberculosis control. Although whole-genome sequencing (WGS) has advanced the detection of resistance-associated mutations, the contribution of structural variants (SVs) remains inadequately characterized due to the inherent limitations of short-read sequencing technologies in resolving repetitive genomic regions and large insertions or deletions. We applied Oxford Nanopore long-read sequencing to clinical MDR-MTB isolates and susceptible controls, complemented by Illumina short-read sequencing. Variants were identified using BCFtools and independently validated with SVIM-asm. Candidate resistance mutations were mapped against the 2023 World Health Organization (WHO) mutation catalogue. Functional validation of identified SVs was performed through heterologous expression in Mycobacterium smegmatis, minimum inhibitory concentration determination, Western blotting, and AlphaFold 3-based structural modeling. We identified two unclassified SVs within WHO-catalogued resistance genes: an IS6110 insertion in Rv0678 (c.59_60ins1358bp, p.Gln22fs) and a 131-bp deletion in ethA (c.135_265del, p.Trp45fs). While IS6110-mediated disruption of Rv0678 has been previously associated with bedaquiline resistance, the ethA deletion represents a previously undescribed SV. Heterologous expression of the ethA deletion in Mycobacterium smegmatis conferred a 16-fold increase in the minimum inhibitory concentration of ethionamide (256 μg/mL vs. 16 μg/mL for wild-type), and AlphaFold 3 structural prediction provided a structural rationale for the loss of the C-terminal domain essential for monooxygenase activity. This study identifies a novel ethA SV conferring ethionamide resistance and provides functional validation of a specific Rv0678 IS6110 insertion allele, demonstrating the power of long-read sequencing to uncover both known and novel mechanisms of drug resistance in MDR-MTB.

title: Whole-genome sequencing-based characterization of antimicrobial resistance determinants and phenotype-genotype concordance in uropathogenic Escherichia coli isolates from ICU patients in Saudi Arabia.
authors: Almebairik N; Bukhari D; Alhumaidan O; Idrees E; Asiri H; Alanazi F; Alkarni M; Alarjani K; Almaarik B
abstract: Escherichia coli is a leading cause of urinary tract infections (UTIs) and an important reservoir of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) enables comprehensive characterization of bacterial population structure and AMR determinants; however, limited data are available on the ability of WGS-derived resistance determinants to predict phenotypic AMR among urinary E. coli isolates. This study aimed to characterize the population structure and AMR determinants of E. coli isolates recovered from urine samples of intensive care unit (ICU) patients at a tertiary-care hospital in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and to evaluate phenotype-genotype concordance at the individual antimicrobial level. A total of 36 non-duplicate uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) isolates recovered from urine samples of ICU patients between 2024 and 2025 underwent phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) and WGS using the DNBSEQ-G400 platform. Phenotypic non-susceptibility was highest to ampicillin (100%), followed by cefuroxime and cefotaxime (94.4% each). All isolates were susceptible to imipenem, meropenem, and tigecycline, while one isolate was intermediate to amikacin. Extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL) production was detected in 88.9% of isolates, and 94.4% exhibited a multidrug-resistant (MDR) phenotype. Genomic analysis identified 17 sequence types (STs), with ST131 and ST1193 being the most frequent lineages. blaCTX-M genes were detected in 80.6% of isolates, predominantly blaCTX-M-15, and resistance-associated chromosomal mutations in the quinolone resistance-determining regions (QRDRs) were identified in 83.3%. Based on resistance determinants representing three or more antimicrobial categories, 97.2% of isolates exhibited a genotypic MDR profile. Overall phenotype-genotype concordance across individual antimicrobial agents was 90.9%, with high concordance for cefuroxime and cefotaxime (97.2% each), followed by gentamicin and levofloxacin (94.4% each), and low concordance for cefepime and norfloxacin (72.2% each). These findings demonstrate a high burden of AMR among genetically diverse E. coli isolates from a tertiary-care hospital in Riyadh and show that the ability of WGS-derived resistance determinants to predict phenotypic antimicrobial non-susceptibility varies across individual antimicrobial agents.

title: Genetic, biochemical, and structural characterization of a novel KLUS subgroup of CTX-M-type extended-spectrum β-lactamases reveals an evolutionarily distinct lineage with unique functional properties.
authors: Huang Z; Li J; Liu X; Zeng L; Zheng Z; Yu H; Wang D; Yu K; Chen J
abstract: Extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs), particularly the CTX-M family, have progressively undermined the clinical utility of β-lactam antibiotics. Herein, we identified and characterized a novel CTX-M subgroup designated KLUS, and investigated its taxonomic position and functional properties. Phylogenetic analysis combined with genetic distance calculations supported KLUS as a distinct lineage, with inter-subgroup distances significantly exceeding intra-subgroup distances and distinct clustering (bootstrap support >95%), consistent with the previously established family-wide CTX-M classification. Recombinant plasmids harboring each of the four bla KLUS alleles were constructed in E. coli BL21 (DE3), with optimal expression achieved using 1.0 mM IPTG at 30 °C for 5 h. Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) determinations revealed that KLUS-1 through KLUS-3 conferred high-level resistance to ampicillin and ceftriaxone, moderate resistance to cefotaxime, and minimal resistance to ceftazidime (MIC < 0.125 μg/mL). KLUS-4 exhibited enhanced ceftazidime resistance (MIC = 8 μg/mL) and a reduced inhibitor response at the phenotypic level (a 16-fold reduction of the cefotaxime MIC with clavulanic acid, in contrast to KLUS-1, where clavulanic acid reduced the MIC to <0.015 μg/mL). β-lactamase inhibitors reduced cefotaxime MICs far exceeding 16-fold in KLUS-1 through KLUS-3, consistent with ESBL phenotypes. Steady-state kinetic analyses demonstrated subtype-dependent catalytic efficiencies that were highest for ampicillin and penicillin G in KLUS-2/3/4 and for ceftriaxone in KLUS-1, broadly consistent with MIC results. The substantially lower catalytic efficiency for ceftazidime may explain its reduced resistance phenotype. Structural modeling revealed that KLUS enzymes comprise 11 α-helices and 5 β-sheets, with a conserved catalytic cavity and SDN loop. Twenty-three unique amino acid substitutions distinguish KLUS from CTX-M-2. V77I (pre-protein positions 106) is located proximal to the Ω-loop region, and any functional contribution of this conservative substitution remains speculative. These findings expand the known diversity of CTX-M β-lactamases; the clinical significance of KLUS requires further investigation in clinical isolates.

title: Characteristics of Klebsiella spp. from sheep flocks in northern China.
authors: Wang HT; Yu HL; Guo L; Wang XY; Tang LY; Yang MT; Tan WX; Shang KM; Ni HB; Yao GZ; Li Y; Liu R
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Klebsiella spp. are Gram-negative opportunistic pathogens that affect both humans and animals. However, data on their antimicrobial resistance and virulence characteristics in sheep, particularly in China, remain limited.

METHODS: In 2024, 421 sheep fecal samples were collected from six regions in northern China. Klebsiella spp. were isolated and identified, followed by antimicrobial susceptibility testing and PCR screening for virulence-associated genes. The pathogenic potential of selected isolates was evaluated using the Galleria mellonella infection model. Whole-genome sequencing was performed on 26 selected isolates to characterize their antimicrobial resistance and virulence determinants.

RESULTS: Klebsiella spp. were isolated from 120 samples, corresponding to an overall detection rate of 28.5%, including 85 Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates (70.8%, 85/120). All isolates were resistant to sulfamethoxazole, with high resistance to tetracycline (76.7%), florfenicol (42.5%), and ciprofloxacin (41.7%). Resistance to tigecycline (10.0%) and polymyxin B (5.8%) was also observed at lower levels. Overall, 64.2% of the isolates exhibited multidrug resistance. PCR screening revealed virulence-associated genes, including iucA (10.8%), rmpA (8.3%), peg-344 (0.8%), and iroB (3.3%). Based on their virulence-associated gene profiles, 14 isolates were selected for further analysis, of which 11 exhibited high pathogenic potential in the Galleria mellonella infection model. Whole-genome sequencing revealed diverse virulence and antimicrobial resistance determinants. No plasmid-mediated resistance determinants related to polymyxin B (e.g., mcr-like genes) or recognized tigecycline resistance determinants were identified in the genomes. In the isolates analyzed in this study, mutations in lipid A modification and regulatory genes, including arnT and pmrA/pmrB, may have contributed to polymyxin B resistance, while mutations in efflux pump-associated genes, including oqxA/oqxB, acrA, and acrR, may have contributed to tigecycline resistance.

CONCLUSION: Multidrug resistance and pathogenic potential coexist among Klebsiella spp. isolated from healthy sheep in northern China. These findings suggest that sheep-associated Klebsiella may serve as reservoirs of clinically relevant antimicrobial resistance and virulence determinants, highlighting the need for continued surveillance and prudent antimicrobial use in livestock.

title: Capsimycin derivatives from Streptomyces sp. PH9007 as α‑glucosidase inhibitors and insights into their biosynthetic gene cluster.
authors: Wang Z; Wu G; Pan J; Sun R; Cao S; Jin X; Zhong Y; Chen Y; Cao L; Chen X; Feng B; Huang X; Pu H
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The increasing number of individuals with diabetes mellitus (DM) highlights the need to develop new diabetes medications. Polycyclic tetramate macrolactams (PTMs), characterized by a macrocyclic lactam containing an integrated tetramic acid ring, constitute an expanding group of extensively dispersed natural compounds with diverse biological functions.

RESULTS: In this study, two Streptomyces strains were isolated from the roots of the medicinal plant Sinomenium acutum. Using the Global Natural Products Social (GNPS) web platform, three PTMs, namely, capsimycin (4), capsimycin B (5), and capsimycin G (6), were extracted from Streptomyces sp. PH9007, which was isolated from Sinomenium acutum. Compounds 4 and 5 inhibited α-glucosidase, with 4 and 5 exhibiting IC50 values of 484.6 ± 14.10 μM and 366.9 ± 12.85 μM, respectively. Compound 5 also exhibited antibacterial and antifungal activities, with MICs of 16 µg/mL against MRSA, Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 29213 and Candida albicans CMCC 98001. The results of fluorescence quenching, UV-visible spectroscopy, molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations of 5 with α-glucosidase indicated that this compound binds better with α-glucosidase. Whole-genome sequencing of PH9007 revealed a 6, 339, 217 bp chromosome and two plasmids (83, 532 bp and 167, 087 bp) containing 25 biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs), including one exhibiting 56% sequence similarity to the ikarugamycin BGC. Furthermore, bioinformatics analysis revealed that the ikarugamycin BGC is widely distributed in microorganisms.

CONCLUSIONS: Overall, this study highlights that PTM-type compounds may serve as promising compounds for the further development of α-glucosidase inhibitors and lays the foundation for research on their biosynthesis.

title: Population structure of group B Streptococcus from semen reveals virulent and resistant lineages with implications for surveillance.
authors: Merces AC; Costa NS; Oliveira LMA; Botelho ACN; Barros LG; Silva LMB; Teixeira LM; Fracalanzza SEL; Khan U; Bentley S; Jamrozy D; Pinto TCA
abstract: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is a major agent of perinatal infections. Although extensively studied as a pathogen in pregnant individuals and neonates, little is known about GBS from male adults, despite occasional reports of its occurrence in semen. We characterized 120 GBS isolates obtained from semen samples in Brazil between 2017 and 2022 to determine serotypes, antimicrobial susceptibility profile, virulence-associated determinants, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) diversity and phylogenetic relationships with isolates from other clinical sources. Serotype V was the most frequent, followed by Ia, Ib, III, II and IV. Resistance was observed for tetracycline (84.1%), erythromycin (30.8%), levofloxacin (8.3%) and 12.5% exhibited multidrug resistance (MDR). The most common sequence types (STs) were ST1, ST144 and ST19. The isolates clustered into five major clonal complexes (CC1, CC17, CC19, CC23 and CC24) and six singletons. Serotypes, antimicrobial resistance and virulence-associated determinants markers varied across CCs. Resistance determinants detected included tetM, mefA, msrD, ermA and ermB. Levofloxacin-resistant isolates contained mutations in gyrA and/or parC and were predominantly linked to the serotype V/ST19 lineage. All isolates except one carried at least one alpha-like protein (Alp) gene. Phylogenetic analysis of isolates from semen, rectovaginal samples, urine and invasive infections showed that isolates clustered according to CC regardless of clinical source. CRISPR1 analysis revealed intra-clonal diversity, as isolates within the same CC displayed different CRISPR compositions. These findings indicate that GBS isolates recovered from semen belong to established GBS lineages also identified in other clinical sources and support the co-circulation of GBS lineages across different human niches.

title: Molecular epidemiology of MRSA and MSSA in Czech hospitals, 2023: complex genomic epidemiology of CC398 in humans and resurgence of penicillin susceptibility.
authors: Rozsypalkova A; Mrazkova P; Cepelikova J; Drozenova J; Amlerova J; Balejova M; Vitkova I; Fackova D; Neradova K; Sivakova A; Riedlova D; Fiserova K; Bartonikova N; Dvorakova L; Mednansky M; Tkadlec J; Drevinek P; Melter O; Tkadlec J
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Staphylococcus aureus causes a broad spectrum of infections, yet the clonal epidemiology of MSSA remains poorly characterized relative to MRSA. We conducted the first WGS-based national survey of both MRSA and MSSA in the Czech Republic to define contemporary population structure following the COVID-19 pandemic.

METHODS: Between September and December 2023, 450 clinical and carriage S. aureus isolates were prospectively collected from 14 major hospitals (175 MRSA; 275 MSSA); 248 clinical isolates underwent WGS, with resistance, virulence, mobile genetic elements, SCCmec type and clonal complex assignment determined alongside whole-genome MLST and maximum-likelihood phylogeny.

RESULTS: MRSA population was less diverse than MSSA (Simpson's Index of Diversity 0.871 versus 0.986). The historically dominant CC5/ST225-MRSA-II declined sharply, from 80%-90% to 59% of MRSA. CC398 emerged across both phenotypes as three genomically distinct, co-circulating subpopulations: penicillin-susceptible human-adapted MSSA, Panton-Valentine leukocidin (PVL)-positive CA-MRSA (ST1232) and livestock-associated MRSA. PVL-positive MRSA were identified across multiple lineages in 11 hospitals, reflecting a diverse CA-MRSA landscape without dominance of a single clone. Strikingly, nearly half of MSSA isolates (47.6%) were penicillin-susceptible, genotypically confirmed by blaZ absence. Penicillin susceptibility was not associated with reduced invasive potential and spanned multiple clonal backgrounds, most prominently CC398 and CC97.

CONCLUSIONS: This study reveals a significant shift in S. aureus epidemiology: decline of the dominant hospital MRSA clone, emergence of CC398 across the hospital-community-animal interface, and a resurgence of penicillin-susceptible MSSA that challenges the assumption of near-universal penicillin resistance and supports reconsidering penicillin for susceptible infections.

title: Antimicrobial resistance of Shigella spp. in South Australia and its detection using WGS.
authors: Torpy H; Mudhar AK; Leong LEX; Moore C; Hocking H; Rowe E; Papanicolas LE
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The use of WGS for antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) is limited by incomplete understanding of the correlation of genetic variants with phenotypic antimicrobial resistance (AMR).

OBJECTIVES: A 5 year retrospective review of Shigella isolates in South Australia was undertaken to compare the results of phenotypic AST with WGS-derived AMR to determine the ability of WGS to infer phenotypic resistance.

METHODS: Pure colonies from confirmed Shigella isolates were selected and DNA extracted using the automated QIASymphony platform. Isolates were sequenced using an Illumina NextSeq platform. The Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD) was used with the AMR screening tool 'ABRicate' to screen assemblies for the presence of intrinsic AMR genes. In addition, the AMRFinderPlus tool with NCBI's compiled database National Database of Antibiotic-Resistant Organisms (NDARO) was used to detect resistance-conferring point mutations, and to verify intrinsic AMR gene screening. The WGS and phenotypic AST results were compared.

RESULTS: There was 96% correlation between phenotypic and WGS-AST. The sensitivity of WGS-AST for prediction of AMR varied according to the antimicrobial: ceftriaxone (100%), azithromycin (100%), ciprofloxacin (100%), ampicillin (88.7%) and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (93.5%). WGS failed to detect resistance in 17 ampicillin-resistant isolates, constituting very major errors. False-positive results included the detection of AmpC blaCMY59 in four ceftriaxone-susceptible Shigella flexneri isolates and genotypic ciprofloxacin resistance in two phenotypically susceptible isolates: one carrying qnrS1 and one carrying four quinolone resistance-determining region point mutations.

CONCLUSIONS: The unexpectedly high rate of false-negative WGS-AST results for detection of ampicillin and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole resistance highlights the importance of local validation studies of WGS-AST for specific organism-antimicrobial combinations prior to its use in AMR surveillance.

title: Synergistic antibacterial effect and improved pharmacokinetics of florfenicol in combination with sulfamonomethoxine sodium.
authors: Ai X; Lan J; Li N; Chen Y; Chen L; Zhang W; Shu G; Lin J; Li H; Xu F; Fu H
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Florfenicol (FFC) and sulfamonomethoxine sodium (SMM-Na) are both broad-spectrum antibiotics for animals. FFC inhibits bacterial protein synthesis, whereas SMM-Na inhibits the bacterial folate pathway, suggesting a potential for synergy. However, the pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic interactions of their combination remain uncharacterized. This study evaluated the in vitro and in vivo interactions between FFC and SMM-Na.

METHODS: The in vitro interaction was assessed against several bacterial strains using the checkerboard method to determine the fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI). The physicochemical stability of the combination was tested. An in situ recirculating intestinal perfusion model in rats was used to assess absorption parameters. Pharmacokinetic studies in rats compared the combination therapy to monotherapies. The therapeutic efficacy was evaluated in a mouse model of Staphylococcus aureus pulmonary infection, with the combination administered at half the individual monotherapy doses.

RESULTS: The FFC/SMM-Na combination demonstrated synergistic effects (FICI = 0.375) in vitro and remained stable for 7 h. Intestinal perfusion showed the combination significantly increased the absorption rate constants (Ka) and effective permeability coefficients (Peff) for both drugs. Pharmacokinetic analysis revealed improved relative bioavailability for both FFC (113.98%) and SMM-Na (113.29%), with distinct pharmacokinetic profiles: FFC showed higher Cmax and shorter Tmax, while SMM-Na exhibited lower Cmax and longer Tmax. In the infection model, the half-dose combination achieved a significant reduction in bacterial load and ameliorated lung pathology.

CONCLUSION: The FFC/SMM-Na combination exhibits synergistic antibacterial activity in vitro, enhances mutual intestinal absorption, improves the pharmacokinetic profiles of both drugs, and achieves comparable in vivo efficacy at reduced doses through a dose-sparing effect. These findings provide a pharmacological basis for the clinical exploration of this combination therapy against bacterial infections.

title: Genetic diversity and resistance profiles of MRSA in community and healthcare settings.
authors: El-Antrawy MA; Shohayeb M; Elsawy LE; Ramadan HA
abstract: This study aimed to characterize and compare methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) strains isolated from community members and healthcare workers (HCWs) in Egypt using antibiotic susceptibility testing, mecA gene detection, SCCmec typing, and ERIC-PCR fingerprinting. A cross-sectional study was conducted between September 2024 and January 2025, during which 450 specimens were collected from Mansoura University Hospitals and the local community, where 71 specimens (30.8%) were confirmed as MRSA. MRSA prevalence was significantly higher among HCWs, 62.5% (50/80), than among community members, 14% (21/150). In general, antibiotic resistance rates were higher in HCW strains. All isolates were resistant to cefoxitin and sensitive to vancomycin.The methicillin-resistant phenotype of the 71 MRSA isolates was confirmed by positive mecA gene tests, with SCCmec Type III prevalent among healthcare workers and SCCmec Type IV predominating in the community. ERIC-PCR fingerprinting demonstrated the isolates' genetic diversity. The dendrogram based on ERIC patterns showed distinct clusters between community and hospital strains, though with some overlap, suggesting possible transmission between the two populations.In conclusion, MRSA strains from HCWs displayed broader antibiotic resistance and greater clonal similarity, while community strains were more diverse and less resistant. The presence of intermixed clusters between community-acquired (CA-MRSA) and (HCW-MRSA) suggested a possible bidirectional transmission pathway, underscoring the blurring of epidemiological boundaries.These results underline the necessity of ongoing molecular surveillance and integrated infection control strategies to track the spread of MRSA in community and clinical settings.

title: Microscale spatial fragmentation promotes bacterial survival under antibiotics.
authors: Benbenisti D; Orevi T; Hamrick GS; You L; Kashtan N
abstract: Most bacteria inhabit fragmented microscale environments rather than well-mixed systems in which antibiotic efficacy is typically defined. Here, we show that microscale spatial fragmentation alone can deterministically promote bacterial survival under antibiotic exposure. A coarse-grained theoretical model predicts that, at fixed bulk cell density and antibiotic concentration, fragmentation generates refuges through two coupled mechanisms: slower growth, which reduces susceptibility to growth-dependent antibiotics, and a finite antibiotic-per-cell constraint that lowers the effective intracellular antibiotic concentration. Using a microdroplet platform spanning five orders of magnitude in volume, we experimentally confirm these predictions for β-lactams; we further demonstrate that the same fragmentation-mediated protection extends to antibiotics with distinct modes of action. Spatial fragmentation thus creates robust, non-genetic antibiotic refuges governed by physical constraints rather than resistance or collective protection, with implications for bacterial persistence in natural and clinical environments and for antibiotic design.

title: Comparison of MALDI-TOF MS and VITEK 2 performance in the identification of brucella strains isolated from blood culture bottles; retrospective evaluation of antibiotic resistance profiles, clinical manifestations, and serological follow-up.
authors: Melez ME; Sağıroğlu P; Altop SÖ; Atalay MA; Yıldız O
abstract:
INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Brucella species cause severe zoonotic infections with an exceptionally high risk of laboratory-acquired transmission. We systematically evaluated and compared the identification performances of two contemporary MALDI-TOF MS platforms and the VITEK 2 automated system, analyzed serial standard tube agglutination (STA) titer kinetics, and determined in vitro antimicrobial susceptibility profiles of clinical blood culture isolates.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: Twenty-five culture-confirmed Brucella isolates recovered from peripheral blood culture bottles between 2019 and 2025 were evaluated using the MALDI Biotyper Sirius (routine MBT Compass library), VITEK MS Prime (IVD database v3.3), and VITEK 2 GN automated identification cards. All sample manipulation and ethanol/formic acid extraction were performed inside a certified Class II Biosafety Cabinet ensuring complete inactivation prior to mass spectrometry. Antimicrobial susceptibility was determined by the disk diffusion method on Mueller-Hinton Fastidious (MH-F) agar according to EUCAST (v. 16.0) guidelines. Clinical data and serial STA titers were retrospectively analyzed.

RESULTS: The MALDI Biotyper Sirius accurately identified all 25 isolates (100%) at the species level as Brucella melitensis, whereas the VITEK MS Prime identified all (100%) at the genus level (Brucella spp.). In contrast, the VITEK 2 GN automated system demonstrated markedly poor diagnostic utility, correctly identifying 92% (23/25) of isolates, failing to identify one isolate ('unidentified'), and misidentifying another blood culture isolate as Roseomonas gilardii. A statistically significant decrease in Wright tube agglutination titers was observed following treatment (median initial titer 1:320 [IQR, 1:160-1:640] vs. median final titer 1:80 [IQR, 1:40-1:160]; p = 0.007). Serological reductions did not differ significantly across therapeutic regimens (p = 0.3219). All isolates (100%) were fully susceptible to rifampin, doxycycline and gentamicin. Resistance rates to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (SXT) and ciprofloxacin were 40% (10/25) and 24% (6/25), respectively. Favorable clinical cure without relapse was achieved in patients receiving SXT-containing regimens despite in vitro resistance.

CONCLUSIONS: The MALDI Biotyper Sirius provides superior diagnostic speed and biosafety via reliable species-level identification using routine spectral libraries. Automated phenotypic misidentifications (e.g., R. gilardii) represent critical biohazards that warrant urgent MALDI-TOF MS verification. High in vitro resistance to SXT highlights potential disk diffusion overestimation in fastidious organisms, emphasizing the necessity of broth microdilution MIC confirmation before precluding vital oral treatment options.

title: Bacillus licheniformis as a therapeutic alternative for Klebsiella pneumoniae infection.
authors: Wang Y; Liu Y; Abbas S; Yang H; Chen W; Gao Q; Peng B; Wan H; Ling S; He H
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a significant zoonotic pathogen. In recent years, the frequent emergence of hypervirulent (hvKP) and multidrug-resistant (MDR) strains has posed serious threats to both human and animal health, becoming a major concern for global public health security. This study characterized the phenotype of a K. pneumoniae strain (KP-01) isolated from a red panda and investigated the protective effects of Bacillus licheniformis against this pathogen through animal experiments, aiming to explore alternative therapeutic approaches for K. pneumoniae infections.

RESULTS: KP-01 was identified as a hypervirulent K. pneumoniae (hvKP) strain, which was susceptible to most clinically relevant antibiotics except for intermediate susceptibility to imipenem and kanamycin. Despite lacking hypermucoviscosity, carried hallmark hvKP virulence genes (iroB, rmpA2, peg-344, and iucA). Pre-treatment with B. licheniformis significantly reduced bacterial burden in infected tissues, suppressed inflammatory cytokine expression, and ameliorated histopathological damage.

CONCLUSION: B. licheniformis exhibits significant protective effects against K. pneumoniae infection and may serve as a potential antibiotic-alternative therapy.

title: Metagenomics analysis reveals horse feces as a reservoir of putative ARG-like sequences.
authors: Jia Y; Yuan P; Zhang Y; Meng S; Li M; Liu W; Nanaei HA; Liu X; Jiang L
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Despite the widespread distribution of horses and their close interface with human environments, the equine antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) reservoir remains insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to comprehensively elucidate the equine resistome by analyzing 104 equine fecal metagenomes sampled across China, thereby establishing a critical baseline for antimicrobial stewardship in equine husbandry.

RESULTS: Through a non-redundant gene catalog approach, we identified 3,264 unique ARG-related coding sequences (CDSs). To detect distant homologs, hidden Markov model (HMM) profiling was applied, revealing 2,420 putatively novel ARG-like sequences. Functional classification indicated that over 90% of these sequences mediate resistance through antibiotic inactivation or target protection, whereas efflux and impaired penetration accounted for less than 10%. Taxonomic profiling attributed these predicted sequences to 23 phyla and 146 genera, with Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, and Proteobacteria identified as the detected taxa. Furthermore, we identified 731 plasmid-associated ARG-like candidates, of which 446 is novel variants, predominantly conferring resistance to macrolides, streptogramins, aminoglycosides, and β-lactams. Experimental validation confirmed that the novel gene abc-f(9) significantly reduced macrolide susceptibility in vitro, elevating the tilmicosin minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of Escherichia coli from 64 to 256 μg/mL.

CONCLUSIONS: These findings provide the first systematic characterization of the equine ARG repertoire, significantly expanding the known global resistome. Our results offer a foundational resource for assessing the risks of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) transmission and implementing informed surveillance strategies in horse farming.

title: Whole-genome sequencing reveals inter-household networks of gut-colonising ESBL-producing Escherichia coli in two rural Malawian districts.
authors: O'Ferrall AM; Lally D; Makaula P; Namacha G; Lewis JM; Musicha P; Goodman RN; Allman E; Moyo SJ; Waddington CS; Kayuni SA; Feasey NA; Musaya J; Stothard JR; Roberts AP
abstract: Infection with extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing Escherichia coli (ESBL-Ec) is a global health concern that disproportionately affects sub-Saharan Africa. Gut mucosal colonisation is thought to precede invasive infection. Understanding ESBL-Ec colonisation and transmission across communities is therefore essential. Here, we investigate the genomic epidemiology and spatial structure of 159 gut-colonising ESBL-Ec isolates from the faeces of 211 people in two rural Malawian villages using longitudinal sampling (2023-24), whole-genome sequencing and household mapping. Colonisation prevalence rose from 34.1% (95% CI: 27.8-41.0) to 54.2% (95% CI: 46.0-62.3) over one year. Isolates belonged to 33 sequence types (STs), most commonly ST38 and ST131, harbouring 46 distinct antimicrobial resistance gene types. Fifteen strains were identified in ≥3 households that were typically separated by short geographic distances ( < 400 m). Of 190 pairwise comparisons between same-strain isolates from different households sampled concurrently within villages, 88.9% differed by ≤10 single nucleotide polymorphisms, consistent with multi-household involvement in community transmission networks. Lineage-specific ST38 and ST131 network analyses linked rural isolates to urban Malawian isolates collected within the last decade. Our findings provide a transferable framework for inferring ESBL-Ec flow in community settings and highlight the need for One Health surveillance and improved sanitation infrastructure to limit transmission.

title: Changes in pregabalin use and overdose after government interventions and media coverage: retrospective observational study.
authors: Cairns R; Noghrehchi F; Pearson SA; Schaffer AL; Brett J; Buckley NA
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate trends in pregabalin use and overdose in Australia and examine temporal relationships with media coverage (December 2018), prescribing and dispensing restrictions (April 2020), and boxed warnings (February 2021).

DESIGN: Retrospective observational study of dispensing and overdose data, with changepoint, interrupted time series, and latent class analysis.

SETTING AND PARTICIPANTS: Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme data (PBS; 10% random sample of people with drug subsidies) and overdose calls (self-harm, recreational use, and misuse) reported to Australia's largest Poisons Centre (50% national sample), 2016-24.

MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Population adjusted rates of dispensing and overdose, timing of breakpoints and rate ratios, proportion of people who use pregabalin at high risk of misuse.

RESULTS: 227 864 people were dispensed 3 441 851 pregabalin prescriptions in the PBS 10% sample and 4871 pregabalin overdose calls were made to the Poisons Centre. Pregabalin use peaked in 2018 before plateauing and declining. Three breakpoints were found in dispensing data, with major decreases in level and slope: December 2018, May 2020, December 2021. The combined rate ratio for dispensing was 0.748 (95% confidence interval 0.700 to 0.800). Compared with the projected historical trend in the absence of interventions (counterfactual), approximately 118 390 (93 960 to 140 940) fewer pregabalin prescriptions were recorded nationally in December 2021, and an ongoing reduction of 0.7% (0.5% to 0.9%) was found each month. All breakpoints were associated with declines in overdose rates, with a combined rate ratio of 0.532 (95% CI 0.406 to 0.695). This reduction corresponded to approximately 41.3 (26.9 to 52.4) fewer pregabalin overdose calls in December 2021 and an ongoing reduction of 1.6% (1.0% to 2.3%) each month. Latent class analysis of 57 744 people dispensed pregabalin in the 12 months after the final breakpoint revealed four groups. The high risk group (7790, 13.5%) were more likely male, younger, dispensed more pregabalin, with shorter refill interval and high rates of opioids and benzodiazepine co-use (5120 (65.7%) and 2455 (31.5%), respectively).

CONCLUSIONS: Pregabalin use and overdose in Australia have declined in recent years. Major decreases in trend corresponded with media coverage (December 2018) and prescribing and dispensing restrictions (May 2020). The third breakpoint may be a delayed impact of boxed warnings (implemented February 2021). These findings suggest that regulatory and risk communication measures may contribute to reducing pregabalin related harm.

title: Analytical performance and workflow impact of the FASTinov QUICKprep kit for direct bacterial identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing from positive blood cultures.
authors: Tittel-Elmer M; Renzi G; Schrenzel J
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Rapid pathogen identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) from positive blood cultures are essential for the timely optimization of antimicrobial therapy in patients with bloodstream infections. The FASTinov QUICKprep kit enables recovery of viable microorganisms directly from positive blood cultures, allowing both identification and AST without prior subculture. We evaluated the analytical performance and workflow impact of the FASTinov QUICKprep kit using 112 positive blood cultures processed in a routine clinical microbiology laboratory. Direct identification was performed by matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time of flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS), and AST was performed using the automated RADIAN system. Results were compared with those obtained using the laboratory's standard subculture-based workflow. Identification accuracy, categorical agreement for AST, reporting times, and turnaround times (TATs) were assessed. Overall, the sensitivity and specificity of direct bacterial identification were 93.4% and 100%, respectively. The QUICKprep workflow enabled same-day identification for all evaluable samples and reduced the median TAT from 7.75 h to 3.0 h. Direct AST performed from QUICKprep-derived pellets demonstrated high categorical agreement with the reference method across 86 isolates. Most discordant AST results involved heteroresistant gram-negative subpopulations and were adjudicated in favor of the QUICKprep results by Etest. Importantly, AST results were consistently available within 24 h irrespective of sample arrival time, whereas the conventional workflow showed substantial delays for cultures received later in the day. In conclusion, the FASTinov QUICKprep kit provides reliable direct identification and AST from positive blood cultures while substantially reducing turnaround times. Integration of this approach into routine clinical microbiology workflows may facilitate earlier optimization of antimicrobial therapy and support antimicrobial stewardship efforts.

IMPORTANCE: Bloodstream infections remain a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Thus, efficient pathogen identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing are critical to optimizing targeted therapy and antimicrobial stewardship. Despite advances in laboratory automation, routine procedures for positive blood cultures remain dependent on secondary subculture growth. Our study proposes relevant and practical benefits regarding the integration of a subculture-independent workflow for bloodstream infection diagnosis and its potential contribution to improving clinical outcomes.

title: Decoding the cefazolin inoculum effect: phenotypic and genotypic insights beyond the MIC.
authors: Srivastava P; Valentine J; Ma C; Jackam G; Baldridge LI; Berti AD; Wozniak DJ; Leininger J; Ventresca RL; Akter F; Morrisette T; Li J; Kebriaei R
abstract: The cefazolin inoculum effect (CzIE) is a clinically relevant in vitro phenomenon that may compromise cefazolin efficacy in high-inoculum methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) infections such as bacteremia and infective endocarditis. We aimed to define mechanisms underlying CzIE beyond BlaZ-dependent enzymatic pathways. We evaluated CzIE in 198 MSSA isolates (single center) by comparing minimum inhibitory concentrations at standard and high inoculum. The inoculum effect index was used as a quantitative measure of the CzIE to validate the operational definition and assess its concordance with the classical definition of CzIE. Whole-genome sequencing was used to define β-lactamase gene (blaZ) allotypes, accessory gene regulator (agr) genotypes (I-IV), and clonal lineages. CzIE was observed in 16.16% of isolates, with Type A (71.9%) and Type C (28.1%) blaZ allotypes predominating among CzIE-positive strains. These isolates were enriched within clonal complex CC8 and CC30. Twenty-four-hour time-kill experiments combining cefazolin with BlaZ inhibitor (sulbactam) demonstrated initial killing followed by regrowth in CzIE-positive isolates, while complete eradication was observed in CzIE-negative isolates. Population analysis profiles (PAP) revealed the expansion of cefazolin-non-susceptible subpopulations at high inoculum, consistent with phenotypic heterogeneity. agr typing identified agrIII as the predominant genotype among CzIE-positive isolates, and agr dysfunction was significantly associated with CzIE-positive phenotype. Together, these findings suggest that CzIE is driven not only by BlaZ-mediated activity but also by agr-dependent regulatory pathways. These observations highlight the potential clinical importance of CzIE and support further investigation into its implications for therapeutic optimization and improved patient outcomes.IMPORTANCECefazolin inoculum effect (CzIE) represents an underrecognized potential determinant of therapeutic failure in methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) infections, yet it remains absent from routine susceptibility testing frameworks. We demonstrate that CzIE is not solely driven by blaZ-mediated activity but is strongly associated with agr-dependent regulation and population heterogeneity. Our findings suggest that standard MIC testing can underestimate cefazolin failure under high-inoculum conditions commonly encountered in invasive diseases. Importantly, identification of CzIE-positive isolates could inform therapeutic decision-making, including selection of alternative β-lactams or adjunctive strategies to suppress tolerant subpopulations. Integration of CzIE assessment with genomic markers such as blaZ allotype and agr genotype may enable more precise prediction of treatment response. These data provide a framework for incorporating CzIE into diagnostic workflows and guide future studies evaluating its clinical utility. Ultimately, recognizing CzIE as a multifactorial phenotype may improve antibiotic selection, reduce treatment failure, and enhance outcomes in serious MSSA infections across patient populations.

title: One Health, no silos: integrating veterinary, human, and environmental stewardship strategies to close the AMR diagnostic gap in the United States.
authors: Tibbetts R; Maddock KJ; Cole SD; Gefroh SJ; Meier BM; Suchanek AL
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a growing global crisis that threatens the health of humans, animals, and the environment. It has been projected that if not urgently and judiciously addressed, there could be up to 10 million deaths each year by 2050 caused by AMR infections. AMR is not a static or easily eradicated issue tied to a singular source; it emerges from intersecting pressures across human, animal, and environmental health and is exacerbated by the misuse and potential excessive use of antimicrobials. This review highlights the importance of an integrated, One-Health approach in tackling AMR, underscoring the need for a coordinated antimicrobial stewardship process that centers on optimal diagnostic approaches spanning all sectors. Significant gaps in diagnostics persist between human and veterinary medicine, especially with regard to diagnostic capacity, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and standardized reporting. In environmental settings, additional challenges include suboptimal effluent and waste management, continued reliance on antimicrobials for non-therapeutic purposes, and inconsistent soil and water management practices. Taken together, these issues hinder the ability to manage AMR, while the siloed nature of these three primary sectors complicates data integration and ultimately weakens global surveillance and mitigation efforts. To improve One Health antimicrobial stewardship strategies, we must strengthen diagnostic capacity, harmonize antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) methods across human and veterinary health, and integrate surveillance systems to include environmental sources worldwide. Further development and investment in rapid diagnostics, standardized protocols, and collaborative data-sharing frameworks is crucial in addressing local and global AMR to ensure the effectiveness of antimicrobials for future generations.

title: Genomic epidemiology and pathogenic potential of Elizabethkingia meningoseptica: a comparative genomic analysis with experimental characterization of a clinical isolate.
authors: Wang Z; Xu S; Zhao X; Yang Y; Li B; Li R; Chen Z; Shi W; Zhang P
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To characterize the population structure, antimicrobial resistance landscape, and virulence potential of Elizabethkingia meningoseptica based on publicly available genomes and a clinical isolate E0725.

METHODS: We analyzed 96 public genomes together with E0725 for core-genome single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), average nucleotide identity (ANI), antimicrobial resistance genes, and virulence genes. E0725 was further evaluated by antimicrobial susceptibility testing, biofilm formation, Galleria mellonella infection, serum resistance, bile salt tolerance, and oxidative-stress assays.

RESULTS: The 97 strains belonged to multiple genetic lineages with weak geographic clustering and few near-clonal clusters. BlaB-, GOB-, CME-, and RASA-like β-lactamases and conserved core virulence genes were widely present, whereas variation mainly involved accessory resistance genes and cell-surface structure genes. E0725 was multidrug-resistant and showed strong biofilm formation, serum resistance, bile salt tolerance, and lethality in G. mellonella, but was sensitive to hydrogen peroxide.

CONCLUSION: E. meningoseptica is genetically diverse, with a conserved intrinsic resistance backbone and variable accessory genomic features. The clinical isolate E0725 exhibited strain-specific phenotypic traits associated with biofilm formation, serum tolerance, and host-associated adaptation. Accurate identification, isolate-specific susceptibility testing, genomic surveillance, and management of hospital water systems should be prioritized for infection control.

CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

title: Co-dissemination of anti-phage defence systems and multidrug resistance is associated with the seventh-pandemic Vibrio cholerae defensome.
authors: Hoque MM; To J; Leo D; McDougald D; Matson JS; Espinoza-Vergara G
abstract: Anti-phage defence systems in Vibrio cholerae are recognized as cargo on mobile genetic elements carrying antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and virulence genes, but a population-scale view of how the V. cholerae defensome partitions between the pandemic O1 clade and the environmental non-O1 reservoir has been missing. We analysed 1,740 RefSeq V. cholerae genomes (773 O1, 967 non-O1) sampled from 1934 to 2022 across 60 countries. Cataloguing defence systems with DefenseFinder, we found that the non-O1 reservoir harboured 283 subtypes and 55 families absent from any O1. This asymmetry persisted after collapsing each core-genome lineage to a single representative, although it partly reflected the greater diversity of non-O1. O1 favoured abortive infection systems (36.8% vs 14.1% in non-O1; P<0.001). Defence and prophage burden were inversely related within O1 (R=-0.15) but weakly positive in non-O1, and a five-decade reconstruction revealed mirror trajectories of rising defence diversity and declining prophage burden in O1, coincident with SXT/R391 integrative conjugative element-borne AMR. A bipartite network identified strong defence-AMR associations (Phi up to 0.80), nominating AbiE, AbiJ, AvcID, Menshen, Retron-I_A and Lamassu-Fam as candidate co-acquired cargo; though much of this is clonal, the strongest associations falling to 0.51 to 0.68 after de-duplication. Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection clustering resolved seven defensome lineages, and a Random Forest classifier trained on defence profile predicted multidrug resistance status with cross-validated area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.96, generalizing across O1 (0.92), non-O1 (0.93), decades (0.88) and regions (AUC=0.92); a five-system signature (AbiE, BREX-I, CBASS-II, AvcID and AbiJ) achieved AUC=0.91. Together, these data show that the pandemic defensome has expanded in step with the AMR-bearing mobilome rather than with prophage burden, with defence and resistance genes co-inherited on seventh pandemic El Tor elements. Their association reflects shared lineage history rather than a causal or mechanistic link, and the defensome serves as a descriptive genomic correlate of multidrug resistance.

title: Genomic characterization of IncC plasmid-mediated triple carbapenemase-producing Providencia hangzhouensis ST222.
authors: Ikhimiukor OO; Prussing C; Cummings K; Marcinkiewicz AL; Kennedy SY; Cebelius J; Nazarian EJ; Musser KA
abstract: Providencia hangzhouensis is a recently described species within the Providencia genus that is most closely related to Providencia rettgeri and is infrequently isolated from human infections. Its clinical relevance and epidemiology remain poorly understood. Here, we describe two P. hangzhouensis isolates recovered from urine specimens from two epidemiologically linked adult patients. Carbapenemase production in both isolates was determined using the modified carbapenem inactivation method. The presence of carbapenem resistance genes, bla NDM-1, bla KPC-2 and bla VIM-24, was identified by multiplex real-time PCR and whole-genome sequencing. Both isolates belong to the novel ST222 and carry all three carbapenem resistance genes on an IncC plasmid. Genetic environment analysis revealed complex integration of mobile genetic elements; notably, bla NDM-1 was localized within the variable region of an insertion sequence common region 1 element, bla KPC-2 was located within a putative Tn3-like transposon and bla VIM-24 was identified as a gene cassette within a second class 1 integron. Epidemiological data uncovered evidence of horizontal transfer of the IncC plasmid involving a Citrobacter freundii ST185 isolate. The convergence of multiple antimicrobial resistance genes, including those conferring resistance to last-line antimicrobials, underscores the potential threat posed by this emerging drug-resistant pathogen.

title: In vitro activity of manogepix against Candida spp. displaying elevated echinocandin MIC results.
authors: Winkler ML; Kimbrough JH; Edeker S; Klauer A; Karr MH; Rhomberg P; Castanheira M
abstract: Fosmanogepix is the prodrug of manogepix, an antifungal agent with a novel mechanism of action targeting the cell wall anchoring protein Gwt1. Fosmanogepix is currently in a Phase 3 clinical trial for the treatment of candidemia and invasive candidiasis (CIC). Echinocandins are first-line recommendations for empiric treatment of CIC, but resistance rates are rising, particularly in Candida glabrata. Given its unique mechanism of action, manogepix might retain activity against Candida spp. isolates that are non-susceptible to echinocandins, although supporting data are limited. Here, we collected 129 Candida spp. isolates from worldwide surveillance testing between 2017 and 2024 that were either resistant or non-wild type (WT) to ≥1 echinocandin when applying the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute breakpoints or epidemiological cutoff values. Isolates included 74 C. glabrata, 19 C. albicans, 14 C. auris, 14 C. tropicalis, 3 C. dubliniensis, 2 C. guilliermondii, and 1 each of C. krusei, C. lusitaniae, and C. parapsilosis. Sequencing of the gene encoding the echinocandin target was performed in all isolates and 75/129 (58.1%) had ≥1 alteration in a hotspot region of FKS1 and/or FKS2. Manogepix maintained low minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) across all isolates with only one C. auris isolate with a MIC above the prior WT-upper limit-defined value of 0.03 mg/L. This isolate had an alteration in Tac1B but wild-type Gwt1. All isolates were WT for amphotericin B and fluconazole resistance varied depending on species from 0% to 100%. The continued clinical development of manogepix for the treatment of CIC is warranted, including against resistant isolates based on these data.

title: Let sleeping dogs lie? Domestic carnivores as potential sentinels for One Health surveillance of antimicrobial resistance: the example of Réunion Island.
authors: Rabaly C; Wilkinson DA; Miltgen G; Belmonte O; Etheves A; Maurines-Carboneill C; Sellier A; Doizy A; Rieux A; Garrigos T; Squarzoni C; Albrechtova K
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase- and carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (ESBL-E and CP-E, respectively) are global public health threats, prioritized by the WHO for urgent action. We assessed prevalence, risk factors and genomic context of ESBL-E and CP-E carriage in domestic carnivores on Réunion Island and compared resistant isolates with human isolates to evaluate pets' role in islandwide antimicrobial resistance transmission.

METHODS: Combining the methods of classical microbiology (selective culture, MS identification, disc-diffusion antimicrobial susceptibility testing) and WGS (using in-house Nanopore technology), we compared 55 ESBL-E isolates originating from 881 domestic carnivores obtained in an island-wide cross-sectional survey with 40 human isolates obtained through an existing ESBL surveillance network and from healthy volunteers. We evaluated the risk factors for ESBL-E carriage in domestic carnivores by fitting multivariate generalized linear models applied to data from anamnestic questionnaires.

RESULTS: The prevalence of ESBL-E/CP-E carriage was 6% in carnivores (dogs: 8%; cats: 3%). The dominant ESBL gene across hosts (dogs, cats, humans) was blaCTX-M-15, followed by blaCTX-M-27. Three carbapenem-resistant isolates were detected in dogs, including the blaNDM-1 gene. Risk factors for animal ESBL-E/CP-E colonization included intact reproductive status, recent antibiotic therapy and free-roaming behaviour. Animal-originating ESBL-producing Escherichia coli exhibited greater genetic diversity than human-origin isolates, suggesting multiple introduction sources and environmental influences.

CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that domestic carnivores should be routinely included in surveillance networks, as their lifestyle and close contact with humans may allow trends in their enteric antimicrobial-resistant flora to foreshadow trends in the human resistome.

title: Real-world outcomes of Citrobacter freundii, Klebsiella aerogenes, and Enterobacter cloacae bacteremia treatment (ROCKET): a contemporary analysis of treatment strategies.
authors: Jawanda J; Shields RK; Balasubramani GK; Clarke L; Creager H; Falcione BA; Marini R; O'Donnell M; Peng L; Shah S
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To determine comparative effectiveness of piperacillin/tazobactam and cefepime for the treatment of bacteremia due to Enterobacterales at moderate risk for clinically significant AmpC production.

METHODS: A retrospective multicentre study was conducted among adults with bacteremia due to Enterobacter cloacae complex, Klebsiella aerogenes, or Citrobacter freundii complex from 2017 to 2025. Treatment-emergent resistance was defined as a ≥4-fold MIC increase or a categorical change in susceptibility within 90 days.

RESULTS: Seven hundred twenty-eight patients met inclusion criteria. The median (IQR) age was 67 years (55-74), and 35% (252/728) were immunocompromised. Cefepime was used for definitive therapy in 47% (342/728), followed by piperacillin/tazobactam in 18% (129/728) and carbapenems in 16% (115/728). Overall, 30-day mortality was 12% (88/728). Patients receiving piperacillin/tazobactam had a higher median (IQR) Pitt bacteremia score (2 [1-3] versus 1 [0-3], P=0.017) than those receiving cefepime, but rates of 30-day mortality (14% [18/129] versus 11% [37/342], P = 0.345) and relapsed infection between days 5-14 (3% [4/129] versus 2% [5/342], P = 0.266) were similar. After inverse probability of treatment weighting, 30-day mortality rates between patients treated with piperacillin/tazobactam and cefepime were not significantly different (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.57-1.92). Treatment-emergent resistance to definitive therapy occurred in 1% (5/342), 2% (3/129), and 3% (4/115) of patients treated with cefepime, piperacillin/tazobactam, and carbapenems, respectively.

CONCLUSIONS: In the largest study to date of bacteremia due to E. cloacae complex, K. aerogenes, or C. freundii complex, treatment-emergent resistance was uncommon, and outcomes did not differ significantly between patients treated with piperacillin/tazobactam and cefepime.

title: Real-world experience with cefepime/zidebactam under compassionate use.
authors: Dubey DK; Swaminathan S; Tirlangi PK; Polati VR; Soman R; Sirsat R; Ghafur A; Gaikwad R; Nagvekar V; Manesh AS; Mohammed I; Limaye HS; Shah PH; Mittal A; Patil PY; Gupta N; Agrawal U; Soneja M; Sridharan S; Madan S; Mitra SK; Sahu M; Sunavala AJ; Toraskar KK; Singhal T; Tayade AR; Gupta N; Sebastian AP; Rahulan V; Narreddy S; Ulloa ER; Miller WR; Krishna V; Savla HS; Sarda RN; Bansal N; Inamdar SB; Kadnur HB; Shetty S; Deswal V; Adderson EE; Aitken SL; van Duin D; William T; Shorr A; Veeraraghavan B; Lodise TP
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Cefepime/zidebactam is a β-lactam/β-lactam enhancer combination with activity against carbapenem-resistant (CR) Gram-negative pathogens, including metallo-β-lactamase (MBL)-producing organisms. Before regulatory approval, cefepime/zidebactam was available through a compassionate-use programme for patients with CR Gram-negative infections who had limited available treatment options.

METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, multi-country analysis of patients who received cefepime/zidebactam through compassionate use between 2022 and 2025. Data included demographics, comorbidities, acute complications, prior antibiotic exposure, infection characteristics, microbiology, treatment details, and investigator-assessed outcomes.

RESULTS: Eighty-five patients were included (median age 48 years; 57.6% in an intensive care unit at initiation). Primary infections included pneumonia/respiratory infection (30.6%), bone and joint infection (24.7%), and complicated urinary tract infection/pyelonephritis (14.1%). Pseudomonas aeruginosa was the predominant pathogen (77.6%), followed by Klebsiella pneumoniae (14.1%) and Acinetobacter baumannii (11.8%); infections involving at least two Gram-negative pathogens occurred in 10.6%. Among isolates with available genotypic data, MBLs were common and predominantly NDM. The cefepime/zidebactam minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC)50 and MIC90 were 8 and 32 mg/L, respectively. Investigator-assessed clinical success at the end of therapy was achieved in 88.2% of patients (95% CI, 79.7-93.5), and microbiological eradication in 89.4% (95% CI, 81.1-94.3); on-therapy mortality was 10.6% (95% CI, 5.7-18.9). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in five patients (5.9%, 95% CI, 2.5-13.0), with one discontinuation.

CONCLUSIONS: In this uncontrolled compassionate-use case series, cefepime/zidebactam treatment was accompanied by high investigator-assessed clinical success and microbiological eradication in patients with severe infections caused by CR Gram-negative pathogens. These observations require confirmation in prospective controlled studies.

title: Global genomic surveillance and temporal trends of carbapenemase-encoding β-lactamase genes in Klebsiella pneumoniae using NCBI pathogen detection data.
authors: Ofori SA
abstract: The global spread of carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae is weakening the effectiveness of last-resort antibiotics and making severe infections increasingly difficult to treat. This study examined the geographical distribution, temporal patterns and co-occurrence of carbapenemase genes among K. pneumoniae genome assemblies deposited in the National Center for Biotechnology Information Pathogen Detection database. Genome metadata and antimicrobial resistance genotype information were retrieved between January and February 2026. After data cleaning, 67,057 unique genome assemblies from 123 countries contributed 77,975 carbapenemase-gene detections. Gene frequencies were summarised by continent, country, year and sample source. Poisson and negative binomial regression models were used to examine temporal patterns from 2013 to 2025. Genome-level co-occurrence was assessed using phi correlation coefficients, Jaccard similarity, odds ratios and Fisher's exact tests. blaKPC was the most frequently detected gene, with 39,832 detections (51.08%), followed by blaNDM with 24,412 (31.31%). blaNDM was the dominant gene in Africa, accounting for 1,101 detections (52.68%), whereas blaKPC was dominant in the Americas, Asia, Europe and Oceania, accounting for 59.29%, 56.50%, 38.37% and 38.77% of detections, respectively. Urine and blood were the main sample sources, representing approximately 30% and 22% of the analysed genomes, respectively. Yearly trend analysis showed increases in blaNDM, blaOXA-232 and blaOXA-181. The strongest negative association was found between blaKPC and blaNDM (φ = -0.69), although genomes carrying either gene frequently contained additional antimicrobial resistance genes. These findings demonstrate clear geographical and temporal differences in carbapenemase genes among genome assemblies deposited in NCBI pathogen detection. However, differences in sequencing capacity and database submissions across countries and years should be considered when interpreting the findings. Continued genomic surveillance, antimicrobial stewardship and stronger infection prevention and control measures are needed, particularly in underrepresented regions.

title: Phenotypic and genomic characteristics of Salmonella isolates from 99,780 wet market workers in Shanghai.
authors: Yang Z; Zhou Y; Yang S; Pei Y; Liu Y; Zhao C; Wang J; Chen J; Wang W; Chen M; Xu X; Wang Y
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Salmonella enterica (S. enterica) poses an increasing public health threat. To better understand and assess the prevalence and AMR patterns of Salmonella carried by asymptomatic individuals, whole-genome sequencing and phenotypic analysis were used to investigate the epidemiology and AMR patterns within Salmonella isolates from 99,780 wet market workers in Shanghai, China. A total of 116 Salmonella isolates (0.12%) were isolated from 99,780 wet market workers in 2023 across six districts in Shanghai, China. The predominant serovars were S. I 1,4,[5],12:i:- and S. London. Antimicrobial phenotypic tests showed that 17.24% and 11.21% of these isolates were resistant to third-generation cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones, respectively, with marked serovar disparity. The prevalence of qnrS1, blaCTX-M-55, mph(A), and fosA7 was 31.03%, 5.17%, 12.93%, and 12.07% of these isolates, respectively. Phylogenetic analysis indicated that S. I 1,4,[5],12:i:- ST34 strains diversified into five distinct clades, each harboring a unique resistance gene array. Two isolates carried the tigecycline resistance gene tet(X4) that were highly homologous to plasmids from both human and porcine Salmonella in China, with tet(X4) flanked by ISCR2 and IS1-family elements. To our knowledge, this is the first study to uncover the prevalence (0.12%) of Salmonella among 99,780 wet market workers, and the first detection of tet(X4)-harboring Salmonella in asymptomatic carriers in Shanghai. These findings underscore the critical role of asymptomatic carriers in the community spread of resistant S. enterica and provide crucial baseline data for future genomic surveillance and control strategies.

title: O-antigen loss modulates meropenem resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae through metabolic and redox reprogramming.
authors: Huang J; Wei DW; Song Y; Vollmer D; Tian X; Zhou T; Liang J; Jing S; Zhang G; Wang C; Zhu J; Vollmer W; Feng J
abstract: Carbapenems are last line β lactam antibiotics for multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infections, yet the adaptive routes by which Enterobacterales survive carbapenem stress remain incompletely understood. Here we show that prolonged subinhibitory meropenem exposure promotes O antigen loss in Klebsiella pneumoniae, predominantly via insertion sequence-mediated disruption of O-antigen biosynthesis genes, thereby enhancing carbapenem resistance. O-antigen deficiency is accompanied by envelope-associated redox remodeling and reprogramming of central metabolism, mitigating meropenem-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation and oxidative killing. This adaptation also conferred collateral sensitivity to aminoglycosides, associated with increased outer-membrane electronegativity and altered porin expression that may promote aminoglycoside uptake. Analysis of public genomes further revealed O-antigen locus disruptions in subsets of K. pneumoniae and Escherichia coli isolates. Together, our findings establish O-antigen deficiency as a surface-remodeling adaptation that enhances carbapenem resistance through coordinated metabolic and redox reprogramming, while exposing an aminoglycoside vulnerability that warrants further evaluation.

title: Risk factors and antifungal resistance in Candidozyma auris bloodstream infections in Southern China.
authors: Yi S; Chen Z; Wu R; Wu F; Zhang J; Liu P
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Candidozyma auris, also known as Candida auris, is an emerging multidrug-resistant fungal pathogen that represents a major global health concern; however, its risk factors and antifungal resistance patterns in bloodstream infections (BSIs) in Southern China remain insufficiently characterized. Therefore, this study aimed to identify risk factors and antifungal resistance patterns associated with C. auris BSIs.

METHODS: A retrospective analysis was performed on 137 patients with candidemia at a large tertiary hospital in Southern China between October 2023 and September 2025. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression followed by multivariate logistic regression was used to identify independent risk factors, and antifungal susceptibility testing was performed. Minimum inhibitory concentrations were determined and interpreted in accordance with the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute M27-A3 guideline.

RESULTS: C. auris was identified as the predominant pathogen, accounting for 39.4% (54/137) of candidemia cases, indicating an evident regional predominance and substantial burden. Independent risk factors included hypertension (OR = 6.283, 95% CI: 2.466-17.719), mechanical ventilation (OR = 4.329, 95% CI: 1.585-12.980), use of two or more antibiotics at infection onset (OR = 5.991, 95% CI: 2.349-16.686), and glucocorticoid therapy (OR = 3.100, 95% CI: 1.196-8.509). The 30-day mortality rate associated with C. auris infection was 18.5%. Lower C-reactive protein levels were independently associated with C. auris BSIs (OR = 0.987, 95% CI: 0.978-0.995), potentially reflecting a distinct host inflammatory response rather than representing a predisposing risk factor. Antifungal susceptibility testing revealed universal resistance to fluconazole (100%), while susceptibility to echinocandins was retained.

CONCLUSIONS: This study identified C. auris as an emerging leading cause of candidemia in this region, characterized by different clinical risk factors and high antifungal resistance, highlighting the importance of early identification and targeted infection control strategies.

title: Suspected Schizophyllum commune Pulmonary Disease in an Apparently Immunocompetent Host: A Case Report and Literature Review.
authors: Liu J; Jiang W; Duan J; Zhang L; Yang X; Yang W
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Schizophyllum commune causes allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis (ABPM) and other respiratory disorders. Its detection in a respiratory specimen, however, does not establish whether it is responsible for the illness.

CASE PRESENTATION: An apparently immunocompetent 45-year-old man developed cough and wheezing two weeks after cleaning a moldy basement without respiratory protection. Symptoms persisted despite moxifloxacin, with marked blood eosinophilia and elevated total IgE. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) detected S. commune and Haemophilus influenzae. BALF fungal culture was not performed, and an endobronchial biopsy showed no fungal elements. Symptoms resolved during combined corticosteroid, antibacterial and antifungal treatment. The patient continued oral voriconazole after discharge but stopped it without medical advice during the fourth month. Cough and wheezing recurred approximately two weeks later, with an absolute eosinophil count of 17.83 × 109/L and no interval change on chest computed tomography (CT). Voriconazole was resumed together with a 10-week course of oral prednisone acetate, and symptoms resolved. The interval from starting voriconazole to final discontinuation was six months, including the interruption. The patient remained symptom-free during 12 months of follow-up after treatment ended. This interval reflects the individual clinical course and should not be interpreted as a recommended treatment duration.

CONCLUSION: This case illustrates the difficulty of interpreting BALF mNGS detection of S. commune in a patient with recurrent wheezing and eosinophilia. Neither ABPM nor invasive infection was established. Concurrent corticosteroid and antifungal treatment limited assessment of the contribution of each drug.

title: Seasonal dietary shifts drive gut microbiome and metabolome adaptation in wild Northern Pike (Esox lucius).
authors: Yang Y; Wu X; Feng H; Zheng Y; Wang Z; Wu R; Zhang J
abstract: The gut microbiome of fish faces challenges in maintaining stability during seasonal dietary shifts, which directly impacts host nutrition and fitness. In this study, environmental DNA metabarcoding, metagenomics, and metabolomics were employed to characterize seasonal differences in diet, gut microbiome composition, metabolites, and digestive enzyme activity of Esox lucius between spring and autumn. E. lucius exhibited broadly and opportunistically in spring but shifted to a markedly narrower in autumn. Microbiome composition exhibited marked seasonality, with spring dominated by Mycoplasma and Yersinia, whereas autumn were characterized by Aeromonas, Acinetobacter, environmental bacteria, and were accompanied by increased trypsin and lipase activities, which suggested a capacity for enhanced lipid and protein digestion for winter energy storage. Metabolomic analysis revealed enrichment of sphingolipid metabolites in autumn, which implicated in lipid metabolism and immune regulation. Furthermore, the autumn exhibited a greater diversity and abundance of antibiotic resistance genes. Our results demonstrated that seasonal dietary variation, digestive enzyme adaptation, microbiota reshaping, metabolite-mediated signaling collectively enabled E. lucius to regulate digestive physiology, as well as efficiently assimilating nutrients and maintaining energy balance in response to fluctuating resource availability in wild. Our study offers valuable insights into the ecological adaptation mechanisms of cold-water fish species.

title: Population genomics of the endangered Peruvian algarrobo (Neltuma pallida) reveals low genetic diversity and a recent bottleneck in a protected dry-forest population.
authors: La Torre Ramirez RD; Caycho E; Saucedo-Bazalar M; Saldaña CL; Bieker VC; Arbizu CI; Orjeda G
abstract: The Pomac Forest Historic Sanctuary (SHBP), a protected area on the northern coast of Peru, conserves biodiversity representative of Equatorial dry forests. SHBP is mainly composed of algarrobo (Neltuma pallida), a species adapted to the variable climate conditions and known for its multiple ecological functions and ecosystem services. Algarrobos face an unprecedented population decline despite their remarkable natural adaptation, worsened by their ongoing habitat degradation and overexploitation. In this study, we aim to characterize the genomic diversity of the protected forest in the SHBP to establish a baseline for future monitoring and research. Results show that the algarrobo population in the SHBP is unstructured, has low inbreeding indices, an average autosomal heterozygosity of 0.19%, and a per-site nucleotide diversity of 0.0023. Patterns of low genetic diversity are associated with a recent bottleneck decline starting around four generations ago. Potentially deleterious variants with varying effects, possibly playing a role in population adaptability were predicted. In conclusion, our results provide reference genetic indices for future monitoring of algarrobo in its native range and raises questions about the impact of recent habitat degradation on its genome.

title: Temporal enrichment of bacterial monoamine oxidase gene aboard the international space station and neuromodulator impacts of dopamine-driven ammonium formed by space isolate Leifsonia virtsii on Caenorhabditis elegans.
authors: Mayuri N; Dhanyashree HR; Shastry RP; Venkateswaran K; Miliotis G; Singh NK; Stothard P; Arun AB; Hameed A
abstract: Dopamine regulates neurological functions, whereas its deficiency is linked with cognitive impairment and neurodegenerative diseases. The spatiotemporal distribution of dopamine-degrading microbes and the implications of dopamine catabolites on eukaryotes remain unexplored. Here, we demonstrate dopamine metabolism in Leifsonia virtsii F6_8S_P_1AT, an Actinomycetes isolated from the crew quarters aboard the International Space Station (ISS), and reveal dopamine catabolite-driven modulation of cognition and chemotaxis in Caenorhabditis elegans. L. virtsii shared a high 16S rRNA gene sequence similarity (>97.9%) and OrthoANI values (79.44-84.96%) with the Leifsonia species, isolated from terrestrial and aquatic habitats. A key gene encoding monoamine oxidase (MAO) involved in dopamine catabolism was found in 61.5% of validly established Leifsonia species, including L. virtsii, but not in ISS co-isolate L. williamsii F6_8S_P_1BT. Analysis of the ISS metagenome revealed temporal enrichment of MAO-associated signatures across Microbial Tracking studies (MT1 to MT3, 2015-2022), driven predominantly by candidate MAO homologs taxonomically associated with Actinomycetota in MT3, whereas strong F6-8S-P-1A-like MAO signals were restricted to two MT2 libraries. Dopamine input stimulated MAO gene expression in L. virtsii at early growth phase, and was found to complement cell division, biofilm establishment and extracellular NH4 + formation in L. virtsii. MAO expression decreased with increasing time/NH4 + concentration, whereas expression of marker genes representing DNA synthesis and transcription (gyrB), translation (tuf) and biofilm formation (cslA) exhibited concurrent upregulation. Dopamine-driven NH4 + formation further altered cognition and chemotaxis in C. elegans. Our analysis suggests that the dopamine metabolic pathway detected in L. virtsii is not an ISS-specific trait and rather represents a phenotype retrieved from Earth. The present study provides direct evidence of spatiotemporal flexibility and heterogeneous dopamine-metabolizing capacity among Actinomycetes. The findings further demonstrate that a dopamine catabolite can modulate chemosensory interactions in a eukaryotic model and highlight the succession and persistence of MAO-bearing taxa aboard ISS.

title: Cell-associated viral community composition and its functional potential in a dimictic lake on the Canadian shield.
authors: Collis CC; Cameron ES; Müller KM; Emelko MB; Tromas N; Nissimov JI
abstract: The Turkey Lake Watershed (TLW), located in Northern Ontario, forms a cascading lake system that drains into Lake Superior. Historically, the TLW has served as a key research site for studies on acid rain and climate change. Despite its long-standing ecological importance, investigations into its microbial communities remain limited, and to date, no studies have explicitly examined the viral component of this watershed. Viruses have been frequently implicated in nutrient cycling in aquatic environments and strongly influence their microbial hosts. Therefore, viral ecology offers a powerful way to extend the environmental legacy of the TLW by identifying the biological mechanisms through which long-term changes in acid deposition, climate, hydrology, carbon chemistry, and forest disturbance propagate through microbial food webs. First steps can be a preliminary view into the type of viruses that are present, and information on which microbial hosts they may be infecting. We conducted a seasonal metagenomic survey of Big Turkey Lake (BTL)-one of the primary lakes within the TLW-from summer 2018 to winter 2020. Our study characterized the diversity and composition of cell-associated viral communities, predicted potential host relationships, and identified auxiliary metabolic genes (AMGs) to better understand the functional roles of these viruses. The results revealed a dynamic viral community that varied across seasons. Most viral contigs were classified as Caudoviricetes, while members of Phycodnaviridae emerged as important non-bacteriophage contributors to the viral assemblage. We reconstructed six draft viral metagenome-assembled genomes (vMAGs), ranging in size from 11 to 45 kbp, all identified as Caudoviricetes, with two being potential temperate phages and a third containing ribosomal genes. Notably, AMGs associated with lipid metabolism were detected exclusively in winter, suggesting a potential season- or niche-specific role for these genes in BTL.
