AMGs related to phosphorus acquisition were present in all samples, suggesting a potential coupling between transport dynamics of dissolved organic matter and phosphorus previously described in the TLW, and the host-virus dynamics described here. Together, these findings provide the first insight into the viral ecology of the TLW and establish a foundation for future studies investigating the roles of viruses in shaping the microbial dynamics in this important habitat.

title: Nutritional intervention trial of yeast mannans derived from baker's yeast enriches Bacteroides and Parabacteroides with concurrent reduction of Klebsiella pneumoniae.
authors: Moreno ML; Taft DH; Tompkins TA; Dahl WJ
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Supplementation with a yeast cell wall fraction rich in mannans is well tolerated in adults without gastrointestinal disease; however, limited research has examined its selective utilization by the gut microbiota and associated health benefits. The aim of this analysis was to investigate the specific effects of yeast mannans on the composition and metabolic function of the gut microbiota.

METHODS: Fecal samples from an open-label study of adults consuming 15 g of yeast mannans per day were profiled for fecal microbiota composition using whole metagenome sequencing, and fecal and urine metabolomics were analyzed by direct infusion and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (DI-MS/MS and LC-MS/MS).

RESULTS: Differential abundance testing identified 46 species whose relative abundances increased with the yeast mannan intervention, primarily in the genera Bacteroides and Parabacteroides. Thomasclavelia spiroformis showed the largest fold increase. Four species decreased in relative abundance, with a greater-than-2-fold decrease in Klebsiella pneumoniae, with 45% of participants showing no detection following the yeast mannan intervention. Minor metabolomic changes were noted, including increased urinary excretion of N-acetylalanine, alanine, and caproic acid, and decreases in fecal concentrations of ether-linked phosphatidylcholines C36:4 and C40:1.

DISCUSSION: Yeast mannan supplementation selectively enriched several Bacteroides and Parabacteroides, saccharolytic commensals that may outcompete Klebsiella pneumoniae, an opportunistic pathobiont capable of causing extraintestinal infections.

title: SOS-independent prophage induction pathways and their contributions to antibiotic resistance gene dissemination: advances and controversies.
authors: Sima J; Li S; Bian Q; Chen Y; Ji S; Yan Y; Zhao Z; Liu A; Shi X
abstract: Temperate bacteriophages integrate into bacterial chromosomes as prophages, which are widespread across sequenced bacterial genomes and serve as key mobile genetic elements mediating horizontal gene transfer and the global dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). For decades, prophage induction has been thought to rely almost entirely on the canonical SOS DNA damage response triggered by DNA-damaging agents such as fluoroquinolones and mitomycin C; however, accumulating experimental evidence shows that multiple SOS-independent regulatory circuits also drive the lysogeny-to-lysis switch in response to non-DNA-damaging physiological and environmental cues. In this mini-review, we classify SOS-independent prophage induction pathways into five major categories: quorum sensing-mediated regulation, metabolic and oxidative stress-triggered activation, induction by sub-inhibitory concentrations of non-DNA-damaging antibiotics, spontaneous induction driven by stochastic gene expression noise, and modulation by physiological and environmental factors such as bile acids and osmotic stress. We summarize the molecular basis of each pathway and examine available empirical evidence linking these induction routes to phage-mediated ARG dissemination across clinical, intestinal, and environmental microbial ecosystems. We further outline four core unresolved debates in the field: the relative quantitative contribution of SOS-independent versus SOS-dependent induction to resistance spread, the mechanistic classification of sub-inhibitory antibiotic effects, the gap between bioinformatic predictions of prophage-associated ARGs and their functional transmissibility, and the limited taxonomic scope of current mechanistic research. We conclude by discussing implications for antimicrobial resistance stewardship and highlighting priority directions for future quantitative and functional investigations.

title: Variation in rhizosphere microbial communities and nitrogen- and phosphorus-cycling functional genes among rubber plantations in Yunnan, China.
authors: Geng S; Yang J; Shi X; Zhang Q; Yang C
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Rhizosphere microorganisms are important participants in soil nutrient transformation. However, variation in rhizosphere microbial community composition and nitrogen (N)- and phosphorus (P)-cycling functional gene profiles among rubber plantations in Yunnan Province remains unclear.

METHODS: Metagenomic sequencing was used to compare rhizosphere microbial community composition and N- and P-cycling functional gene profiles among the rubber plantations located in five major natural rubber-producing areas in Yunnan Province, China: Gengma (MD), Ximeng (XM), Mengla (ML), Jinghong (JH), and Jiangcheng (JC).

RESULTS: Bacterial and fungal community composition and N- and P-cycling functional gene profiles differed significantly among the five rubber plantations. JC exhibited higher fungal diversity and richness, but its bacterial diversity was significantly lower than that in MD. The bacterial communities were dominated by Pseudomonadota, Acidobacteriota, and Actinomycetota, and the relative abundance of Acidobacteria was significantly enriched in JC compared to JH. Furthermore, Mucoromycota, Ascomycota, and Basidiomycota were the dominant phyla in the fungal community. At the functional level, compared to JC, key genes associated with N cycling were significantly enriched in ML, including N assimilation (glnA, gltB, gltD), dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (narG, narH, nirB), nitrification (nxrA, nxrB), and denitrification (napA, napB). Furthermore, the nosZ gene was also significantly enriched in MD compared to JC. Regarding the P cycle, compared to JC, genes associated with high-affinity phosphate transporters (pstA, pstB, pstC) and polyphosphate degradation (ndk) were significantly enriched in MD, whereas the organic phosphorus mineralization-related gene phnX exhibited the opposite trend. Meanwhile, compared to MD, the polyphosphate degradation-related gene ppk2 was significantly enriched in ML, whereas the inorganic phosphorus solubilization-related gene pqqC exhibited the opposite pattern. Hierarchical partitioning identified soil pH, total phosphorus (TP), and total potassium (TK) as the primary factors significantly associated with variations in bacterial community composition and P-cycling functional gene profiles.

CONCLUSION: In summary, the composition of rhizosphere bacterial and fungal communities, as well as the functional gene profiles related to N and P cycling, differed significantly among the investigated rubber plantations. These variations were closely associated with soil physicochemical factors. These findings may provide a microbiological basis for further developing site-specific nutrient management strategies in rubber plantations.

title: proMGE2-a planetary-scale resource of mobile genetic elements in microbial (meta)genomes.
authors: Grekova A; Schudoma C; Letunic I; Kim CY; Podlesny D; Fullam A; Schmidt TSB; Orakov A; Mende D; Schiller J; Erbstein KOE; Bartmanski B; Zimmermann-Kogadeeva M; Zimmermann M; Kuhn M; Bork P; Khedkar S
abstract: proMGE is a resource of prokaryotic mobile genetic elements (MGEs) that systematically catalogues MGEs from prokaryotes, their intercellular spread, antimicrobial resistance gene carriage, and MGE nesting interactions. We present proMGE2 featuring a 6X expansion, a total of >16.4 million MGEs from 670k high-quality isolate genomes, and 180k metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), spanning diverse MGE categories: transposons and insertion sequences, phages, phage-like elements, conjugative elements, mobility islands, and integrons. proMGE2 includes MGEs from MAGs derived from environmental microbiomes, encompassing ~50k samples across several major habitat types. proMGE2 provides a standardized MGE reference collection of >5 million non-redundant MGE sequences drawn from our curated database, and enables identification of MGEs in user-provided genomes. proMGE2 captures MGE diversity and their functional potential at unprecedented scale to support future research of mobile genetic elements and transfer of genetic material in microbes. The database is available at http://promge.embl.de/.

title: A specialized microbiome enriched in nitrification and halogen cycling potential resolved from multi-omics investigation of a Caribbean suboxic and acidic marine sinkhole.
authors: Boer MD; Peets P; van Eijnatten AL; Nelson CE; do Canto Brum de Menezes Pena MM; Karancz S; Humphreys MP; van Duyl FC; Meesters EH; Snoek BL; Melkonian C; Haas AF; Dutilh BE
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The Luymes Sinkholes, located on the Luymes Bank northwest of Saba, represent a unique marine environment characterized by distinct biogeochemical gradients. Most noticeable is an acidic (pH ≈ 6.25) and suboxic (O2 < 60 µmol/kg) submerged 'lake' at ~ 220 m depth exhibiting extreme deviations from standard oceanographic patterns, including elevated inorganic carbon, nitrate, and phosphate, and a lower temperature (20.3 ºC vs 26.4 ºC). To determine how the microbiome within the submerged acid lake adapted to these unique conditions, we collected 59 coupled samples of size-filtered (0.22 µm) planktonic microbes for shotgun metagenomics and solid-phase extracted dissolved organic matter for untargeted metabolomics from 21 stations at depths ranging from 2 to 600 m during a 10-day research cruise in December 2019.

RESULTS: We identified a distinct microbial community within the submerged acid lake different from the non-acidic sinkholes, with increased abundances of Nitrospinota, Thermoproteota, Planctomycetota, and Actinobacteriota. We also found three enriched classes of dissolved compounds within the submerged acid lake: (1) large, (2) low-polarity, and (3) halogenated metabolites, including iodides and halobenzoic acids. Correlations between microbial taxa and metabolite classes show potential links between nitrifying archaea and halogenated compound cycling. We further supported these findings using the functional annotation of metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) and protein clusters showing enrichment of nitrification and halogen cycling genes, suggesting the presence of specialized degradation and biosynthetic pathways, directly connecting microbial metabolism to the observed geochemical conditions.

CONCLUSION: These findings demonstrate that the submerged acid lake contains specific microbially driven biogeochemical processes under acidified and low-oxygen conditions, providing a natural model for future extreme ocean acidification scenarios. With this multi‑omics approach, we were able to connect the microbial metabolism with this unique environment, thereby expanding our understanding of how both are interconnected. Video Abstract.

title: Gut microbiota dysbiosis in Post-COVID condition symptoms: relation with chronic fatigue and functional limitation.
authors: Carpallo-Porcar B; García-Martínez L; Jiménez-Sánchez C; Calvo S; Roig FJ
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Post-COVID Condition (PCC) is a heterogeneous clinical syndrome in which chronic fatigue and functional limitation are among the most disabling manifestations. Alterations in the gut microbiota have been proposed as contributors to PCC pathophysiology; however, it remains unclear whether distinct clinical PCC phenotypes are associated with specific microbiota signatures.

RESULTS: This cross-sectional pilot study analysed gut microbiota composition and predicted functional capacity in 50 participants from Aragón (Spain), including 30 patients with PCC and 20 healthy controls. PCC patients were stratified according to the presence of Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS)-like symptoms and functional limitation assessed using the 6-Minute Walking Test. Alpha and beta diversity did not differ significantly between groups (Figs. 2 and 3). Differential abundance analysis identified taxon-level differences between groups. Escherichia/Shigella was enriched in PCC-CFS relative to controls, both overall and in the subgroup without functional limitation, representing the most consistent signal. Additional differences included higher Streptococcus and Veillonella in controls, and higher Flavonifractor and Hungatella in PCC-NCFS. After adjustment for digestive symptoms and vaccine dose, these associations attenuated and none remained significant, indicating that they may be partly driven by confounding.PICRUSt2 functional predictions suggested differences in pathways related to nucleotide and amino acid metabolism; however, none remained significant after correction for multiple testing and should therefore be considered exploratory.

CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest the presence of phenotype-associated taxonomic differences within PCC despite the absence of global diversity alterations. The results should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating due to the limited subgroup sample sizes. Larger studies incorporating metagenomic and metabolomic approaches are needed to validate these observations and clarify their potential clinical relevance.

title: ArchaeaHQ: a curated reference database of archaeal genomes.
authors: Bespiatykh D; Leão P
abstract: Archaea have proven to be major players in biogeochemical cycles across diverse ecosystems, yet we still see an underrepresentation of archaeal genomes in the datasets used by popular computational biology tools. Here, we present ArchaeaHQ, a quality-controlled, systematically curated reference database of 25,584 archaeal genomes compiled initially from 43,045 assemblies from all four archaeal kingdoms retrieved from NCBI: Methanobacteriati (Euryarchaeota), Thermoproteati (TACK), Nanobdellati (DPANN) and Promethearchaeati (Asgard). All genomes in the database passed standardized quality control, requiring ≥70% completeness and ≤10% contamination. A total of 44.0% of genomes in ArchaeaHQ achieved ≥90% completeness, while 92.7% exhibited ≤5% contamination. ArchaeaHQ comprises 18,701 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs; 73.1%) and 6,883 isolate genomes (26.9%). Approximately 76% of MAGs are assigned to 17 ecologically meaningful categories based on sampling origin, and around 65% of genomes include geographic metadata. ArchaeaHQ is available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.32266599 for download and at https://vee-lab.eu/archaeahq for online browsing. This resource was designed to provide an analysis-ready reference set for metagenomic, biogeochemical and ecological studies, comparative genomics analyses and the development of archaeal-specific bioinformatic tools.

title: Microbiome-targeted strategies for Alzheimer's disease: multi-omics signatures, mechanistic links, and intervention evidence.
authors: Huang X; Zhang X; Zhu Q
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is increasingly studied in relation to gut microbial mechanisms because microbial metabolism, mucosal barrier function, and peripheral immune activation may influence neuroinflammation and host metabolic stress. This review evaluates microbiome-linked evidence in AD with emphasis on studies that combine metagenomics, metabolomics, inflammatory markers, neuroimaging, cerebrospinal fluid or blood biomarkers, and cognitive phenotyping. Current data support several recurring but not yet causal axes, including bile acid transformation, short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), bacterial product-related inflammatory signaling, and barrier dysfunction. We also review microbiome-targeted interventions, including diet and prebiotics, strain-specified probiotics and synbiotics, oligosaccharide-based agents, gut-restricted antimicrobials, and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT). The strength of evidence differs substantially across these strategies: sodium oligomannate has been tested in a phase 3 trial, whereas many probiotic, antimicrobial, and FMT approaches remain early clinical, preclinical, or mechanism-generating. Future trials should define a priori microbial, metabolite, immune, and brain biomarker endpoints; control diet, medication, and comorbidity confounding; and validate candidate signatures across independent cohorts before using microbiome profiles for screening or treatment selection.

title: Improving Talaromycosis Infection Diagnosis and Prognosis with Metagenomic Next-Generation Sequencing.
authors: Zhang L; He X; Xu L; Xiao J; Lin J; Song B; Chen L; Chen G; Liu K
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early diagnosis and timely initiation of appropriate antifungal treatment are critical for improving the prognosis of talaromycosis infection. We aimed to test whether metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), versus conventional microbiological testing (CMT), improves talaromycosis diagnosis and management in HIV-negative patients via higher sensitivity and faster detection.

METHODS: We retrospectively investigated the clinical data of patients with Talaromyces marneffei (T. marneffei) infection in six hospitals in Fujian, China, between July 2015 and June 2024. The diagnostic performance and clinical impact of mNGS were compared with those of CMT.

RESULTS: Seventy-four patients were included, with 38 cases in the mNGS group and 36 cases for CMT group, based on the method that established the definitive diagnosis. The median duration from hospitalization to confirmed diagnosis was significantly shorter in the mNGS group than in the CMT group (5.0 vs 12.0 days, p < 0.0001). The turnround time for mNGS was shorter than that of CMT (1.0 days vs 6.5 days, p < 0.0001). The mNGS detected more mycobacteria and other fungal infection co-infections than CMT (36.8% vs 13.9%, p = 0.033; 26.3% vs 5.56%, p = 0.025). The mNGS group has a trend of lower mortality compared with the CMT group (18.4% vs 38.9%, p = 0.072). In addition, the length of stay was significantly shorter in the mNGS group than in the CMT group (14.5 days vs 21.0 days, p = 0.007).

CONCLUSION: mNGS facilitates rapid diagnosis and improves administration of targeted antimicrobial therapy, thus improving the prognosis of T. marneffei infection. The clinical utility of mNGS for talaromycosis in at-risk populations should be investigated in prospective and large studies.

title: Metagenomic next-generation sequencing improves pathogen detection in culture-negative infections: a diagnostic performance study.
authors: Tayeb HT; Abouelhoda M; Alqasabi A; Magrashi A; Nafe G; Alzahrani T; Alzeer S; Bakheet R
abstract: The conventional microbiological diagnosis is frequently insensitive, time consuming and targeted. Patients with underlying immune suppression and those who have recently been on antibiotics often have culture-negative infections. In recent years, metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) has emerged as a novel, pathogen-agnostic diagnostic approach. A total of 136 clinical specimens were submitted for metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) between August 2022 and January 2024. Of these samples, 86 from 73 patients were included in this retrospective study. Thirteen patients had more than one specimen included in the study. All specimens were processed using conventional microbiological methods and analyzed using mNGS technology, either by using Illumina next-generation sequencing technology or Oxford Nanopore long-read technology. The diagnostic performance characteristics, including sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV), were calculated for both methods. The agreement between the two methods was evaluated using Cohen's kappa coefficient. The paired comparisons were made using the McNemar test. The areas under the ROC curves for both methods were calculated, and the multivariable logistic regression analysis was used to identify the variables that were independently associated with mNGS positivity. Here, conventional microbiology identified pathogens in 16.3% of samples, whereas mNGS identified pathogens in 45.3% of samples. The sensitivity and specificity of mNGS were 57.1 and 84.2%, respectively. By McNemar testing, there was significant detection of pathogens by mNGS (p = 0.0015). The agreement between two methods was poor (kappa = 0.20). The ROC curve for mNGS results showed moderate diagnostic accuracy with an AUC of 0.71. By multivariable logistic regression, immunocompromised status (OR 2.8, 95% CI 1.3-6.0, p = 0.018) and positive imaging findings (OR 3.1, 95% CI 1.4-6.9, p = 0.010) were independently associated with mNGS positivity. mNGS is able to identify more pathogens in culture-negative cases than conventional methods. There is scope for mNGS to be used in a complementary fashion, whilst relying on conventional methods as the primary tool for diagnosis of infections. Notably, the greatest additional information will come from the use of mNGS in immunocompromised patients.

title: Antimicrobial resistance in environment and wastewaters of a swine slaughterhouse - tracking ESKAPE bacteria and ESBL-/carbapenemase-producing Escherichia coli.
authors: Manfreda C; Guarneri F; Ferri G; Di Vittori C; Olivastri A; Piccioni MA; Ianieri A; Alborali GL; Vergara A
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: This study investigated the occurrence, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) profiles, and genomic features of selected ESKAPE bacteria and ESBL-/carbapenemase-producing Escherichia coli isolated from wastewater and floor swabs in a swine slaughterhouse in Central Italy.

METHODS: By integrating microbiological and genomic analyses across different operational phases, the study observed persistence and dissemination of antimicrobial resistant bacteria (ARB) within the abattoir environment.

RESULTS: E. coli was the most prevalent species (39.6%) across all matrices, confirming its role as an indicator of fecal and environmental contamination. Despite cleaning and depuration, few ARB and antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) persisted, particularly in wastewater, reflecting the partial efficacy of conventional sanitation and treatment measures. The antimicrobial susceptibility tests revealed high resistance against ampicillin (47.2%), tetracycline (41.2%), and trimethoprim (34.0%), with multidrug resistant isolates occurring in nearly one-third of samples. Whole-genome sequencing identified the resistome, e.g., bla TEM, bla CTX-M, and bla OXA-48 genes. The detection of bla NDM in treated wastewater underscores the potential for environmental dissemination of carbapenemase producers. Phylogenetic analyses revealed clonal persistence of OXA- and ESBL-producing E. coli and Acinetobacter baumannii across samples, while livestock-associated MRSA ST398 indicated localized contamination events.

DISCUSSION: These findings demonstrate that slaughterhouse ecosystems can function as active reservoirs and transmission nodes for AMR.

title: Aerobic methane oxidation by microorganisms exacerbates neurotoxic methylmercury accumulation in rice paddy fields.
authors: Chen KH; Liu HW; Hao YY; Sun R; Yang M; Liu Q; Jia H; Liu YR
abstract: Aerobic methane (CH4) oxidation is the dominant biological sink for CH4 in wetland soils and is increasingly linked to diverse biogeochemical processes; however, whether and how aerobic CH4 oxidation influences the production of the neurotoxin methylmercury (MeHg) through microbial mercury (Hg) methylation remains poorly understood. Here, we combined a ~3300 km field survey across the main rice-producing areas of China with 13CH4-DNA-stable isotope probing (SIP) to investigate the microbial linkage between aerobic CH4 oxidation and Hg methylation in paddy fields. Field observations showed positive relationships between CH4 oxidation activity and the ratio of MeHg at a continental scale, as well as between gene abundances of CH4 oxidation (pmoA) and Hg methylation (hgcA). Microcosm experiments further demonstrated that CH4 addition significantly increased MeHg production by 40.7-177.7% and enhanced hgcA gene expression by 49.5-416.0% across three typical paddy soils. Moreover, 13CH4-DNA-SIP analyses identified 112 hgcA-containing operational taxonomic units (OTUs) that incorporated 13CH4-derived 13C, of which 75.0-85.5% were affiliated with the families Geobacteraceae, Anaerolineaceae, and unclassified Desulfobacterales. Integrated analyses of 13C-metagenome-assembled genomes and metabolomics indicated that this carbon transfer was likely mediated by metabolic handoffs from methanotrophs to Hg-methylating microorganisms through intermediates (e.g., malate and fumarate) released during aerobic CH4 oxidation. Soil incubation and pure-culture experiments further confirmed the functional significance of methanotroph-derived metabolites, as their addition significantly enhanced MeHg production. These findings highlight microbial metabolic handoffs as an important mechanism linking aerobic CH4 oxidation and Hg methylation, with implications for developing synergistic strategies for MeHg pollution mitigation and carbon reduction.

title: Evaluation of the DISQVER metagenomic sequencing platform for detection of microbial cell-free DNA in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid.
authors: Cox CR; Wolf MJ; Norgan AP; Yao JD; Patel R; Simner PJ

title: Gut microbiome and metabolite profiling in term SGA infants: a multi-omics approach to physical development.
authors: Li S; Yu Z; Jin Y; Ma K; Sha L; Qian M; Chen X; Han S
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Early-life gut microbial composition and fecal metabolic profiles may be altered in infants born small for gestational age (SGA), but evidence specifically concerning term SGA infants remains limited.

OBJECTIVES: To characterize gut microbial composition, predicted microbial functions, and fecal metabolite profiles in term SGA infants and explore their associations with early growth.

METHODS: This prospective nested case-control study included 62 term infants (31 SGA and 31 appropriate for gestational age [AGA]). Fecal samples were collected at 3 months. Untargeted metabolomics was performed in the full cohort, and shotgun metagenomic sequencing was conducted in a nested subset of 20 infants (10 SGA and 10 AGA). Differential taxa, KEGG orthologs (KOs), metabolites, and cross-omics correlations were analyzed.

RESULTS: Alpha diversity did not differ significantly between groups, whereas microbial composition and species-level abundance patterns differed between SGA and AGA infants. Functional analysis identified 135 differential KOs, including 36 with higher and 99 with lower abundance in the SGA group. These KOs were mapped to 25 metabolic pathways, including galactose, butanoate, D-amino acid, aromatic amino acid, fructose-mannose, pyruvate, propanoate, and lipid metabolism. Twelve fecal metabolite features differed between groups, including 5'-methylthioadenosine, taurocholate, β-alanine, and 17α-hydroxypregnanolone. Exploratory integration identified connections among microbial species, KOs, and metabolites. Several microbial and metabolite features showed nominal associations with 6-month growth indices, but most cross-omics and metabolite-growth associations did not remain significant after false discovery rate correction.

CONCLUSIONS: Term SGA infants showed differences in gut microbial composition, predicted metabolic potential, and fecal metabolite profiles at 3 months. Associations with subsequent growth were exploratory and require validation in larger longitudinal studies.

title: Investigating the biotechnological potential of thermophiles using integrated culture-dependent and metagenomic approaches from Tapovan hot springs for industrial thermozymes.
authors: Bhatt D; Shelat R; Bharwad K; Singh NK; Joshi C; Bagatharia S; Shekh S; Patel A
abstract: Hot springs are prolific reservoirs for bioprospecting novel biomolecules with industrial relevance. The present study reports the first integrated culture-dependent and culture enriched and sequencing based assessment of microbial diversity and metabolic potential at the Tapovan hot spring (Uttarakhand, India). Fifteen genera belonging to five major phyla were identified from soil and water samples using both culture-dependent culture-enriched and culture-independent (16S amplicon sequencing) approaches. Based on 16S rRNA gene sequencing of culturable isolates, Paenibacillus phoenicis, Paenibacillus naphthalenovorans, Paenibacillus faecis, and Aeribacillus pallidus were preliminarily identified; their presence at Tapovan extends the known geographical and ecological range of these species. Additional genome-based research will be necessary to confirm their taxonomic identity and ecological importance. Qualitative and quantitative enzyme screening revealed that isolates produced key industrial enzymes including amylase, cellulase, xylanase, mannanase, and pectinase. Importantly, most characterised strains demonstrated the ability to produce multiple enzymes simultaneously, reflecting broad metabolic versatility. These findings demonstrate the potential of Tapovan hot spring as a source of thermostable, multi-functional enzymes, and indicate the need for further genome level characterisation of its thermophilic community for biotechnological exploitation.

title: Cell-free expression and NGS-powered substrate profiling reveal a thermostable metagenomic meganuclease from an extreme environment with novel specificity.
authors: Dorrazehi GM; Penner M; Athanasiou C; Boursinhac L; Mobarec JC; Webster CI; Papworth M; Hollfelder F
abstract: As an alternative to historical enzyme isolation, metagenomic databases (e.g. MGnify) provide information on vast unculturable microbial diversity, including extreme environments, and constitute an enormous source of functional proteins. Conservative mining of these data by close sequence homology alone tends to identify merely different versions of known enzymes. Here we present a discovery strategy for meganucleases based on wider capture of less homologous enzymes in metagenomic databases, and incorporating metadata with their homology. We use cell-free expression to bypass host incompatibility and the need for purification, along with deep sequencing for experimental assessment of substrate specificity and cleavage pattern, thereby circumventing classical gel-based profiling. Specifically, we discovered the temperature-stable (>55°C), intron-encoded LAGLIDADG meganuclease I-MG11 that recognizes a GC-rich 17 base pair sequence to generate 4-nt palindromic 3'-overhangs-the first monomeric meganuclease to produce such overhangs. Co-folding models of I-MG11 bound to DNA provide a structural context for enzyme-DNA interactions, highlighting differences from other monomeric LAGLIDADG meganucleases (e.g. I-SceI) shaped by InDels (insertion-deletions) in the DNA-binding region that may cause specificity changes. Our strategy streamlines general bona fide identification and annotation of meganucleases, while the unique properties of I-MG11 expand the toolbox of molecular genome engineering.

title: gcPathogen 2.0: an expanded multi-omics database advancing global pathogen surveillance and One Health research.
authors: Chen Q; Guo C; Wang L; Fan G; Qu X; Li S; Feng M; Ma J; Tong Z; Song H; Wu L
abstract: Launched in 2024, gcPathogen established a critical foundation for the genomic surveillance of human pathogens. Here, we present gcPathogen 2.0, a major multi-omics update designed to address key analytical bottlenecks, including the integration of genomic and transcriptional profiles, systematic tracking of cross-habitat distribution, and large-scale discovery of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs). This release expands coverage from 1134 to 1506 pathogenic species, spanning 557 bacteria, 508 fungi, 258 viruses, and 183 parasites, and increases total genomic records past 2.3 million. By incorporating 12 597 transcriptomes across 148 species, gcPathogen 2.0 bridges the gap between gene carriage and functional expression for risk assessment. Furthermore, the platform integrates 285 925 pathogen metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) spanning human, animal, and environmental niches. Mapped across 68 Environment Ontology (ENVO) habitat categories, these MAGs enable comprehensive tracking of cross-habitat distribution of pathogens, antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), virulence factors (VFs), and mobile genetic elements (MGEs). Leveraging a nonredundant reference set curated from seven public databases, we identified over 77 million AMPs belonging to >55 000 families across 438 bacterial pathogens. Finally, pan-genome analyses of 440 bacterial species map intraspecies functional distributions across core, accessory, and unique gene repertoires. gcPathogen 2.0 is publicly accessible at https://nmdc.cn/gcpathogen/.

title: Beneficial microbes in plant salt stress tolerance: mechanisms, antioxidant defense, and multi-omics insights.
authors: Shree S; Chaudhary A; Kumar S; Singh K; Dubey N
abstract: Salinity stress represents a significant environmental challenge that affects plant growth, resulting in adverse impacts on crop productivity and overall yield. Salt accumulation in plants affects cellular homeostasis and provokes osmotic and ionic imbalance. It stimulates higher reactive oxygen species (ROS) production leading to oxidative stress damage and eventual cellular dysfunction. Beneficial microorganisms like plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria, arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, endophytic fungi, and rhizosphere-associated microbes have recently emerged as resources for sustainable solutions to enhance plant resiliency against salinity stress. Their effects can involve osmotic adjustment, ion sequestration, oxidative-stress mitigation, phytohormone regulation, and rhizosphere-mediated stress buffering. The mechanisms to impart such benefits may include improved nutrients acquisition, assist in osmotic regulation, modulation of phytohormones signaling, and maintenance of cellular ion homeostasis. Often, beneficial microorganisms carry the potential to trigger both enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidant defense mechanisms. These responses contribute to oxidative-stress mitigation, yet, their interpretation requires contemplation of fine balance between oxidative damage and plant responses. For example, selected microbial inoculation studies have reported changes in the activity of crucial antioxidant enzymes, like superoxide dismutase, ascorbate peroxidase, catalase, and glutathione reductase. However, the magnitude and the direction of these responses are context dependent. Multi-omics approaches, including amplicon and shotgun metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, host transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, have expanded our understanding of the taxa, genes, transcripts, proteins, and metabolites associated with plant-microbe interactions under salinity. Therefore, here an effort has been made to present the evidential support for reported microbial effects and their proposed mechanisms of salt tolerance, with a focus on enzymatic and non-enzymatic defense mechanisms and the learnings of multi-omics studies. Frontier integrative mechanisms, including microbiome engineering, synthetic microbial consortia, and systems biology frameworks, are discussed for cultivating climate-resilient crops and sustainable agricultural systems in the salt-affected environments.

title: Current research status of risk assessment models for oral squamous cell carcinoma based on microbiome databases.
authors: Li GL; Zhang ZC; Lyu XM; Li MX; Lin PY; Yu HS; Zhu YY; Zhang GH; Duan CG; Cheung Y; Li W; Zhang ZJ; Xu TS; Chen F; Huang MW
abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is one of the most common oral malignancies. Due to insidious early symptoms, high invasiveness, and frequent cervical lymph node metastasis, patient survival remains poor. Recent studies demonstrate significant associations between oral dysbiosis and OSCC. To address limited early screening and suboptimal survival rates, this review systematically summarizes OSCC microbiome research and disease risk assessment applications. Studies reveal marked oral dysbiosis in patients with OSCC, characterized by enrichment of Fusobacterium and Porphyromonas, reduced Neisseria abundance, and altered community stability. These promote tumorigenesis through chronic pro-inflammatory signaling, the production of carcinogenic metabolites, and direct oncogenic pathway interference. Consequently, the oral microbiome offers non-invasive, sensitive biomarkers for early detection. We identify and distinguish four categories of predictive models in the current literature: (1) detection/discrimination of prevalent OSCC, (2) prediction of malignant transformation from oral potentially malignant disorders, (3) prediction of recurrence or metastasis after treatment, and (4) prognostic models for survival prediction. Existing databases include comprehensive and OSCC-specific collections with multi-omics integration. Risk assessment models encompass traditional statistics, machine learning, deep learning, and multimodal fusion, and have shown promising performance in retrospective cohorts. However, standardized databases are lacking, and existing models face confounding interference, limited generalizability, and insufficient interpretability. Furthermore, current predictive models are predominantly based on 16S rRNA sequencing (bacteriome-centric), whereas comprehensive risk assessment requires integrating interkingdom entities, including fungi, viruses, and archaea, through metagenomic and virome profiling. Critically, the distinction between promising retrospective discrimination and validated prospective clinical utility remains a major translational barrier. Future directions include developing standardized longitudinal databases, integrating multi-omics, using explainable artificial intelligence, and conducting prospective validation studies to achieve personalized precision treatment.

title: Feed additives as systems-level modulators of the ruminant host-microbiome interaction: a multi-omics perspective on efficiency, resistance, and reproduction.
authors: Fijabi O; Morenikeji OB; Ivey SL; Loest C; Idowu M; Ashley R; Ogunade IM; Taiwo G
abstract: Ruminant livestock face converging pressures from climatic variation, antimicrobial agents, and the imperative for sustainable intensification. However, the molecular imprints through which nutritional interventions modulate host-microbiome interactions across physiological contexts remain fragmented across disciplinary themes. Here, we synthesize evidence from metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metabolomics, and host transcriptomics to propose that feed additives operate as systems-level modulators of a functionally integrated rumen-liver-immune-reproductive axis, rather than acting on isolated metabolic pathways. Prevotella, Butyrivibrio, Ruminococcus, and Fibrobacter recurrently emerged across studies to be associated with feed efficiency, immune modulation, resistome dynamics, and reproductive fitness. However, their relationship is context dependent and not causal. Furthermore, hepatic transcriptomic and microRNA (miRNA)-mediated regulatory networks could serve as a molecular bridge connecting ruminal fermentation events to systemic phenotypic outcomes. The ruminant resistome may also represent a potential interface with public health rather than an isolated ecological phenomenon, given the capacity for horizontal gene transfer through mobile genetic elements, although the extent of transmission to humans remains to be quantified. Early-life microbial programming and reproductive tract microbiome composition also represent tractable intervention windows for precision management. This integrated framework could reframe feed additive research from a single pathway to a systems-level perspective, offering a basis for precision ruminant production.

title: Isolation and characterization of novel Klebsiella phages from Benin and their antibiofilm activities on multidrug resistant and hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae strains.
authors: Agbankpe AJ; Fabiyi K; Hounmanou YMG; Nougbologni GR; Balarabe R; Michniewski S; Hougbenou JB; Deguenon E; Dougnon V; Bankolé H; Baba-Moussa L; Nazir R; Clokie MRJ
abstract: Hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae represents a growing clinical threat, particularly where multidrug resistance limits treatment options. This study aims to characterize Klebsiella phages isolated in Benin and evaluate their efficacy in reducing bacterial cell growth, biofilm inhibition and biofilm disruption. To achieve this objective, we isolated Klebsiella phages by enriching samples of hospital effluent, pig droppings, and stool, using clinical multidrug resistant and hypervirulent K. pneumoniae strains as hosts. These phages were characterized using transmission electron microscopy, whole-genome sequencing, and biological assays. Then, we evaluated their antibiofilm activity and stability under harsh conditions (pH and temperature) in vitro. So, we report the isolation and characterization of three novel lytic phages from Benin (Kp1Bj_HH11_M23, Kp2Bj_LN294_M23, and Kp10Bj_LN54_14). These Myoviruses, belonging to the genera Marfavirus and Jiaodavirus, display broad host range activity against multidrug resistant and hypervirulent K. pneumoniae strains with various capsular serotypes including KL114, KL53, KL8, KL62, KL64, KL124, KL102, KL57, KL39, KL48, KL17, KL20, KL2, KL30, KL51, KL105, KL146, KL28, KL122, KL38, KL3, and KL163. Genomic analysis confirmed the absence of virulence and antimicrobial resistance genes. The phages exhibit rapid adsorption, short latency periods (5-10 min), and high burst sizes (119-2208 PFU/cell). All three phages have significantly biofilm disruption effect in vitro (Kp1Bj_HH11_M23, biofilm disruption rate of 98.46 %, p-value = 0.0170; Kp2Bj_LN294_M23, biofilm disruption rate of 65.56%, p-value < 0.0001; Kp10Bj_LN54_14, biofilm disruption rate of 99.96%, p-value = 0.003). Their stability across a wide range of temperatures and pH further supports their potential for therapeutic development. Together, these data highlight the value of locally sourced phages as candidates for tackling region-specific antimicrobial resistance challenges.

title: Metagenomic insights into carbon and nitrogen cycling functions in an integrated rice-crayfish farming system with straw return.
authors: Wang F; Chen Z; Zhou X; Liu X; Jiang Y; Fang G; Su Y; Rong C; Ji S; Hou G
abstract: Straw return is an important strategy for agricultural residue utilization, and functional microbial communities are known to play a pivotal role in straw decomposition and nutrient cycling. Nevertheless, the decomposition dynamics and associated microbial functional outcomes in rice-aquaculture systems remain poorly documented. This study established a rice-crayfish integrated system with straw return and assessed the mechanisms of straw decomposition and the resulting improvement on soil fertility through soil physicochemical characterization, enzyme activity assays, and metagenomic sequencing. Soil samples were obtained in July (PF7, the rice transplanting stage following the crayfish farming period) and November (PF11, the post-harvest field drying period), with surrounding ditches as controls (CK7 and CK11). The results showed that straw was effectively decomposed, releasing potassium and nitrogen nutrients, while urease and cellulase activities were markedly increased in the paddy field. Metagenomic analysis revealed that Pseudomonadota was the dominant phylum, whereas Euryarchaeota and Nitrososphaerota exhibited the most pronounced changes, with their abundances in PF11 being 0.23-fold and 10.57-fold of those in CK11, respectively. In the C cycle, C degradation was the most abundant pathway, in which amino acid degradation (primarily derived from crayfish farming) dominated, followed by aromatic compound degradation (associated with straw decomposition). For the methane metabolic pathway, the greenhouse gas emission potential was reduced, as evidenced by lower mcrA abundances in PF than in CK. N cycling was primarily mediated through organic N metabolism (81.63-84.14%), with the remaining fraction dominated by nitrification and denitrification. Furthermore, the relevant analysis consistently indicated that C cycling genes occupy more central positions and TN showed a negative effect on these genes. Collectively, this integrated system was associated with straw decomposition, facilitated terminal organic C and N mineralization, while greenhouse gas-related functional potentials were reduced, supporting sustainable straw utilization in rice-crayfish agroecosystems.

title: Compound microbial intelligent membrane fermentation reshapes the bacterial community and reduces antibiotic, metal, and biocide resistance genes and virulence factors in duck litter.
authors: Sun T; Mei G; Li M; Mo J; Zhang C; Ma Y; Zhao J; Peng S; Lin F; Chen JL; Li Z
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Contaminated duck litter is a leading cause of flock disease and a bottleneck for the sustainable development of large-scale dry-rearing systems.

METHODS: We applied shotgun metagenomics to litter from four positions within each of three independent compound microbial intelligent membrane fermentation beds, with unfermented litter from the same three batches as the control. We investigated the bacterial community alongside the abundance of antibiotic, metal and biocide resistance genes (ARGs, MRGs and BRGs) and of virulence factor genes (VFGs).

RESULTS: Fermented litter was consistently enriched in thermophilic and thermotolerant taxa and in beneficial genera such as Paenibacillus and Bacillus, while opportunistic pathogens including Streptococcus, Mycobacterium and Escherichia were clearly reduced. The total burden of the ARG and VFG classes fell in every fermented position, and representative determinants were consistently depleted: floR, qacEdelta1 and sul2 among the ARGs, ruvB among the MRGs, mexF, ideR and sodA among the BRGs, and htpB, clpV and katA among the VFGs. A small number of genes, tet(L), fexA and bacA among them, rose in the most active zones, indicating structural remodeling of the resistance reservoir rather than uniform removal. Fermentation was not spatially uniform: the upper and edge layers were more active, and the center-lower layer remained closest to the unfermented control.

CONCLUSION: Intelligent membrane fermentation reduced the overall abundance of resistance and virulence determinants in the litter microbiome, and spatial uniformity is important for the process. Because these data are DNA-based, they describe the abundance of resistance and virulence determinants and not resistance or virulence phenotypes.

title: Whole-genome characterization and genomic stability of Mastadenovirus F40 and F41 in pediatric gastroenteritis.
authors: El-Shahidy SM; Zakaria AM; Ibrahim MA; Diab AM
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Human adenovirus types 40 and 41 (HAdV-40 and HAdV-41), belonging to the species Mastadenovirus faecale, are among the leading viral causes of acute gastroenteritis in children. Despite their clinical importance, whole-genome data on circulating strains remain limited. This study investigated the epidemiological and genomic characteristics of enteric Mastadenoviruses detected in children with acute gastroenteritis.

METHODS: A total of 632 stool specimens collected from hospitalized children with acute gastroenteritis were screened using a multiplex gastrointestinal real-time PCR panel. Five representative Mastadenovirus-positive samples underwent shotgun metagenomic sequencing followed by genome reconstruction, phylogenetic analysis, pairwise sequence identity comparisons, genome-wide variant analysis, amino acid substitution profiling, and recombination analysis.

RESULTS: Mastadenoviruses were detected in 60/632 (9.5%) children, with the highest positivity observed among those aged 1-3 years. Co-infections occurred predominantly involving bacterial pathogens. Complete or near-complete genomes were recovered for all five sequenced isolates with high sequencing depth (2,806 × -34,120 ×), genome coverage (94.8%-100% at ≥ 10 ×), and nucleotide identity (99.19%-99.78%) relative to genotype-matched reference genomes. Phylogenetic analyses identified two HAdV-F40 and three HAdV-F41 isolates. Gene-specific phylogenies of the hexon, penton base, fiber, and DNA polymerase genes consistently confirmed genotype assignment. Pairwise sequence identity analysis and recombination analysis further supported classification with no evidence of intergenotypic recombination.

CONCLUSIONS: The sequenced enteric Mastadenovirus isolates exhibited high genomic conservation with limited within-genotype diversity and no detectable evidence of recent recombination. The concordance between gene-specific phylogenies, sequence identity analyses, and whole-genome comparisons supports the robustness of current molecular typing approaches and expands the limited genomic data available for circulating HAdV-F40 and HAdV-F41 strains.

title: Scellmate enables contamination aware curation and host mobilome linkage analysis of large SAG datasets.
authors: Wang Y; Xu X; Chen X; Zhang Y; Zheng W; Zhang T
abstract: Single-cell genomics enables cell-resolved insights into in-situ microbial communities, yet single amplified genomes (SAGs) are often fragmented, taxonomically ambiguous, and prone to contamination, limiting their biological interpretation. Here, we present Scellmate, a scalable, semi-supervised framework that integrates whole-SAG curation, species-level taxonomic anchoring and SAG-mobilome linkage analysis for large-scale SAG datasets. Following benchmarking of its SAG curation and SAG-eMGE linkage modules using in silico and four-strain mock SAG datasets, respectively, Scellmate was applied to 11,976 sewage-derived SAGs. This approach yielded 4,198 SAGs passing Scellmate's whole-SAG curation, which captured pronounced heterogeneity masked by bulk methods. At the species level, we resolved extensive hidden diversity within abundant taxa such as Aliarcobacter that was unresolved by matched metagenome-assembled genomes; at the strain level, we pinpointed a distinct Agathobacter rectalis cluster carrying specialized carbon-utilization pathways, suggesting niche differentiation. Leveraging these curated SAGs, we identified 6,474 host-mobilome linkages across 2,378 SAGs; these linkages not only showed high concordance with host-association data within the Integrated Microbial Genomes (IMG) system but also significantly expanded species-level host assignments. Furthermore, we detected frequent inter-species sharing patterns of diverse cryptic plasmids within the order Bacteroidales. Together, this work demonstrates that high-throughput single-cell genomics, empowered by the robust framework, resolves fine-scale heterogeneity and host-mobilome dynamics, advancing culture-independent microbiome research.

title: Temperature effects on life history strategies for rapid growth potential of leaf epiphytic bacteria.
authors: Wang Q; He X; Han B; Shi L; Hu H; Liu F; Nie J; Chen Y; Zhou J; Li Y; Zhao K; Ni K; Zhang L; Jia S; Shao X
abstract: Phyllosphere bacteria, occupying both epiphytic and endophytic habitats, constitute a critical plant-atmosphere interface. However, their community assembly and life-history strategies (LHSs) in response to temperature increase remain poorly understood. Here, we compared leaf phyllosphere bacterial communities with those in other plant compartments across four representative plant species from an alpine meadow on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. By combining observations along an elevational gradient with a controlled warming experiment, we found that temperature was closely associated with the deterministic assembly of leaf phyllosphere bacterial communities. Elevated temperature corresponded to shifts in taxonomic composition, diversity, assembly process, cross-compartment bacterial source, and co-occurrence network. Furthermore, elevated temperature was associated with a shift toward r-strategists in leaf phyllosphere bacterial LHSs, evidenced by higher ribosomal RNA operon (rrn) copy numbers for rapid growth potential and corroborated by genome assemblies of four warming-responsive epiphytic isolates and metagenomic sequencing. Based on 880 public 16S rRNA gene datasets from 45 locations on six continents, we identified a global increase in the rrn copy number in leaf epiphytic bacterial communities across diverse plant species, which was associated with elevated temperatures and enhanced diurnal fluctuation. Finally, we proposed a concept of four LHSs (growth, stress tolerance, competition, and resource acquisition) based on functional inference from 16S rRNA data, supported by the assembled epiphytic bacterial genomes and metagenomes. Collectively, our findings established a trait-based framework for understanding responses of leaf phyllosphere bacteria to future warming.

title: Molecular profiling of repeated self-sampled blood reveals dynamic immune phenotypes in young adults.
authors: Bendes A; Björkander S; Kere MM; Merid SK; Kumar A; Dahl L; Pottinger TD; Yu Z; Gardell A; Vogt A; Kim C; Pan-Hammarström Q; Bergström A; Kull I; Merritt AS; Ekström S; Lövquist A; Murrell B; Roxhed N; Melén E; Schwenk JM
abstract: Although population-based studies of circulating blood proteins have provided profound insight into human biology, transient changes to time-dependent exposures often remain elusive. Here, we perform a longitudinal dried blood spot (DBS) self-sampling study in 808 young adults (aged 24-27, 64% females) from the Swedish Barn [Children], Allergy, Milieu, Stockholm Epidemiology cohort. In total, we collected ~2400 samples from 2020 to 2022. Each sample was profiled for SARS-CoV-2 serological, anti-interferon autoantibodies (AAbs), and 365 inflammation-related proteins. We subsequently linked these samples to registry-confirmed infection and vaccination exposures, physiological traits, genetic variation, and blood counts. We show that data-driven seroclustering captures the response to both infection and vaccination exposures, while stable AAbs against interferon receptors IFNAR1 and IFNGR2 associate with the duration of self-reported COVID-19 symptoms. Genome-wide mapping reveals 664 protein quantitative trait loci (pQTL) across 65 proteins, with cis-pQTLs associated proteins showing greater longitudinal stability. Paired pre- and post-exposure samples indicate temporal changes in protein levels after infection (LAP3) and vaccination (TIMP3). This multi-molecular epidemiological profiling of self-sampled blood captures dynamic immune trajectories and shorter-term variability in a population of young adults.

title: cgMLST typing reproducibility is maintained across diverse whole-genome sequencing workflows in a multi-country HERA2 surveillance pilot.
authors: Cabal Rosel A; Galanopoulos AP; Polemis M; Henczkó J; Pappa O; Karligiotou E; Malliarou M; Chochlakis D; Hyden P; Daza Prieto B; Stöger A; Polzer D; Ungvári E; Tóth Á; Ruppitsch W; Juric D; Ferencak I; Tabain I
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) has become indispensable in infectious disease surveillance, yet its implementation across laboratories remains heterogeneous. Six laboratories from four European countries participated in 2023 in a pilot ring trial as part of the HERA2 project, using a standardized panel of 25 bacterial isolates representing five public health-relevant species. The aim was to assess the comparability and reproducibility of laboratory-specific WGS workflows and to determine whether workflow-related variability affected cgMLST-based interpretations relevant for routine surveillance and outbreak investigations.

METHODS: Participating laboratories applied their established wet-laboratory workflows, including different sample-processing, DNA-extraction and library-preparation methods and sequencing platforms. Illumina sequencing was performed by all laboratories, while Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) sequencing was available in two. To specifically evaluate variability introduced by wet-laboratory procedures, all raw sequencing data were centrally processed using the same bioinformatic pipeline. Reproducibility was primarily assessed using cgMLST allelic distances to the Lab 1 Illumina comparator assembly and concordance of cluster assignments, complemented by analyses of sequencing and assembly variability.

RESULTS: Despite substantial differences in wet-laboratory workflows and technical sequencing characteristics, retained Illumina records showed only small cgMLST allelic differences across laboratories (0-2 alleles) and concordant cluster assignments. Sequencing and assembly metrics varied according to laboratory, species, and technical factors, but this variability did not prevent concordant Illumina-based cluster interpretation among records meeting predefined minimum quality requirements. ONT results were more species-dependent, and several records, particularly for Salmonella enterica, did not achieve the required cgMLST target completeness. These ONT findings should be interpreted in the context of the technology available at the time of the 2023 ring trial.

CONCLUSIONS: Our results suggest that complete standardization of wet-laboratory workflows may not be required to achieve comparable Illumina-based cgMLST results across laboratories. Rather, laboratories may retain validated local workflows provided that the resulting sequencing data meet appropriate minimum quality requirements. This supports a pragmatic approach to multi-laboratory genomic surveillance that prioritizes data quality and fitness-for-purpose over uniformity of individual wet-laboratory procedures.

title: The microbiome of draught no- and low-alcohol beer.
authors: Roselli GE; Smart KA; Crow M; Powell CD
abstract: The microbiological ecosystem of commercially available draught dispensed no- and low-alcohol beers was evaluated, with a focus on identifying predominant microorganisms with spoilage potential and characterizing variation in community structure. More than 50 samples, representing 20 no- and low- alcohol beers (7 different beer styles: lager, India pale ale, pale ale, wheat, radler, pilsner and amber ale; and 17 brands) were collected for analysis across 12 different public houses (accounts) in Nottingham, UK. Bacterial and fungal identification was achieved via third generation sequencing technologies, using amplicon-based nanopore sequencing (Oxford Nanopore Technologies). Analysis of samples indicated that species of Acetobacter, Brettanomyces and Saccharomyces were core microbiome members. The account from which a beer was sampled was shown to harbor distinct microbial communities and was the dominant factor in determining microbial community structure, explaining 72.6% of variation. This is the first study to apply third-generation sequencing technology for the analysis of draught no- and low-alcohol beers. The findings underscore the vulnerability of draught products to microbial spoilage, and highlight the importance of implementing strict hygiene control focused on draught lines, taps, keg couplers and nozzles, especially when dispensing microbiologically sensitive no- and low-alcohol beverages.

title: Absolute quantification and profiling of cellular tRNAs by nanopore sequencing and a deep learning classifier.
authors: Ueda H; Maeda M; Okada S; Noguchi R; Dasgupta B; Yamamoto R; Furuta M; Nishi A; Nagao A; Sakaguchi Y; Miyauchi K; Suzuki T
abstract: Transfer RNAs (tRNAs) link mRNA codons to amino acids during translation. Their abundance and modification states are dynamically regulated and influence translation efficiency, mRNA stability, and proteostasis. Accurate profiling of tRNAs is essential, but deep sequencing suffers from modification-induced biases during cDNA synthesis, while nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) still faces challenges in accurate tRNA profiling. Here, we develop an end-to-end deep learning model, termed nano tRNA classifier, that directly uses nanopore-DRS ionic current signals to classify tRNAs without basecalling. The model achieves 98.2% classification accuracy with high read retention across all Escherichia coli tRNA species. Using an equimolar mixture of native tRNAs as a ground-truth reference, we correct read-count bias, enabling absolute quantification and profiling under diverse culture conditions. We further develop binary classifiers that detect specific tRNA modifications at the single-molecule level with high accuracy. This nanopore-based platform integrates accurate tRNA classification, absolute quantification, and single-molecule modification detection.

title: Genomic and phenotypic assessment of functional and safety properties of Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus PMK4 isolated from Cameroonian infant faeces.
authors: Djodjeu Kamega LC; Foko Kouam EM; Tchabou Tientcheu ML; Hall LJ; Kaktcham PM
abstract: The gut microbiota is a complex community of microorganisms that plays a crucial role in maintaining short- and long-term health. However, a perturbed microbial ecosystem is associated with a range of diseases, including increased risk of infections. Probiotic-based strategies may help restore microbiome function, but candidate strains require robust functional and safety evaluation. Here, we performed integrated genomic and phenotypic characterisation of beneficial properties of Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus PMK4, isolated from the stool of a healthy Cameroonian infant. Whole-genome sequencing and comparative pangenomic analysis against 13 L. rhamnosus genomes were used to infer functional potential, with in silico safety screening conducted using ResFinder, CARD and VFDB. Beneficial-relevant phenotypes were assessed through tolerance to simulated gastrointestinal conditions, adhesion-associated traits (hydrophobicity, aggregation), antimicrobial activity, nutrients utilisation profiling and safety-related assays. The L. rhamnosus PMK4 genome (2,935,039 bp), contains strain-specific loci predicted to support acid stress tolerance and epithelial adhesion. Functional annotation indicated the presence of genetic potential for carbohydrate metabolism, stress response, adhesion-related functions, and biosynthesis of secondary metabolites including acids, terpenes and vitamins. No acquired antibiotic resistance determinants or virulence genes were detected. Consistent with genomic predictions, PMK4 showed high survival under simulated gastrointestinal conditions, strong auto-aggregation capacity, moderate hydrophobicity and co-aggregation, and broad antagonistic activity against a range of enteropathogens. The strain also utilised a wide range of substrates, including complex carbohydrates and proteins, suggesting metabolic versatility relevant to microbe-microbe and microbe-host interactions in the gut. Together, these data support L. rhamnosus PMK4 as a promising indigenous probiotic candidate with a favourable safety profile and functional potential.

title: A core genome multilocus sequence typing scheme for Bacteroides fragilis: insights into population structure and genomic epidemiology.
authors: Delvallez G; Diancourt L; Criscuolo A; Amara M; Brisse S; Dupuy B; Guglielmini J
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Bacteroides fragilis strains are important members of the human gut microbiota and represent major opportunistic pathogens responsible for a wide range of anaerobic infections. Their clinical relevance is reinforced by diverse antimicrobial resistance mechanisms and a complex population structure comprising two major phylogenetic lineages, Division I and Division II. Although whole-genome sequencing is increasingly used for bacterial surveillance, no standardized core genome multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST) scheme is available for B. fragilis, limiting high-resolution and comparable genomic analyses. In this study, we developed a cgMLST scheme comprising 2,342 highly conserved loci applicable across both Divisions. The scheme was developed from 433 publicly available genomes with diverse geographic origins, sample types, and isolation periods. It was subsequently evaluated using 118 newly sequenced infection-associated isolates from France not included in scheme development. Clustering analysis identified an accurate single-linkage threshold of 400 allelic mismatches, providing balanced resolution for population structure analyses and high concordance with core genome phylogeny and classical MLST sequence types. Well-defined clusters were identified within both Divisions, with genetic profiles indicative of long-standing evolutionary divergence. These clusters showed no clear association with geographic origin, isolation source, or sampling period. Notably, some clusters were enriched in nim-positive and multidrug-resistant (MDR) isolates, including one in particular that emerged as a genetically divergent MDR-associated lineage within Division II. This cgMLST scheme provides a standardized and high-resolution framework for B. fragilis genotyping. Its implementation in the publicly accessible BIGSdb-Pasteur platform (https://bigsdb.pasteur.fr/) will support global genomic surveillance and future epidemiological studies.

IMPORTANCE: Bacteroides fragilis strains hold a position of relevance within the human gut microbiota, as they represent a major cause of severe anaerobic infections. Defining genotypes is essential for tracking infections and monitoring the emergence and spread of antimicrobial resistance. In this study, we developed a core genome multilocus sequence typing scheme for B. fragilis and applied it to a large collection of isolates from diverse origins. Our results reveal a structured population with well-defined and genetically conserved clusters across both Divisions, consistent with a long-standing population structure. Notably, several clusters were enriched in antimicrobial resistance determinants and multidrug-resistant isolates. This study also provides an easy-to-use resource for global surveillance and future epidemiological investigations of this clinically important pathogen.

title: Engineered DNA materials shape microbial physiology and ecological selection
authors: Meisch, L.; Velaz Martin, M.; Moench, S. A.; Weigel, S.; Vollmers, J.; Jaeger, P. S.; Kaster, A.-K.; Rabe, K. S.; Niemeyer, C. M.
abstract: Extracellular DNA (eDNA) is both a structural component of microbial biofilms and a potential reservoir of genetic information, yet its role as an ecological material remains largely unexplored. Here we establish engineered extracellular materials as determinants of microbial physiology and community assembly across increasing biological complexity. A three-dimensional DNA hydrogel altered bacterial stress-associated responses, elicited species-dependent phenotypes and transcriptional changes in a defined consortium, and shaped community succession in wastewater-derived microbiomes. Distinct responses to surface-bound oligonucleotides reveal that DNA presentation matters beyond its mere presence. Strikingly, metagenomic sequencing identified rare, hydrogel-specific candidate junctions linking material-derived DNA to microbial genomic sequences, suggesting a previously unexplored interface between extracellular DNA materials and microbial genetic information. These findings reveal a dual role for engineered DNA: its material organization shapes microbial physiology and ecological selection, while its encoded sequences may engage with microbial genomic processes.

title: Glycine-Proline driven flexibility and interface-dependent conservation of six-residue {Omega}-loops in protein complexes
authors: Tajane, S. V.; Pohane, S.; Dey, S.
abstract: {Omega}-loops are six- to sixteen-residue, non-regular structural motifs that occur in protein structures, connecting regular regions and forming a well-defined, ordered structural segment. They are functionally important because of their strategic location on the protein surface, where they are often associated with molecular recognition, ligand binding, and catalytic activity. Their non-regular nature enables them to adopt different conformations, which makes them important in protein dynamics and allosteric communication. In this work, we have curated six-residue {Omega}-loops from diverse protein-protein complexes of varying stability and found them to be abundant across all. We identified 1205 hydrogen-bonded and 6518 non-hydrogen-bonded {Omega}-loops, leading to an average of ~1.7 {Omega}-loops per structure. Glycine and proline were the most enriched residues in the loop, with proline preferentially positioned at the fourth position and glycine distributed across multiple positions, supporting their roles in chain reversal and conformational flexibility. Using ProteinMPNN-based sequence-design modelling and Rate4Site evolutionary-rate analysis, we show that {Omega}-loops occupy a relatively constrained sequence space, with interface loops in obligate homodimers and heterodimers more conserved than non-interface loops; the opposite trend was observed in transient and crystal dimers. Mapping known pathogenic and benign mutations onto the {Omega}-loop present in human proteins, together with a case study of the TEM1 {beta}-lactamase {Omega}-loop, further illustrates how small sequence changes within these loops can produce crucial structural and functional consequences, leading to altered enzyme activity and antibiotic resistance. Altogether, we report that {Omega}-loops are not merely connectors of secondary structure but are structurally constrained, evolutionarily significant elements that contribute to protein folding, stability and function.

title: Genomes of Solenogastres Shed Light on Ancestral Molluscan Biomineralization Genes
authors: Yap-Chiongco, M.; Kocot, K. M.
abstract: Aplacophora (Solenogastres + Caudofoveata) is a group of worm-like molluscs that lack a shell and instead are covered with aragonitic spines and scales called sclerites. Sclerites are also found along the girdle in chitons (Polyplacophora) and are a synapomorphy for Aculifera (Aplacophora + Polyplacophora), which is the sister taxon of all other shell-bearing molluscs (Conchifera). However, whether the same genetic mechanism underlies the process of biomineralization in aculiferans and conchiferans is unknown. To investigate evolution of genes involved in biomineralization across Mollusca, we re-sequenced the genomes of two species of Solenogastres, Epimenia babai and Neomenia megatrapezata, producing near-chromosome-level assemblies through PacBio HiFi and Hi-C scaffolding. Using a combination of orthology inference and similarity searches against a known SMP database we identified 1,244 putative SMP orthogroups across Mollusca, 292 of which were present in at least one solenogaster genome. SMPs undergoing significant expansion/contraction at key nodes were further investigated. Of these, 15 were found in at least one solenogaster genome and included families containing chitin-binding, von Willebrand factor A, and C-type lectin domains. Across Mollusca, Solenogastres showed the highest number of significant losses in all gene families, including the SMPs investigated. Targeted searches for structural, silk-like proteins in Aculifera show further reductions in Solenogastres (16-17) compared to caudofoveates (29) and chitons (46-80). Altogether, our results support a conserved but reduced biomineralization toolkit underlying sclerite formation in Solenogastres and identify candidate genes for further proteomic and functional study.

title: Reversible decrease in swimming motility accompanies emergent β-lactam antibiotic resistance in Escherichia coli
authors: Stabryla, L.; Ackerman, W.; Dootz, J. N.; Servetas, S. L.; Jackson, S. A.; Kralj, J. G.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) threatens global health, food security, and development; however, the evolutionary and molecular pathways that drive AMR remain poorly understood, limiting our ability to advance diagnostics and rapidly detect newly emerging resistance. In this report, we employed laboratory evolution of an environmental Escherichia coli strain (NIST 0056) under B-lactam antibiotic pressure (ampicillin and cephalexin) to specifically investigate the relationship between resistance genotype and motility phenotype. Within 10 passages, populations evolved varying levels of B-lactam resistance (including high-level resistance > 32 ug/mL) and showed consistent, dose-dependent reductions in swimming motility. Whole-population genome sequencing revealed large deletions in marR, SNPs in efflux pump gene acrB and fumarate reductase gene frdD, and mutations with evidence of amplification in the chromosomal class C B-lactamase gene ampC, collectively linking these efflux-mediated, B-lactam resistance mechanisms to loss of motility. Notably, motility reductions were more pronounced in individual clones than in the mixed populations (p < 0.005, Mann-Whitney; two-tailed test). Following removal of antibiotic pressure, motility was restored and AMR-associated mutations decreased in frequency, suggesting fitness costs associated with resistance. In aggregate, our results demonstrate that reduced swimming motility accompanies specific efflux-driven, B-lactam resistance mechanisms. Further work will investigate if the behavior is generalizable across flagellated Enterobacteriaceae. Because these rapid changes are amenable to high-throughput measurement, swimming motility may offer a tractable physiological metric for AMR detection in environmental surveillance.

title: Integrated genotyping, annotation and epigenetic characterization of transposable elements with GraffiTE
authors: Goubert, C.; Laflamme, R.; Eveleigh, R.; Ragoussis, I.; Wheeler, T.; Lettre, G.; Bourque, G.; Groza, C.
abstract: Genotyping, annotating and characterizing TE variation leaped forward with long-read sequencing (LRS) and de novo assembly. LRS techniques also reveal CpG methylation, which enables measuring the impact of TEs on epigenomes and sheds light on the role of TEs as regulatory sequences. Yet, TE genotyping tools discard the valuable allele-specific epigenetic information. We introduce GraffiTE v1.1, the first Nextflow pipeline that genotypes SVs, annotates polymorphic mobile elements (MEI), and maps epigenetic data to TEs using pangenome graphs in one command. GraffiTE v1.1 is designed to map any epigenetic information that is based on LRS stencils, including Fiber-seq. We demonstrate the capabilities of GraffiTE v1.1 by analyzing genomes and methylomes obtained from 20 Quebec residents of French-Canadian descent. In these genomes, TE annotation yields 4,908 Alu, 704 LINE1, 112 SVA and 21 HERVK (HML-2) distinct polymorphic mobile elements (MEIs). We also identify 10 fixed HERVK insertions that vary between solo LTR and provirus, or in proviral copy number. We determine that these MEIs contribute 144,748 additional CpGs not present in the reference. From this, we identify 480 Alus, 67 LINE1s, 12 SVAs and 2 HERVKs in hypomethylated states. We note that Alus and SVAs are more methylated than other LINE1 and HERVK. Lastly, MEIs dating reported a mean of age 1.08 Mya (median: 640 kya) and beta regression identified a moderate demethylating effect of age on MEIs (effect: -0.069 log-odds per log10 years, P < 6.08 x 10-19). Our results show that the methylation level of a LINE1 MEI is expected to decrease from 86.4% to 80.8% in the first Mya. In conclusion, GraffiTE v1.1 genotypes SVs, annotates MEI, and characterizes their epigenetic state at the scale of populations by leveraging the full potential of LRS. While we showcase its application in human data, the pipeline can be deployed in any model for which a TE library is available.

title: Interconnected reservoirs of multidrug-resistant bacteria and plasmids within hospital plumbing infrastructure
authors: Annavajhala, M. K.; Hokunson, T. W.; Terzoglou, K.; Uhlemann, A.-C.; Gomez-Simmonds, A.
abstract: Hospital sinks and wastewater streams are hotspots for contamination and colonization with multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria (MDR-GNB). While hospital water systems may facilitate MDR-GNB transmission during outbreaks, longitudinal population dynamics of environmental MDR-GNB and their long-term relationship with patient isolates remain unclear. Here we aimed to characterize the diversity and abundance of MDR-GNB within the hospital built environment and evaluate their relationship with clinical isolates. We performed nanopore sequencing on MDR-GNB cultured from sink drains (n=523) and wastewater (n=146) at a New York City hospital between March-August 2023. We assessed spatial and longitudinal genomic strain and plasmid dynamics and quantified relatedness to historical clinical isolates from the same hospital (n=602). Sink drains (54-73%) and wastewater (100%) demonstrated widespread, longitudinal colonization with MDR-GNB, driven primarily by carbapenem-resistant GNB including opportunistic organisms and Enterobacterales encoding blaKPC. While bacterial colonization differed across environmental niches, we identified both MDR-GNB strains and resistance plasmids that were shared between clinical and environmental sources, as well a distinct interplay between clinical and wastewater versus sink drain samples. This study supports the role of hospital plumbing as an important reservoir for clinically relevant MDR-GNB, but highlights differences across environmental sources, which may impact surveillance approaches.

title: Hybrid RY-mers increase aDNA alignment sensitivity
authors: Tolstoganov, I.; Sahlin, K.
abstract: One of the key steps in ancient DNA data analysis is the accurate identification of endogenous short reads that originate from the ancient genome. Currently, this step is performed using general-purpose sequence aligners, such as BWA-aln, with parameter settings optimized for sensitivity. This approach results in increased runtime, even relative to standard DNA alignment workflows, and is not sufficient for aligning samples that are highly divergent from a reference database. We introduce hybrid RY-mers, a seed construct designed to incorporate aDNA-specific sequence damage. We adapt hybrid RY-mers to the existing concept of multi-context seeds and implement them in the read aligner strobealign. On simulated genomic and metagenomic datasets, we show that hybrid RY-mers result in higher mapping accuracy, while also reducing runtime by 4-6 times compared to the state-of-the-art aDNA alignment method BWA-aln. Furthermore, substituting aDNA aligner MALT in the metagenomic tool-suite aMeta with our new alignment approach demonstrated that aMeta gave a faster and less memory consuming detection of ancient taxa present in the samples.

title: Metagenomic Insights into the Fecal Microbiome, Resistome, and Mobilome of Beef Cattle in Cow-Calf Operations in Florida, United States
authors: Ali, A.; K. Edison, L.; Bittar, J. H. J.; Denagamage, T.; Lee, A. C. Y.; Jeong, K. C.; Hernandez, J. A.; Kariyawasam, S.
