abstract: Food-producing animals are a focus of One Health approaches to antimicrobial resistance (AMR) as reservoirs of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria (ARB) and antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs). We hypothesized that microbial composition, ARGs profiles, and mobile genetic element (MGE) profiles would differ by operation size and animal age group. Fecal samples from 162 cows and calves were combined into 54 composite samples, each comprising three animals of the same age group. Across operation sizes, Bacillota (51.4-64.9%), Bacteroidota (12.0-17.3%), Pseudomonadota (10.3-16.5%), and Actinomycetota (3.3-10.9%) were predominant phyla. Alpha diversity did not differ among operation sizes; however, cows exhibited greater observed richness, Shannon diversity, and Simpson diversity than calves (all P < 0.001). Microbial composition did not differ significantly among operation sizes (PERMANOVA, R{superscript 2} = 0.065, P = 0.609) but differed significantly between cows and calves (R{superscript 2} = 0.200, P < 0.001). Seventy-five ARGs representing 14 resistance classes were identified. Normalized ARG hit rates were higher in small operations (0.444) than in medium (0.278) and large operations (0.222; P = 0.088), whereas calves exhibited a higher estimated marginal mean normalized ARG hit rate than cows (0.383 vs. 0.247 hits/million reads; P < 0.001). Of 1,054 curated ARG hits, 23.9% occurred on predicted plasmid contigs, 0.9% on predicted viral contigs, and 7.1% on contigs containing insertion sequences. Overall findings demonstrate differences in fecal microbiome diversity and ARG abundance between cows and calves and indicate that predicted plasmids are associated with a notable proportion of ARG hits in Florida beef cow-calf operations.

title: MitoScope: a comprehensive mitochondrial genome analysis workflow for long-read sequencing data
authors: Zakarian, C.; Smith, J. D.; Wong, C. H.; Frazar, C. D.; Ryke, E.; McGee, S. R.; Richardson, M.; Weiss, J. M.; Munson, K. M.; Hoekzema, K.; Mack, T.; Kwon, Y.; Ou, J.; Neph, S. J.; Sohn, M.-H.; Minkina, A.; Bennett, J. T.; Stergachis, A. B.; Eichler, E. E.; Wei, C.-L.
abstract: The mitochondrial genome (mtDNA), rich in repeats and prone to nuclear mitochondrial DNA segments (NUMTs), is implicated in cancer, metabolic syndromes, and neurodegeneration, yet short-read sequencing yields incomplete catalogs, mapping artifacts, and false heteroplasmies. We introduce MitoScope, a scalable end-to-end long-read mitochondrial analysis workflow that integrates mtDNA-read selection, heteroplasmic variant detection, assembly, copy number estimation, read-level haplotyping, and NUMT profiling. Applied to benchmarking data from the Somatic Mosaicism Across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network, we reveal high sensitivity and precision compared to existing methods and successfully uncover known mitochondrial biology relevant for variant interpretation, aging, and human disease.

title: A Y-specific translocated gsdf copy is a candidate master sex-determining gene in common dab (Limanda limanda)
authors: Edvardsen, R. B.; Barvik, M.; Furmanek, T.; Perrichon, P.; Rubin, C.-J.
abstract: Sex-determining systems in flatfishes are highly diverse, and even closely related species can differ in both sex-determining loci and heterogametic systems. In common dab (Limanda limanda), the genetic basis of sex determination has not yet been established. Here, we investigated sex determination using pooled whole-genome sequencing combined with long-read genome sequencing of females and males from Iceland and Norway. Genome-wide allele-frequency analyses identified sex-associated regions consistent with male heterogamety (XX/XY), with the strongest signal on chromosome 16. Comparison of the existing reference assembly, which represents an X haplotype at this locus, with a haplotype-resolved male PacBio HiFi assembly revealed a [~]21.5 kb Y-specific insertion on chromosome 16. The insertion showed complete coverage in male pools but little or no coverage in female pools from either population. It contained a translocated genomic segment including a copy of gonadal soma-derived factor (gsdf) and a predicted gene of unknown function. Comparative genomic analyses were consistent with this segment originating from an autosomal gsdf-containing region on chromosome 1. Given the recurrent recruitment of gsdf as a sex-determining factor in teleosts, we designate the Y-linked copy gsdfY and identify it as the strongest candidate for the master sex-determining gene in common dab. Additional broad sex-associated differentiation on chromosome 19 was restricted to the Icelandic samples and may reflect population-specific expansion of the sex-linked region, although its structural basis remains unresolved. Together, these findings provide the first genomic characterization of sex determination in common dab and demonstrate how gene duplication and translocation can contribute to the evolution of novel sex-determining systems in flatfishes.

title: Contig-Resolved Genetic Context of Antimicrobial Resistome in Sediments of Two Contrasting Wastewater-Impacted Rivers
authors: Kashyap, A.; Sonkar, V.; Nambi, I. M.; Thatikonda, S.
abstract: River sediments harbor diverse antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinants; however, gene abundance alone provides limited insight into their genomic context, mobility potential, and associated bacterial hosts. This study employed an assembly- and read-mapping metagenomic framework to surface-sediment metagenomes (40.78 Gb clean data) from two contrasting wastewater-impacted Indian rivers, Adyar (Chennai) and Musi (Hyderabad), retaining sample-, contig- and open reading frame level provenance. ARG-carrying contigs (ACCs; n = 2,402) were annotated for mobile genetic elements (MGEs), biocide/metal resistance genes (BMRGs), virulence factor genes (VFGs), nitrogen-cycling genes (NCycGs), and putative host taxonomy. The resistomes exhibited substantial diversity (264 ARG subtypes) and spatial heterogeneity, with subtype richness in the Adyar (up to 171 subtypes) than in the Musi, where richness progressively declined downstream. Rank IV determinants dominated ARG abundance (77.82%), whereas Rank I determinants accounted for only 9.89%. MGEs were detected on just 3.12% (75/2,402) of ACCs, predominantly comprising plasmid-like contigs and proximal ARG-MGE associations. Co-occurrence with BMRGs was observed on 386 ACCs, whereas VFGs were uncommon (26 ACCs) and primarily represented dual-annotated efflux and envelope-integrity determinants rather than independent virulence loci. NCyc annotations were sparse (12 ACCs), with no evidence of complete nitrification or denitrification pathways. Taxonomic classification resolved 217 ACCs to the species level, with no matches to curated human pathogenic bacteria. Only two Acinetobacter-assigned ACCs exhibited both genus-level pathogenicity and mobility evidence. These findings highlight the importance of integrating mobility and host-taxonomic information to distinguish baseline environmental resistance from potential priorities for AMR surveillance.

title: Batch, Prefetch, Skip, Orient, Squeeze: Faster, Smaller k-mer dictionaries via the Spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform
authors: Diseth, A. C.; Alanko, J. N.; Mackenzie, J.; Puglisi, S. J.
abstract: Looking up k-mers in an index is a core operation in genomics, underlying read mapping, metagenomic classification, and many other tasks. Queries are often streaming: the k-mers come from a longer sequence such as a sequencing read, and consecutive k-mers overlap. The fastest index for such queries is currently the hashing-based SSHash; indexes based on the spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform (SBWT) are competitive in space but slower. We show how to make SBWT indexes both faster and smaller. First, we process queries in small batches and prefetch the memory each will need next, hiding the latency of the dependent random accesses that dominate a lookup; together with a new rank structure that reads one cache line per query, this makes k-mer lookups about seven times faster than unbatched SBWT search. Second, we extend batching to streaming search and show that one failed lookup can rule out many k-mers of a read at once, which removes the need for the longest common suffix array. Third, we build an SBWT that stores only one orientation of each k-mer, thereby halving its size, with a modified search that exploits how rarely the orientation changes along a read. Finally, we adapt a compact subset rank structure to batched search. On the collections of the SSHash benchmark, and on two collections up to 15 times larger, our fastest index answers streaming queries for 31-mers faster than SSHash on every read set, by up to 4.9 times, using 12 bits per canonical k-mer against SSHash's 7.4-11.1. We also show that a 6.1-bit index is still faster than SSHash on most read sets, and that our smallest index needs about 4 bits per canonical k-mer. Unlike that of SSHash, the space of our indexes barely varies across collections. Our code is available at https://github.com/anadis504/sbwt-squeeze-rs.

title: Gene-resolved metagenomics reveals partitioned nitrogen transformation potential in a landfill leachate sequencing batch reactor microbiome
authors: Rattray, S.; Blake, L.; Ingrey, N.; MacArthur, I.
abstract: Landfill leachate can contain high concentrations of ammonia and organic nitrogen requiring treatment before discharge. Sequencing batch reactors (SBRs) promote biological nitrogen removal through alternating aerobic and anoxic conditions, but taxonomic profiling alone cannot resolve how nitrogen transformation and competing retention pathways are distributed across microbial communities. This study applied gene-resolved metagenomics to a sludge sample collected from a UK landfill leachate SBR. Nitrogen-metabolism genes were linked to contig-level taxonomic assignments and metagenome-assembled genome bins to examine nitrification, denitrification, dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA), and assimilatory nitrate reduction (ANR). Nitrogen-transformation potential was partitioned across dominant and minor taxa. Nitrospirota and Pseudomonadota were the most abundant classified phyla, whereas Actinomycetota represented only 4% of the community but included Actinomycetes, which showed the highest within-taxon proportion of nitrogen metabolism associated genes. amoABC was assigned only to Nitrosomonas and Nitrososphaerota, whereas denitrification genes were more widely distributed but frequently occurred as partial pathways. nosZ was detected only in the minor phyla Chloroflexota, Acidobacteriota and Myxococcota. DNRA and ANR-associated genes occurred across multiple lineages; nirA in Nitrospira and DNRA-associated nirBD elsewhere within Nitrospirota suggested nitrifier-associated lineages may also encode nitrogen retention potential. Gene-resolved metagenomics identified candidate low-abundance contributors, restricted distributions of genes associated with ammonia oxidation and nitrous oxide reduction, and nitrogen-retention potential not apparent from taxonomic composition alone. Because the study examined DNA-level potential in a single sludge sample, expression, reactor chemistry and longitudinal data are needed to establish pathway activity and operational relevance.

title: Northern palsa and peat ecosystem microbiomes are potentially supported by hydrogen and carbon monoxide metabolism
authors: Tuomela, N.; Thomas, D. N.; Kaartokallio, H.; Välikangas, T.; Hultman, J.
abstract: Northern peatland and permafrost ecosystems are facing rapid changes, with increasing temperatures, permafrost thaw and shifts in hydrology. Characterizing microbial communities and metabolic potential from the soils and associated water bodies is crucial to understanding the changes in biogeochemical cycling in these ecosystems. For this, samples were collected and sequenced from subarctic palsa and peat soils, along with samples from associated thaw ponds and streams. Metagenomics was utilized in describing the microbiome and its metabolic potential in these environments. Palsa soils hosted microbial communities that were distinct from the peatland soils, ponds and stream waters. Soils and their adjacent ponds shared taxa, and peat soils and ponds also shared taxa with the streams, unlike palsa soils which were likely more hydrologically isolated. Based on metabolic marker gene ratio for denitrification [(nirS+nirK)/nosZ], palsa soils had the strongest potential to be a source of nitrous oxide (N2O) out of all the sample types. Marker genes for hydrogen gas (H2) and carbon monoxide (CO) utilization were abundant across soil environments and metagenome assembled genomes, suggesting that trace gas oxidation is likely one of the key energy sources for microbiomes. In the palsa ponds and peat soils pmoA, marker gene for methanotrophy, was the most abundant compared to the other sample types.

title: Women's health outreach using a rapid and fieldable Nanopore-based microbiome profiling workflow.
authors: Boden, S.; Waldekker, C.; Kaijen - Lambers, M. E. H.; van den Braak, N. P. W. C. J.; Brackel, D. C. J.; Wijnstroom-de Quartel, L.; Pinheiro-Keulers, L.; Klaassens, E. S.; de Bot, C. M. A.; van Gestel, M. A.; Schrauwen, E. J. A.
abstract: Background In recent years, scientific interest in the vaginal microbiome has increased due to its impact on women's health. Colonization of the Lactobacillus species in the vagina may contribute to protection against vaginal infectious diseases. In order to create public awareness regarding vaginal health and to provide insights into the vaginal microbiome, a rapid field microbiome analysis using Nanopore sequencing was evaluated at Lowlands, a three-day music festival in the Netherlands. This study aimed not only to evaluate a rapid sequencing workflow, but also to explore citizen science as a tool for health promotion and public engagement in women's health. Methods The workflow at Lowlands contained the following steps; (i) Dialogue concerning vaginal health, with invitation to participate. (ii) Informed consent and questionnaire to investigate knowledge on vaginal health, life-style and contraceptive usage; (iii) self-collection of a vaginal swab; (iv) DNA isolation using QuickExtract DNA extraction solution; (v) Ultrafast amplification of the 16S rRNA gene using NextGenPCR thermal cycling using 16S Barcoding kit 24 V14; (vi) Library preparation and sequencing was performed according to the manufacturers protocol using R10 chemistry; (vii) For data-analysis, MABA16S was used, with slight modifications. This workflow was established within 4 hours and results were communicated with interested participants.

title: EMtrace: offline nanopore metagenomics on a laptop for rapid viral diagnostics, genome recovery and 16S profiling
authors: Weinstein, I.; Smura, T.; Leppanen, O.; Krupinska, M.; Vauhkonen, H.; Sironen, T.; Grzybek, M.; Vapalahti, O.; Kant, R.
abstract: Nanopore sequencers produce reads within minutes, but metagenomic analysis remains challenging where internet access is limited, data are sensitive or computing resources are modest. EMtrace is an offline pipeline that runs on a laptop during sequencing: it classifies MinKNOW reads, estimates taxon abundance by expectation-maximization (EM) and assembles reference-based consensus genomes. We benchmarked it against five virome and four 16S rRNA tools on simulated, mock-community and clinical data. On field isolates and 16 SARS-CoV-2 clinical samples, EMtrace had the highest species-level F1 score (1.00 and 0.97) and one false-positive species, against 3-7 for the comparators. It recovered divergent viruses as completely as ViMOP, and low-titre field libraries more completely, at [≥]99.7% identity. In replayed runs, it identified the target virus in the first 4,000-read batch (5-13 min). With a shared 16S reference, EMtrace reported two to three times fewer false-positive species than Emu.

title: A chromosome-level, haplotype-resolved genome assembly of the impressed tortoise, Manouria impressa
authors: Wang, J.; Li, Q.
abstract: Background. The impressed tortoise, Manouria impressa (Gunther, 1882), is an Endangered, largely fungivorous tortoise of the montane forests of Southeast Asia and one of the two living species of the basal testudinid genus Manouria. It is one of the least-studied tortoises, and no chromosome-level genome was available for the genus. Findings. From 68.5 Gb of PacBio HiFi reads (28x), 9.8 Gb of Hi-C read pairs and RNA-seq of heart and lung from a single female, we assembled a 2.42 Gb primary assembly with a contig N50 of 86.9 Mb and a scaffold N50 of 138.6 Mb. Hi-C scaffolding followed by quantitative curation -- every scaffold join scored against the within-contig contact-decay expectation -- placed 94.5 % of the sequence in 26 chromosomes, matching the testudinid karyotype (2n = 52); the remaining 335 scaffolds are unplaced. Consensus accuracy is QV 67.9 (Merqury), k-mer completeness 95.1 %, and 99.3 % of vertebrate BUSCO genes are complete. Two phased haplotype assemblies (scaffold N50 87.8 and 91.6 Mb; QV 69.1 and 68.5; 99.2 % combined k-mer completeness) and the 18.1-kb mitochondrial genome were assembled from the same data. Repeats mask 48.6 % of the genome (LINEs 11.5 %, LTR retrotransposons 10.0 %, DNA transposons 7.6 %, SINEs 2.6 %, unclassified families 15.4 %); 24,875 protein-coding genes were predicted from RNA-seq and OrthoDB protein evidence (97.6 % complete vertebrate BUSCOs), 89.0 % of them functionally annotated. Conclusions. This haplotype-resolved reference, with its curation evidence and scripts, provides the first chromosome-level genomic resource for Manouria and a foundation for conservation genomics and for studies of the dietary specialisation of this fungivorous tortoise.

title: DNA-MGC+: A versatile codec for reliable and resource-efficient data storage on synthetic DNA
authors: Khabbaz, R.; Mateos, J.; Antonini, M.; Kas Hanna, S.
abstract: The biochemical processes underlying DNA data storage, including synthesis, amplification, and sequencing, are inherently noisy, leading to insertion, deletion, and substitution errors as well as sequence dropouts that challenge reliable data retrieval. Here we introduce DNA-MGC+, a DNA storage codec designed for reliable and resource-efficient retrieval under diverse operating conditions. We evaluate DNA-MGC+ across various in silico and in vitro settings. In comparison with selected representative codecs, the results show that DNA-MGC+ consistently improves key performance metrics under explicit reliability constraints, including required sequencing depth, read cost, decoding time, storage density, and error-correction capability. In silico experiments show that DNA-MGC+ supports reliable decoding at error rates up to 24% for a 15-KB file, while separate scalability experiments demonstrate reliable decoding of files up to 200 MB at a 5% error rate. In vitro experiments involving a 24-KB file and electrochemical synthesis show that different DNA-MGC+ configurations achieve minimum sequencing depths below 3x and read costs below 3.5 nts/bit under both Illumina and Nanopore sequencing.

title: Skiver: Reference-free quality control of metagenomic sequencing datasets using (k,v)-mer sketches
authors: Gu, Z.; Sharma, P.; Wong, L.; Nagarajan, N.
abstract: Quality control is essential in numerous Bioinformatics pipelines, yet existing approaches often depend on inefficient mapping to reference genomes or potentially uncalibrated quality scores. We present skiver, a reference-free, alignment-free quality control tool that uses (k, v)-mer sketches. By deriving consensus from sketched (k, v)-mers, skiver estimates survival and hazard rates that capture the positional distribution of errors. Across simulated and real datasets from multiple sequencing platforms, skiver accurately estimates overall error rates, error-type proportions, and quality-score calibration. An iterative outlier-filtering strategy enables robust performance on complex datasets with multiple strains, alleles, and repetitive regions.

title: RICO enables integrated analysis of ribosomal DNA copy number and methylation from nanopore long-read sequencing
authors: Yuen, Z. W. S.; Leeder, N.; Udumanne, T.; Garvie, A.; Wong, L.; Weiss, E.; van Loon, L.; Ganley, A.; Hannan, R.; Eyras, E.; Hein, N.
abstract: Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) provides the structural and catalytic core of ribosomes and is encoded by ribosomal RNA genes (rDNA) arranged in tandem repeat arrays. rDNA copy number (CN) is highly dynamic, representing a clinically relevant form of structural variation, but its accurate quantification has been challenging due to its highly repetitive and GC-rich nature. Here, we present RICO (RIbosomal dna Integrated COpy number and methylation analysis), a novel computational pipeline for integrated estimation of rDNA CN and methylation using Oxford Nanopore long-read sequencing. RICO leverages long sequencing reads that span entire rDNA repeats, mapped to an rDNA-augmented reference genome, and normalizes coverage using a single-copy gene panel. We demonstrate that RICO provides accurate rDNA CN estimates in simulated datasets and reproducible measurements across human samples, with strong agreement to short-read sequencing and PCR-based methods. Furthermore, RICO reproduces a ~40% reduction in rDNA CN in Atrx-knockout mouse embryonic stem cells, consistent with established effects of ATRX loss on rDNA CN. RICO also captures an increased total and active rDNA CN in malignant cells from a MYC-driven B-cell lymphoma mouse model, in agreement with prior studies. Applying RICO to independent human cohorts, we uncover that individuals with higher total rDNA CN consistently exhibit higher fractions of highly methylated rDNA copies, suggesting a dosage compensation mechanism that potentially maintains a similar number of active rDNA copies across individuals. Together, RICO enables integrated analysis of rDNA CN and methylation state, providing a scalable framework for investigating rDNA regulation across population and disease studies. RICO is available at https://github.com/comprna/RICO.

title: Language-guided domain adaptation improves protein sequence representations for antimicrobial resistance analysis
authors: Ye, R.; Li, L.; Geng, Z.; Song, S.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR), particularly antibiotic resistance in bacterial pathogens, complicates infectious disease management. Because bacterial resistance is often mediated by protein functions, including antibiotic inactivation and efflux, protein sequence analysis provides a molecular basis for digital AMR surveillance and therapeutic intervention. We developed BacLLM, a language guided protein representation framework that integrates annotation-derived functional knowledge into protein language model representations for AMR analysis in WHO priority bacterial pathogens. Through sequence enhancement, semantic enrichment of UniProt annotations, and cross modal contrastive learning, BacLLM transfers LLM encoded annotation priors into the sequence encoder. Compared with baselines, BacLLM provided more informative representations for resistance-gene identification and mechanism prediction, captured resistance associated mutational signals at single-residue resolution, and preserved taxonomic relationships not reflected by phenotype based clinical groupings. Moreover, BacLLM recovered resistance associated functional organization within a TolC-centered protein association network, prioritizing proteins with low sequence identity to TolC but predicted structural similarity to TolC. Extending from AMR characterization to therapeutic prioritization, BacLLM also improved strain-level phage host matching for phage therapy candidate prioritization. Together, these findings establish BacLLM as a protein representation framework supporting AMR surveillance, functional characterization, and therapeutic candidate prioritization.

title: spearfish: ultrafast Δ-mapping of long reads to redundant transcriptomes
authors: Abdelgawad, H.; Martayan, I.; MARCHET, C.; Patro, R.
abstract: In a transcriptome, isoforms share most of their sequence, and gene families add further near-copies. Yet most long-read mappers treat each isoform as a separate target and repeat seeding, chaining and alignment for each. We introduce spearfish, a long-read mapper built for this redundancy. Its delta mapping ({Delta}-mapping) computes each target's alignment-score difference from the best candidate. It skips sequence that all candidates share, which cannot change the difference, and aligns where they differ once per distinct sequence rather than once per target. Seeds come from locally consistent parsing (LCP), so every isoform that contains an exon receives the same seeds in its interior. Collapsing them gives a core graph, a de Bruijn-like graph whose size is bounded by the distinct exonic sequence plus a small term per splice junction, independent of the number of isoforms. Over this graph, spearfish computes the exact colinear chaining score of every candidate transcript, sharing dynamic-programming state among transcripts via a procedure which we prove is equivalent to chaining on each transcript separately. Across RNA-seq experiments, using 32 threads, spearfish maps reads 24-102x faster than minimap2 in under a quarter of the memory, and 2.5-11.5x faster than lr-kallisto's pseudoalignment. On simulated reads it ranks the true transcript first more often than minimap2 on HiFi reads and at least as often on ONT reads. When using spearfish's {Delta}-mapping with oarfish for abundance estimation, the abundance estimates match or improve on those that make use of minimap2's alignments on both simulated reads (with or without primers and poly(A) tails) and on seven SG-NEx runs with spike-ins, and quantification is 4.1-8.8x faster than lr-kallisto in going from reads to abundances.

title: Clofarabine enforces dual host-pathogen translational arrest and disarms enteric bacterial virulence
authors: Deans, N. D.; Naylor, K. L.; Srour, S.; Mallick, B.; Pham, T. K.; Edmunds, G. S.; Sheffield, J. W.; Ansell, O. F.; Edington-Siddon, C. D.; Burt, E. A.; Stafford, G.; Collins, M.; Humphreys, D.
abstract: Enteropathogenic and enterohaemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EPEC/EHEC) cause severe global diarrhoeal disease, exacerbated by rising antimicrobial resistance. Pathogenesis relies on attaching and effacing lesions, where bacteria generate actin pedestals to adhere, replicate, and destroy intestinal microvilli. To identify novel anti-virulence candidates targeting this process, we conducted a high-throughput phenotypic screen quantifying pedestal formation via high-content fluorescence microscopy. We identified the anticancer nucleotide analogue clofarabine as a potent inhibitor of EPEC growth and pathogenesis. Distinct from its oncology mechanism - inducing DNA chain termination and apoptosis - clofarabine competes with bacterial ATP-dependent processes to impede gene transcription, protein synthesis, and Type III Secretion System (T3SS) function. Remarkably, EPEC counteracts this inhibition by cleaving clofarabine, enabling restored protein synthesis and resumed growth. Furthermore, we report for the first time that clofarabine suppresses protein translation in human monocytes, suggesting an uncharacterised translational impact on mammalian cells. These findings reveal host and bacterial translation as interconnected vulnerabilities to purine antimetabolites, offering a novel strategy to disarm enteric pathogens while uncovering a bacterial enzymatic mechanism for neutralizing host-targeted therapeutics.

title: Integrating Long-Read Structural Variant Analysis with single-nucleus RNA-seq to Elucidate Gene Expression Effects in Disease
authors: Kim, K.; Lin, Z.; Simmons, S. K.; Parker, J.; Kearney, M.; Liao, Z.; Haywood, N.; Zhang, J.; Cline, M. P.; Tuncali, I.; Sharma, M.; Serrano, G. E.; Beach, T. G.; Dong, X.; Popic, V.; Scherzer, C. R.; Levin, J. Z.
abstract: Structural variants (SVs) are a major source of genetic diversity, yet how they impact cell types in complex brain diseases remains largely unexplored, partially due to limitations of short-read sequencing. Here, we addressed this fundamental question in Parkinson's disease (PD). generating long-read whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data for 100 post-mortem brain samples from a PD cohort, constructing a high-confidence catalog of 74,552 SVs. To resolve their functional impact, we integrated single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data from two brain regions from the same samples and focused functional analyses on SVs proximal to genes previously nominated as cis-regulated, potential causal targets of PD-associated GWAS loci. Using expression quantitative trait locus and allele-specific expression analyses, we uncovered SVs significantly associated with expression in specific cell types as well as effects shared across cell types. This study demonstrates the power of uniting long-read WGS with transcriptomics to uncover SVs underlying complex disease architecture with cell type resolution.

title: Assessing the Capacity of Genomic Language Models to Generate Informative Embeddings of Viral Genome Fragments
authors: Kladchenko, A.; Manolov, A.; Popov, N. S.
abstract: Genomic language models (gLMs) trained on large volumes of nucleotide sequences are becoming an alternative to classical methods in metagenomic analysis, particularly for studying genomic "dark matter". In this work, we investigate the ability of four gLMs (DNABERT-2, DNABERT-S, ViraLM, and Evo2-7B) to generate taxonomically informative vector representations of short viral genome fragments. We constructed a balanced reference dataset of viruses based on the ICTV Virus Metadata Resource and compared the representations generated by gLMs with conventional k-mer profiles and MinHash sketches using clustering and neighborhood-based metrics (adjusted Rand index (ARI), precision@k, and CROSS precision@k). On the reference dataset, three of the four gLMs outperformed the 4-mer profile in terms of ARI and precision@5 under the same evaluation protocol. The best performance was generally achieved by intermediate model layers. Conventional k-mer profiles consistently outperformed MinHash sketches. We further evaluated the methods on two viral orders (egoviruses and mriyaviruses) absent from the reference dataset, with model layers and k-mer lengths selected exclusively on the reference dataset. DNABERT-S showed the most consistently strong performance across these two orders, ranking first on mriyaviruses and second on egoviruses, while k-mer profiles with Jensen-Shannon distance remained competitive. We also observed the consistency of representations between forward fragments and their reverse complements. Overall, the best-performing gLMs surpassed conventional baselines, although their advantage depended on the dataset and evaluation metric. The consistently strong performance of DNABERT-S suggests a potential benefit of contrastive fine-tuning and indicates that larger models are not necessarily more effective for generating taxonomically informative representations.

title: Structural signatures of salinity adaptation in Microviricetes capsids
authors: Khot, V. M.; Krupovic, M.; Dutilh, B. E.
abstract: Phages, like their bacterial hosts, have evolved to proliferate across the full range of environments on Earth, but the specific amino acid residues that underlie their environmental adaptations remain elusive. Here, we developed a computational framework that uses structure-based multiple sequence alignments, a random forest classifier, and a phylogeny-aware regression model to find amino acid residues linked to specific environments. Applying this framework to public metagenomic data, we analyzed 1,110 Microviricetes major capsid proteins (MCPs) from the lake and ocean biomes, and found that ocean virus capsids were highly enriched in negatively charged residues on internal and external surfaces. This adaptation likely helps maintain solubility at high salt concentrations and stabilizes ssDNA-capsid interactions by sequestering positively charged ions inside the capsid. At intersubunit interfaces, ocean capsids showed enrichment of cation-{pi} and {pi}-{pi} interactions, which are more resistant to solvation than salt bridges and hydrogen bonds. Amino acid residues in lake capsids were more often substituted by biochemically dissimilar amino acids in ocean capsids than the reverse. Together, these results show that microvirus capsids adapt to high-salt environments through changes in surface charge and substitutions affecting intersubunit interactions. Further, we describe a general approach for studying the adaptation and stability of any protein family under complementary environmental or phenotypic conditions.

title: Highly prevalent cargo genes of F plasmids harbored in pathogenic Escherichia coli
authors: Guirao-Rico, S.; Flament-Simon, S. C.; Madrid, C.; Balsalobre, C.; Huttener, M.; Blanco, J. E.; Blanco, J.; Rozas, J.; Juarez, A.
abstract: Analysis of prevalent orthogroups (OGs) in a collection of F plasmids from extraintestinal Escherichia coli ST131 isolates has led to the identification of two groups of previously uncharacterized cargo genes that may be widely distributed among F plasmids of pathogenic E. coli. Group 1 comprises four OGs whose encoded proteins are predicted to be involved in transport-related functions. The corresponding genes cluster with other genes associated with metabolism and are highly prevalent in extraintestinal ST131 isolates. Group 2 comprises several OGs whose encoded proteins currently have unknown functions. These OGs are present in a large proportion of F plasmids from both intestinal and extraintestinal E. coli isolates. The corresponding genes cluster within an F-plasmid region that also contains genes involved in DNA metabolism, suggesting that the proteins encoded by these newly identified OGs may likewise contribute to F-plasmid DNA biology. Characterizing the functions of these newly identified proteins may improve our understanding of the contribution of F plasmid to E. coli virulence and reveal novel targets for antimicrobial intervention, either by limiting F-plasmid dissemination among multidrug-resistant (MDR) E. coli strains or by directly targeting plasmid-carrying bacteria.

title: Long-read analysis of complete human 5S rDNA arrays reveals a zoned organization with two-state unit methylation linked to chromatin architecture
authors: Kim, H.
abstract: Despite the fundamental importance of the 5S ribosomal DNA (rDNA) to all cellular life, the landscape of its units by position along its array has remained poorly understood. Here, recent telomere-to-telomere long-read sequencing is used to resolve 5S rDNA arrays from flank to flank and to follow the state of each unit along single molecules. The array is zoned at both the sequence and the epigenetic level. Notably, methylation is bimodal at the level of the unit, and the combination of low-methylation and high-methylation units gives rise to the overall methylation pattern of the array. Moreover, the average number of low-methylation units remains relatively constant regardless of array length. Chromatin fiber sequencing (Fiber-seq) data further show that low-methylation units are more accessible, have lower nucleosome occupancy and are more frequently footprinted at the TFIIIB-binding site, consistent with analyses of ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq data from cell lines. Across species, this pattern is shared among apes, whereas other species show diverse patterns. These results provide a unit-resolved view of the human 5S rDNA array and reveal a zone-specific organization of unit methylation that is associated with chromatin architecture.

title: Single-nucleus long-read RNA sequencing reveals isoform usage shifts in mouse acute kidney injury
authors: Oda, Y.; Noonan, M. L.; Dixon, E. E.; Wu, H.; Humphreys, B. D.
abstract: Introduction Single-cell and single-nucleus short-read RNA sequencing has elucidated transcriptomic changes across kidney cell types at the gene expression level. However, its limited read length precludes reliable isoform identification, hindering the characterization of individual protein-coding isoforms and non-protein-coding isoforms. We combined long-read sequencing with single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing technologies to investigate isoform regulation in healthy and acutely injured mouse kidneys. Methods Single-cell and single-nucleus long-read RNA sequencing datasets were generated from kidneys of three healthy adult male C57BL/6J mice. An additional three adult male C57BL/6J mice underwent bilateral renal ischemia-reperfusion injury, and kidneys were subjected to single-nucleus long-read RNA sequencing. Results A total of 1.3 billion reads were generated, with a median read length of 757-884 bases across samples. Single-nucleus libraries yielded a smaller proportion of reads assigned to isoforms than single-cell libraries, reflecting their larger proportion of intronic reads. Nevertheless, single-nucleus libraries detected more distinct isoforms and greater isoform expression diversity, partly owing to the near absence of mitochondrial gene-derived transcripts. Single-nucleus analysis of healthy and injured kidneys revealed that ischemia-reperfusion injury downregulated oxidative phosphorylation-associated genes in proximal tubule cells both at the gene expression level and through shifts in isoform composition. Beyond oxidative phosphorylation-associated genes, Fut9 and Prrc2b were identified as genes exhibiting prominent shifts in isoform usage after ischemia-reperfusion injury. Conclusion Single-nucleus long-read RNA sequencing detected injury-induced shifts in isoform usage in mouse kidney, adding a layer of transcriptomic information that is largely inaccessible to conventional gene-level short-read analysis.

title: The chromosome-scale genome of the drought-adapted Caatinga tree Spondias tuberosa reveals a conserved, unduplicated architecture within Anacardiaceae
authors: Almeida, C.; Lopes, E.; Santos, D.; Rodrigues, G.; Silva, J. V.; Bhatia, A.; Marques, A.
abstract: Spondias tuberosa (umbu) is a tree endemic to the semi-arid Caatinga of north-eastern Brazil, adapted to recurrent drought and high temperatures. Although genomes of mango (Mangifera indica), pistachio (Pistacia vera) and cashew (Anacardium occidentale) are available, comparative analyses of genome evolution across Anacardiaceae remain scarce. We aimed to generate a chromosome-scale reference genome for S. tuberosa and use it to examine genome architecture, meiotic recombination and gene family evolution within the family. We assembled the genome of a single individual using PacBio HiFi and Omni-C (Hi-C) data, mapped meiotic crossovers by single-nucleus RNA sequencing of pollen, and compared the genome with those of six other Sapindales species through orthology, synteny, synonymous substitution (Ks) and gene family expansion/contraction analyses within a dated phylogenomic framework. The assembly anchors 288 Mb onto 16 chromosomes (98.8% BUSCO completeness) and contains 24,232 protein-coding genes, 52.01% repetitive DNA and 1.78 million heterozygous SNPs (0.62%). We identified 1,740 crossovers in 153 pollen nuclei (4.01 cM.Mb1), which were depleted in repeat-rich pericentromeric regions. Ks analyses revealed a whole-genome duplication shared by Mangifera and Anacardium that is absent from S. tuberosa, which retains only the ancient {gamma} triplication. The 97 gene families expanded in S. tuberosa, mostly through tandem duplication, include receptor-like kinases, glutathione S-transferases and disease-resistance proteins, consistent with roles in environmental sensing and stress tolerance. Genome structure has remained highly conserved across Sapindales, except in the mango cashew lineage, which underwent extensive rearrangements following a whole-genome duplication. As sister to the remaining Anacardiaceae sampled and with an unduplicated, largely collinear architecture, S. tuberosa provides a reference for comparative mapping and for transferring genomic information to economically important woody relatives.

title: Fast Pangenome Matching Statistics in Compressed Space with Move Structures
authors: Brown, N. K.; Sanaullah, A.; Shakya, P.; Zhang, S.; Langmead, B.
abstract: Matching statistics and supermaximal exact matches (SMEMs) are key inputs for sequence homology search and classification. Methods such as MONI, PHONI, and ropebwt3 compute these statistics using compressed pangenome indexes, but are substantially slower than methods that compute approximations of matching statistics, such as pseudo-matching lengths (PMLs). PMLs can be computed quickly in a single pass, but SMEM computation can require overlapping forward or backward passes over the query. We present ms2, a suite of algorithms that use "move structures" to compute matching statistics and SMEMs efficiently in compressed space. Our four algorithms compose move structures for the LF, {Psi}, {varphi}, and {varphi}-1 permutations with additional longest common prefix (LCP) array summaries and samples. The algorithms offer different tradeoffs among speed, index size, and support for reporting SMEM offsets. They inherit the move structure's fast, constant-time operations and achieve high throughput by leveraging the move structure's locality of reference. Thanks to recent advances, move structures can be constructed in optimal time and compressed space, including the LCP information needed for "match recovery" during SMEM computation. On 100 haplotypes of human chromosome 22, ms2's fastest algorithm computes matching statistics 35 to 48 times as fast as PHONI's online approach, while using an index of similar size. On the 472-haplotype HPRC2 pangenome and human reads, three ms2 modes achieve speedups of at least 22, 19, and 15 times over ropebwt3, whose index is about 15% the size of ms2's fastest mode. When additionally reporting SMEMs and their offsets, ms2 achieves speedups of 25 to 34 times over ropebwt3. Together, these advances enable online computation of matching statistics and SMEMs at a throughput that supports real-time processing of approximately 21 PromethION nanopore flow cells on a single thread. The ms2 software is open source and available at https://github.com/langmead-lab/ms2. It builds on the open-source TeraTools suite (https://github.com/ucfcbb/TeraTools) and Orbit library (https://github.com/drnatebrown/orbit). Experimental scripts and other details are described in: https://github.com/langmead-lab/ms2-experiments.

title: Saturation barcoding of ribosomal DNA resolves the nucleolar organizer regions of the human genome
authors: Zhao, S.; Wallentin, J.; Potapova, T.; Zheng, S.; Liu, X.; Daza, R. M.; Gerton, J. L.; Shendure, J.; Li, X.
abstract: The nucleolus is the hub for ribosome biogenesis in eukaryotic cells. It is assembled on nucleolar organizer regions (NORs), tandem arrays of ribosomal DNA (rDNA) units. In humans, each rDNA unit is ~45 kb and encodes the 47S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) precursor. Hundreds of rDNA units are present per germline genome, spread across 10 NORs positioned on the short arms of the five acrocentric chromosomes. However, their precise count and structure are unknown. In fact, twenty-five years after the first draft of the human genome, NORs are the only regions of the human genome that remain incompletely resolved, represented in telomere-to-telomere (T2T) reference genomes as gaps or modeled sequences rather than bona fide assemblies. Here we use prime editing to insert degenerate 6-bp DNA barcodes to 99% of taggable rDNA units in a clonal derivative of the leukemia-derived K562 cell line. Following ultra-long-read sequencing, these barcodes serve as molecular identifiers that guide the end-to-end assembly of all 18 NORs of K562s pseudotriploid genome. The assembly yields: (i) a precise rDNA copy number for each NOR (range 5-43; total 290); (ii) the cis- and trans- architecture of intragenomic variation in rDNA sequence, both structural and fine-scale; and (iii) patterns of divergence and homogenization within and across NORs that may have arisen during cancer evolution and the subsequent passaging of this line. Finally, by reading the same tags from RNA, we define the relationship between DNA methylation and Pol I transcription at the resolution of individual rDNA units. Together, our study demonstrates how the final tangles of the human genome can at last be resolved, and opens the door to more extensive investigations of how genetic, epigenetic and functional rDNA variation contributes to health and disease.

title: Rise and Fall of a Superbug: Analyzing the epidemic success of a distinct clone of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium ST117/CT71 in Germany, 2017 - 2024.
authors: Weber, R. E.; Werner, G.; Bender, J. K.; Haldemann, B.; Drechsel, O.; Fischer, M. A.
abstract: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) is a major cause of healthcare-associated infections, yet outbreak analysis remains challenging, particularly for prevalent lineages. One of the most striking examples is the Sequence Type (ST) 117/Complex Type (CT) 71/vanB lineage, whose rapid expansion across Germany coincided with a sharp rise in VRE prevalence observed around 2019. Defining reliable genomic thresholds remains particularly difficult, as current core-genome Multi-Locus Sequence Typing (cgMLST) cutoffs are based largely on expert consensus or limited case series. Here, we evaluate the discriminatory performance of cgMLST and split k-mer analysis (SKA) for resolving relatedness within ST117/CT71 and investigate whether low core-genome diversity represents a lineage-specific trait or a population-wide property of E. faecium. While cgMLST captures the overall population structure of ST117/CT71, SKA provided higher resolution, distinguishing isolates identical by cgMLST. Analysis of 2,505 genomes showed that ST117/CT71 does not exhibit reduced allelic variability compared with other hospital-adapted lineages, suggesting that limited core-genome diversity is a broader population characteristic. Complementary transposon analyses further identified two temporally distinct ST117/CT71 sublineages carrying different Tn1549-like structures. To assess allelic variation within confirmed transmission events, we analyzed 138 outbreak clusters from 96 hospitals. Outbreak-associated isolates showed sharply compressed allelic differences (median = 1), with 90% of pairwise comparisons falling within [≤]9 alleles. Thus, the commonly applied [≤]20-allele threshold risks overestimating genomic relatedness and grouping unrelated isolates. Based on these data, we propose lowering the cgMLST alert threshold to [≤]9 alleles for initial cluster detection of local outbreaks, followed by confirmatory high-resolution analyses such as SKA.

title: Distinct binding modes shape exploitable asymmetries between echinocandin and triterpenoid resistance landscapes in Fks1
authors: Carolus, H.; Wang, N.; Jacobs, S.; Dube, A. K.; Sofras, D.; Lobo Romero, C.; Durand, R.; Spruijtenburg, B.; Meijer, E. F. J.; Van Dijck, P.; Lague, P.; Landry, C. R.
abstract: Echinocandins are the first-line treatment for invasive fungal infections and work by inhibiting the fungal {beta}-1,3-glucan synthase Fks1. Recently, a first-in-class triterpenoid Fks1 inhibitor, ibrexafungerp, was approved for clinical use. The extent to which the difference between these drug classes alters the landscape of resistance mutations in Fks1 is unknown. We used deep mutational scanning (DMS) to quantify the effects of all single-amino-acid variants spanning 159 residues across the three canonical Fks1 resistance hotspots and flanking regions in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Drug selections revealed widespread position-specific cross-resistance and differential resistance, including an ibrexafungerp-specific resistance cluster downstream of hotspot 2 that defines a novel triterpenoid-specific resistance hotspot. We defined this as hotspot 4 and redefined the boundaries of the remaining three canonical echinocandin hotspots, based on the mutational landscape of our DMS analyses. Susceptibility testing of individual FKS1 variants of S. cerevisiae and Candidozyma auris strains confirmed conserved class-specific and cross-resistance patterns. Structure-guided ligand placement, molecular dynamics-based simulated annealing, and DMS-informed pose selection linked drug-specific phenotypes to distinct interaction networks, providing a molecular rationale for the observed differential resistance patterns. These data provide a framework for predicting antifungal resistance, informing treatment strategies and future drug design.

title: RawMod: Modification-Agnostic Detection of DNA Base Modifications from Nanopore Signal Pileups
authors: Srinivasan, B.; Nazar, S.; Gandhi, V.; Zhang, E.; Bachvaroff, T.; Kolmogorov, M.; Place, A.; Firtina, C.
abstract: Summary: Identifying epigenetically modified bases (e.g., methylation) is crucial for many important applications such as discovering mechanisms of cancer development, cell differentiation, and bacterial defense. Nanopore sequencing generates electrical signals that can differentiate canonical bases from modified ones. To detect base modifications from signals, machine learning (ML) methods and statistical approaches are commonly used. These methods can either detect a specific modification type or require an additional unmodified copy of the same DNA as a control group. However, no released model detects modification types beyond those it was trained for, which makes it difficult to detect rare modification types without an unmodified control. Our goal is to accurately identify the presence of modified sites regardless of their modification type, which we define as modification-agnostic detection. To this end, we propose RawMod, a transformer-based modification-agnostic and control-free method for detecting epigenetically modified genomic positions. The key idea of RawMod is to compare the raw signals of many reads at each site with the unmodified reference sequence, using a small model that learns many modification types as a single modified class. Based on our extensive evaluations on the detection of various modification types (5mC, 5hmC, 4mC, 6mA, and 5hmU) using various genomes, RawMod achieves the highest mean AUROC across modifications compared to control-based methods and control-free modification models. A single RawMod model with 0.23M parameters detects five modification types with a mean AUROC of 0.964, against 0.799 for the best released model. When a modification type is withheld from training, RawMod still detects it (AUROC 0.91--0.98), provided another modification of the same base was seen in training. We use RawMod to map 5hmU without a control across a 7.7 Mb contig of the Amphidinium carterae genome, consistent with two published trends. Further, we show that the modification-aware embeddings from RawMod can be used to differentiate read origin (e.g., cell types, tumor/normal origin, and native/PCR-amplified DNA). We discuss how RawMod can enable further work on label-free classification of cell types using these modification-aware embeddings. Availability and Implementation: RawMod is available at https://github.com/STORMgroup/RawMod and at https://huggingface.co/STORMResearch/RawMod. We also provide the scripts to fully reproduce our results on our GitHub page and release our datasets on SquiDBase.

title: Using Oyster Genomics to Understand Human Health
authors: Bargmann, W.; Chen, Z.; Wang, S.; Cawood, M. L.; Parulekar, A.; Martucci, C.; Hoh, J.
abstract: As sessile filter feeders that experience continuous environmental exposure, oysters, particularly Crassostrea virginica, offer a unique opportunity to understand how environmental exposure alters the genome and influence health. Furthermore, oysters must be sorted by size for market value for premium size and taste. However, it requires intensive labor, specialized equipment (tumblers), and is susceptible to environmental risks like pollution. Therefore, it is desirable to produce uniform oysters without machines. However, limitations in the previous reference genome [2] have constrained our understanding of how genes are organized and maintained in oyster populations. To this end, we harvested 240 adult oysters in same location, 120 extremely large size and 120 extremely small, controlled with all confounding factors such as age and water temperature. We perform a genome wide associate study (GWAS) using next generation whole genome sequencing, aiming to discover genomic regions associated with oyster size. Using PacBio HiFi, Illumina, and Hi-C technologies, we generated a 99.7% complete chromosome-level genome assembly for C. virginica (NCBI RefSeq GCF_053477285.1) [75]. We identified a ~13 Mb region on chromosome 1 uniquely expanded in C. virginica and enriched for innate immune and stress-response genes. To evaluate whether these structural features are reflected at the population level, we then conducted a k-mer analysis. This revealed differential sequence patterns by size, including enrichment of bacterial DNA in smaller individuals and host variation at the RNF213 locus within this region. By highlighting genome structure as a mediator of immune resilience, this work supports the use of oysters as sentinels to advance out understanding of how the dynamic reassembly of the genome due to environmental exposures influence health in human populations.

title: BIG-TB: A benchmark for evaluating prediction and interpretability of sequence-based machine learning using Mycobacterium tuberculosis  genomes
authors: Tasmin, M.; Mohanty, S.; Kulkarni, S.; Farhat, M. R.; Green, A. G.
abstract: Foundation models aim to learn useful representations of biological sequences, but are hindered by a lack of benchmarks to jointly evaluate predictive performance and variant attribution on diverse tasks. To this end, we present the Benchmark for Interpretable prediction from Genomes of Tuberculosis, BIG-TB. We curate over 17,000 genomes with high-quality sequencing data and experimentally measured antibiotic resistance phenotypes, combined with a curated list of WHO-catalogue of resistance-associated variants, and provide these data in an ML-ready format. BIG-TB defines two tasks: (1) predictive performance of antibiotic resistance phenotypes, and (2) attribution of predictions to known resistance-conferring variants. Using our tasks, we evaluate DNA- and protein-based foundation models, showing that DNA-based foundation models do not yet outperform simple machine learning baselines (mean test AUC = 0.888 vs. 0.865 for best CNN variant vs. best Evo2 variant across drugs). In a lineage-informed evaluation across DNA and protein modalities, predictive signal for well-characterized drugs was largely preserved (mean AUC 0.846-0.963). Across both evaluation settings, models with the highest predictive performance did not necessarily achieve the strongest recovery of resistance variants, underscoring the value of evaluating both predictive accuracy and biological interpretability. Overall, BIG-TB provides a reusable resource for developing sequence representations that are both accurate and mechanistically meaningful.

title: Panmap: Scalable phylogeny-guided alignment, genotyping, and placement on pangenomes
authors: Kramer, A. M.; Zhang, A.; Ayala, N.; de Sanctis, B.; Karim, L. M.; Hinrichs, A. S.; Walia, S.; Turakhia, Y.; Corbett-Detig, R.
abstract: Pangenomes capture population-level variation but remain computationally challenging at scale. We present Panmap, a tool that leverages evolutionary structure to place, align, and genotype sequencing reads against mutation-annotated pangenomes containing up to millions of genomes. Panmap introduces a phylogenetically compressed k-mer index that stores only sequence differences along branches, enabling efficient comparison of reads to both sampled genomes and inferred ancestors. This approach reduces index size by up to 600-fold and construction time by over three orders of magnitude relative to existing tools. Panmap places a 100x coverage SARS-CoV-2 sample onto 20,000 genomes in 0.4 seconds and onto 8 million genomes in under two minutes. Furthermore, it enables accurate haplotype identification and abundance estimation in metagenomic samples and sensitive placement of ancient environmental DNA without prior alignment. Our approach makes large-scale pangenomes directly amenable to read mapping, genome assembly, alignment-free phylogenetic placement, and metagenomic analysis.

title: Sedimentary ancient DNA expands bioarchaeological evidence and interpretation at Roman Harelbeke
authors: Özdogan, K. T.; Furni, F.; Nota, K.; Erven, J.; Aal, J.; Reurings, S.; den Boef, L.; van Mousch, R.; de Groot, G. A.; Plets, G.
abstract: Sedimentary ancient DNA (sedaDNA) can expand archaeological research by recovering broad biological signals from small amounts of sediment. Here, we apply shotgun sedaDNA metagenomics and target capture (also known as hybridization capture) to disused Roman wells from the vicus of Harelbeke, Belgium, dated to ca. 160-300 CE, and integrate the results with existing bioarchaeological datasets. Moving beyond individual introduced taxa as proxies for Roman influence, we reconstruct community-level profiles spanning consumption-related, synanthropic, and environmental organisms. SedaDNA reproduced most established bioarchaeological signals, including cultivated plants and domestic animals, while also recovering additional environmental taxa that established methods underrepresented. Mitochondrial target capture strengthened selected faunal detections and enabled phylogenetic placement of a pig (Sus scrofa) within the European mitochondrial lineage. The predominance of previously established consumption-related taxa is consistent with subsistence continuity and selective adoption of Roman-introduced resources, although taxon counts alone cannot establish their relative importance. Analytical-effort modeling further indicates that batch-based sedaDNA workflows can provide broad biological profiles at lower cost and time investment than established archaeological methods. Overall, sedaDNA complements conventional bioarchaeology by broadening taxonomic recovery, supporting scalable sampling, and providing a broad-spectrum approach to reconstructing settlement ecology, subsistence, and human-environment interaction.

title: Nanopore-only assembly and methylation profiling of Arabidopsis thaliana across chemistries, basecalling models and assembly workflows
authors: Martin, S.; Peel, N.; Heavens, D.; Lan, Y.; Irish, N.; Horsfield, S. T.; Giolai, M.; Clark, M. D.; Leggett, R. M.
abstract: Over the past decade, nanopore sequencing has progressed rapidly through advances in flow cell chemistry, library preparation, basecalling algorithms and base-modification detection. These developments have increased both throughput and read accuracy, making nanopore-only sequencing increasingly practical for eukaryotic genome assembly and direct detection of DNA methylation. Here, we present nanopore sequencing data, genome assemblies, and methylation analysis for the Columbia (Col-0) accession of the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana and assess how successive improvements in the nanopore sequencing platform have affected read accuracy and assembly quality. Data from earlier R9.4.1 and R10.4 flow cells were sufficient to generate nanopore-only multi-megabase and chromosome-arm scale assemblies, with higher reference-alignment identity achieved with the improved R10.4 chemistry. Super-accuracy rebasecalling increased read quality in both datasets and markedly improved assembly identity and gene completeness. Methylation calls obtained directly from nanopore signal were strongly concordant with a published bisulphite sequencing dataset at shared covered sites, with Pearson's r values of 0.93 and 0.96 for the R9.4.1 and R10.4 datasets, respectively. To assess current nanopore assembly performance, we additionally analysed 14.3 Gb R10.4.1 simplex reads, basecalled with a super-accuracy model and assembled using hifiasm, a contemporary long-read de novo assembler. This produced a five-contig nuclear assembly of 134.93 Mb, with each contig corresponding to one of the five Arabidopsis nuclear chromosomes. The assembly recovered 99.9% complete BUSCO genes and showed 99.98% one-to-one alignment identity to TAIR12, with three chromosomes assembled telomere-to-telomere. These results provide an empirical example of how nanopore-only plant genome assembly has improved across successive workflows and demonstrate the value of nanopore data for simultaneous genome assembly and methylation analysis.

title: Infection-dependent antibiotic response phenotypes emerge during chronic airway adaptation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa
authors: Laborda, P.; Cebrian-Sastre, E.; La Rosa, R.; Molin, S.; Johansen, H. K.
abstract: Objectives Chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa airway infections can persist for years despite intensive antibiotic therapy guided by standard antimicrobial susceptibility testing. While this technique captures the emergence of resistance, it does not reproduce many features of the infection environment, where adaptation acquired during chronic infection may alter bacterial responses to antibiotics in ways that are not fully reflected by conventional susceptibility testing. Here we investigated antibiotic responses of longitudinal clinical isolates under standard laboratory conditions and in an airway epithelial infection model. Methods Six longitudinal pairs of P. aeruginosa isolates from people with cystic fibrosis were analysed. Changes in bacterial growth following exposure to tobramycin, ceftazidime and ciprofloxacin were quantified under standard laboratory conditions and compared with changes in bacterial burden after treatment measured in differentiated airway epithelial cultures maintained under air-liquid interface (ALI) conditions that reproduce key features of the airway infection environment. Representative phenotypes were visualized by confocal microscopy and interpreted in the context of available whole-genome sequencing data. Results Major resistance phenotypes identified by conventional susceptibility testing were largely reproduced in the ALI model. However, concordance between phenotypes observed under standard laboratory and ALI conditions differed between antibiotics. Several isolates classified as susceptible according to conventional susceptibility testing displayed substantial survival in the ALI model, and these discordant phenotypes were observed predominantly among those isolates recovered after prolonged airway persistence. Genomic analyses identified mutations associated with both classical resistance mechanisms and chronic adaptation. Conclusions Phenotypes observed under conventional laboratory conditions do not uniformly predict those observed in the ALI airway conditions. Discordant phenotypes were most apparent among chronically adapted isolates and varied between antibiotics, suggesting that adaptation acquired during chronic infection can alter antibiotic responses in ways that are not fully reflected by conventional susceptibility testing.

title: MicroDUET: a dual-headed genomic foundation model for pathogen surveillance
authors: Barber, M.; Suster, C. J. E.; Lei, J.; Getchell, M.; Wulandari, S.; Sintchenko, V.; Pronyk, P. M.
abstract: Pathogen genomic surveillance works from raw reads, assembled genomes and alignments, representations that are slow and costly to compare at scale. Compact embeddings from genomic language models offer an alternative, but surveillance requires resolving both evolutionary ancestry (phylogeny) and phenotypic capability (function) - which need not co-vary. Here we present MicroDUET, which adapts a 26.6-million-parameter ProkBERT backbone with two 3.5-million-parameter adapter heads: a phylogeny head trained contrastively on genome windows from the same microbes, and a function head trained to identify genes across taxa. On held-out retrieval benchmarks, the phylogeny head returned the correct species for 80.3% and 66.6% of cellular and viral queries, and the function head the correct gene family for 97.3% and 97.2%, reaching 74.4% accuracy on an independent antimicrobial resistance-class benchmark. Across all three benchmarks MicroDUET outranked 17 other genomic encoders. Without training on lineage, clade or drug-susceptibility tasks, MicroDUET identified Mycobacterium tuberculosis and mpox virus lineages and clades (0.965, 0.975 accuracy), discriminated rifampicin resistance without lineage adjustment (AUROC 0.985), and retrospectively identified an emerging mpox lineage as anomalous (AUROC 0.974). MicroDUET operates 10^3 - 10^4 times faster than single-threaded sequence-based alignments. MicroDUET therefore provides a compact, reusable representation for scalable pathogen surveillance and sequence triage.

title: Systematic benchmarks reveal DNA polymerase combinations for high-quality genome assembly
authors: Bein, B.; Gerheim, C.; Gscheidel, N.; Canesin, L.; Ben Hamadou, A.; Schneider, C.; Schell, T.; Yi, X.; Galia-Camps, C.; Hechavarria-Cueria, J.; Lake, J. A.; McLaughlin, I.; Winkler, S.; Greve, C.; Hiller, M.
abstract: Background: A fundamental challenge in biodiversity genomics is generating long-read sequencing data and high-quality genome assemblies from samples lacking gold-standard flash-frozen tissue, including ethanol-preserved specimens, minimally invasive biopsies, and small-bodied organisms. Amplification-based library preparation enables long-read sequencing of such samples, but assembly quality critically depends on the polymerase used for amplification. Results: We present a systematic benchmark of eleven long-range DNA polymerases for PacBio HiFi sequencing and genome assembly across three taxonomically diverse species: a springtail, a sea slug, and a bat. We show that polymerase choice substantially affects assembly contiguity and gene completeness, primarily caused by polymerase-intrinsic GC-dependent amplification bias and read coverage heterogeneity. Five polymerases consistently produced assemblies with comparatively high contiguity and completeness, with some enzymes outperforming the polymerase currently used in the PacBio Ampli-Fi protocol. Importantly, combining reads amplified with different polymerases frequently resulted in superior assemblies, because polymerases complement each other by covering regions where others drop out. Combining reads amplified with different polymerases, we generated haplotype-resolved assemblies of the ~1 Gb giant springtail and ~2 Gb bat genome and improved the sea slug reference genome. Using the human GIAB benchmark, we further show that optimized amplification strategies improve variant-calling accuracy, highlighting their utility in medical and clinical research. To facilitate polymerase benchmarking across additional taxa, we provide the polymeval pipeline (https://github.com/casparbein/polymeval), which automates the computational workflow. Conclusion: Our study demonstrates that optimized amplification-based HiFi sequencing generates assemblies with >1 Mb contig N50 and >90% gene completeness, providing a toolkit to produce long-read genome assemblies from challenging samples.

title: EsViritu is a sensitive and specific profiler for viral pathogen detection and genome recovery in metagenomes
authors: Tisza, M. J.; Simar, S. R.; Zorz, J.; Javornik Cregeen, S. J.; Maresso, A. W.
abstract: Metagenomic sequencing allows for detection of any number of pathogenic viruses from a single sample without a priori knowledge of its contents. This has created a substantial opportunity to characterize pathogens in humans and their environment, but the field is held back by a lack of bioinformatics tools for taxonomic profiling and reconstructing virus genomes. The ideal profiler would simultaneously do two things: report viruses at single-read sensitivity so that ultra-low-abundance pathogens are not missed and hold near-perfect specificity so that a pathogen is never falsely reported. Here we present EsViritu, a taxonomic profiler that pairs an iterative greedy clustering algorithm and lowest-common-ancestor taxonomic refinement with a curated Virus Pathogen Database to reconstruct virus genomes and generate virome profiles directly from reads. We benchmarked EsViritu against four leading metagenomic profilers (Kraken2, Centrifuger, Metabuli, and Sylph), running each program across a full parameter sweep and against the same Virus Pathogen Database for an apples-to-apples comparison. Across synthetic positive controls, pathogen-free negative controls, and mutated mock communities, EsViritu was the most accurate tool at reconstructing community composition: it led or tied every tool on relative abundance accuracy at all taxonomic ranks and led or tied on detection across ranks. Importantly, other tools frequently report the presence of multiple related taxa when only reads for a single genome are present, but EsViritu faithfully records the correct, single taxon and genome. EsViritu achieves read-level sensitivity for sequences as low as 85% average nucleotide identity to the nearest reference and reports essentially no false positives in pathogen-free host and synthetic samples. EsViritu also returns reconstructed consensus genomes whose nucleotide identity to the nearest reference closely tracks ground truth, yielding both a profile and genomes from a single run.

title: Ultra-small bacteria and their phages discovered through metagenomics in a sub-arctic degrading permafrost ecosystem
authors: Tuomela, N.; Demina, T.; Thomas, D. N.; Kaartokallio, H.; Hultman, J.
abstract: Patescibacteriota is a diverse bacterial phylum characterized by ultra-small cell size, streamlined genome, incomplete metabolism and episymbiotic lifestyle. While Patescibacteriota have been detected across a wide range of ecosystem types, their phages are not widely described. We utilized metagenomics to explore these less characterized parts of the microbiome in a sporadic permafrost ecosystem, with samples from palsa and peat soils, small ponds and streams. We retrieved 33 high-quality metagenome assembled genomes (MAGs) of Patescibacteriota, mainly from the classes Minisyncoccia and Saccharimonadia. Minisyncoccia was a dominant class in the thawing soils and thaw ponds, whereas the Saccharimonadia was more abundant in the frozen palsa soil layers. The distribution of the Patescibacteria classes was also reflected in their metabolic potential. For example, gluconeogenesis pathway was complete only in MAGs from the class Minisyncoccia, whereas cytochrome o ubiquinol oxidase was mainly found from the MAGs of the class Saccharimondia. The viral community analysis yielded 16 354 viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs), which represented mainly tailed dsDNA viruses from the class Caudoviricetes. Based on genome size, 16 vOTUs were qualified as jumbophages and one as a megaphage. Similar to the bacterial community, the viral community composition differed across sample types. The most common hosts for bacterial viruses were phyla Pseudomonadota, Acidobacteriota and Actinomycetota. A further 196 vOTUs were in silico linked to Patescibacteriota hosts. The Patescibacteriota phages were diverse, with only two vOTUs representing the same genus. The relative abundance of Patescibacteriota-associated phages was especially high in frozen palsa soils, largely following the same pattern of abundance as Patescibacteriota.

title: Candidatus Pannonibacter alzirae sp. nov. isolated from a septic immunocompromised patient in Brazil
authors: Rocha, I. V.; de Melo, B. S. T.; Pitta, J. L. d. L. P.; de Andrade, C. A. d. N.; de Lima Neto, R. G.; de Faria, A. C. M.; Nunes, M. L.; Wallau, G. d. L.; de Lima Campos, T.; Saraiva, K. L. A.; Carneiro, M. E. B. d. A.; Sobreira, M.; Bezerra, M. F.
abstract: Pannonibacter species. are non-fermentative Gram-stain-negative bacteria, with rare reports of human infections primarily affecting immunocompromised patients. Here, we report the genomic and phenotypic characterization of a novel Pannonibacter species, isolated from a bacteremia episode in a pediatric patient with acute lymphoblastic leukemia in Brazil. Initial characterization of the isolate (here named CBAS 1226) by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry and 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing identified it as Pannonibacter sp., most closely related to P. phragmitetus. However, comparison of its MALDI-TOF spectrum with a commercial reference library revealed compatibility with only two of the five main spectra profiles for P. phragmitetus. This discrepancy motivated comprehensive genomic, biochemical, morphological, and antimicrobial resistance profiling of CBAS 1226. Genomic analysis revealed that Pannonibacter sp. CBAS 1226 is phylogenetically distinct from P. phragmitetus and other known species, with ANI and dDDH values below species delineation thresholds, supporting its proposal as Candidatus Pannonibacter alzirae. It forms small, non-hemolytic, grayish-white colonies on blood agar, similar to its closest relatives P. phragmitetus and P. indicus. Phenotypically, it is distinguished by positive - and {beta}-glucosidase activity, along with the utilization of citrate, L-proline, and 2-ketoglutarate. It is negative for alkaline phosphatase and unable to utilize D-fructose, D-melibiose, esculin, or L-arginine. The isolate exhibited higher MICs for {beta}-lactams, whereas carbapenems and fluoroquinolones showed low MICs. The isolate is capable of forming biofilms and tolerates alkaline conditions, a wide range of temperatures, and different oxygen concentrations. Altogether, this report emphasizes the relevance of additional proteomics- and genomics-based approaches to clarify unusual bacterial infections and describes a new Pannonibacter species with distinct features and the potential to cause opportunistic infections.

title: RAMP-Seq: a single-tube nanopore workflow for co-amplifying full-length 16S rRNA and antimicrobial resistance genes for integrated taxonomic and resistance profiling
authors: Pathak, D.; Jagtap, S.; Godbole, R.; Patel, N.; Mohammed, A.; Jeevanandan, S. P.; Sarkar, D.; Roy, I.; Shridhar, V.; Natarajan, A.; Srikantaiah, V.; Roy, R.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance needs workflows that both identify bacteria and detect resistance genes from a single sample, but current targeted nanopore assays typically split these steps into separate reactions or library preparations. We introduce RAMP-Seq (Rapid AMR Profiling by Sequencing), a workflow that simultaneously amplifies the full-length 16S rRNA gene (~1,500 bp) together with eight resistance determinants (~600 - 700 bp) in a single multiplex PCR and then sequences the resulting mixed-length amplicon pool as a single nanopore library. The eight-primer pair set targets dominant alleles of {beta}-lactamase, carbapenemase, quinolone-resistance and silver-resistance families. Read-length distributions confirmed that both size classes were co-amplified evenly using a single, non-equimolar primer pool. From extracted DNA to the first taxonomically classified reads took 8.2 {+/-} 0.6 h. Full-length 16S sequencing of an eight-member mock community identified all anticipated taxa, and the observed abundances closely followed the expected log-scaled composition (Pearson's r = 0.879). The full nineplex amplicon assay was subsequently tested on three distinct matrices: pooled clinical isolates, spiked human blood, and environmental water samples. Using an equal-mass pool of genomic DNA from eleven multidrug-resistant clinical and repository isolates, the full assay produced genus-level and resistance-gene profiles that were consistent across biological replicates (r = 0.998 and r = 0.824), and it specifically identified all seven panel targets present, confirmed by Illumina whole-genome sequencing. After carbonate-based host DNA depletion, Klebsiella pneumoniae was recovered from spiked human blood at every titration down to 102 CFU/mL, as were all five panel targets carried by that strain. Across five water-sampling sites from a sewage treatment plant (STP) to a connected lake system, microbial communities and resistance-gene profiles were site-specific: influent and effluent communities overlapped little, while the lake inlet and outlet were similar. Target resistance genes were most numerous and abundant in STP influent, fewer in effluent, and rare or absent in lake and well samples. Because bacterial identification relies on amplification of the conserved, near-universal 16S rRNA gene, rather than on species-specific primer sets, RAMP-Seq can detect and taxonomically classify bacteria in a design-agnostic manner. The same single-tube chemistry therefore serves sample types as different as clinical specimens and environmental water and is extendable to longer ribosomal targets and further resistance-gene families.

title: ModBERT: a DNA modification and genetic variant-aware DNA large language model
authors: Bolzan, D.; Davuluri, R. V.; Mahony, S.; AY, F.
abstract: The development of foundation models that learn a general grammar of DNA (DNA language models) has accelerated in recent years. The vast majority of DNA large language models (LLMs), such as DNABERT-2 and Nucleotide Transformer, are pretrained almost exclusively on reference genomes. They therefore cannot represent the two sources of variation most directly tied to regulatory differences between people: genetic variants and DNA methylation. Long-read sequencing (Nanopore and PacBio) now measures both from the same native DNA molecules, but no model is designed to use this joint readout. With this in mind, we developed ModBERT, a DNA language model built on a five-letter probabilistic genome representation in which each position is a distribution over A, C, G, T, 5mC (represented with M). In pretraining, these distributions encode population allele frequencies and CpG methylation levels from 242 individuals in the 1000 Genomes Long-Read Sequencing Consortium, learned with a soft-target masked language modeling objective. We further propose probabilistic fine-tuning, in which the same representation encodes one individual's genotype and methylation. A fine-tuned model can then make person-specific predictions from a single assay. Under this novel fine-tuning framework, we show that ModBERT effectively utilizes methylation information to classify peaks from functional genomic assays, including histone mark (n=11 different marks) and transcription factor binding (n=69 TFs) ChIP-seq data, outperforming ab initio trained models and ModBERT pretrained on sequences without methylation. In silico methylation perturbations yield TF sensitivities that correlate with independent methylation-aware motif models. Using an evaluation design that separates generalization to new loci from generalization to new individuals, ModBERT predicts chromatin accessibility at held-out loci in held-out individuals (AUROC 0.88). Its predicted variant effects agree with likely causal caQTLs (Spearman correlation = 0.52) but not with variants associated only through linkage, a traditionally challenging task.
