Overall, ModBERT establishes a framework for personal-genome language modeling, in which a model reads each individual's genetic and epigenetic sequence rather than a shared reference. This enables in silico dissection of variant and methylation effects on gene regulation and principled prioritization of candidates for experimental validation as population-scale long-read cohorts (e.g., 1KGP and Human Pangenome Reference Consortium) grow.

title: Evolutionarily Conserved Fragments reveal modular architecture and expand functional coverage in bacteriophage proteins
authors: Smug, B.; Szczepaniak, K.; Leconte, J.; Dunin-Horkawicz, S.; Mostowy, R. J.
abstract: Bacteriophage proteins evolve through extensive modular exchange, yet the sequence units underlying this process remain poorly defined. Classical domains are plausible evolutionary modules, but they incompletely annotate phage proteins and may not always coincide with the regions conserved across protein families. Here, we constructed 13,035 Evolutionarily Conserved Fragments (ECFs), grouped into 3,167 families, through large-scale HMM-HMM comparisons of proteins from 5,396 RefSeq phage genomes, without imposing predefined domain boundaries. ECFs overlapped substantially with ECOD and Pfam annotations but formed a heterogeneous spectrum comprising subdomains, domain-equivalent units, composite regions and fragments with no counterpart in either resource. Their relationships were frequently nested, indicating that conserved modules occur at multiple organisational scales. ECFs annotated 50% of phage representative proteins (at least doubling the coverage of either database), with the largest gains in structural and infection-related functions, a pattern replicated in independent metagenomic data. ECF families also showed function-dependent patterns of diversity and spatial segregation and provided functional associations for 23,925 protein families lacking detectable Pfam or ECOD domains. In receptor-binding proteins, ECFs subdivided established domains, delineated previously unannotated structural elements and recovered homologous regions where structural similarity was ambiguous. These results show that the evolutionary building blocks of phage proteins do not always coincide with classical domains, highlighting that evolutionary processes act across multiple scales. ECFs provide a complementary, sequence-derived framework for investigating how complex viral proteins are assembled, diversified and functionally organised.

title: Convergent lignocellulose degradation in terrestrial crabs is driven by distinct host genus-specific microbial communities
authors: Watson-Zink, V. M.; Wilkins, L. G. E.; Eisen, J. A.; Grosberg, R. K.; Ettinger, C. L.
abstract: Background: Restrictions on the types of food available on land have repeatedly triggered the convergent evolution of herbivory in terrestrial animals. This pattern also holds true in many terrestrially adapted crabs, which have independently colonized land more than 17 times since the Cretaceous. Many clades of terrestrial crabs are now almost completely herbivorous, standing in contrast to the ancestral pattern of detrivory. While many bacteria possess efficient pathways for degrading lignin and cellulose, the role of gut microbiomes in facilitating these dietary shifts in terrestrial crabs remains poorly understood. To explore the relationship between microbial community structure and the ability of land crabs to digest lignocellulose, we conducted read-based and assembly-based metagenomic analyses on feces collected from the guts of 14 crab species across six genera, representing a gradient of terrestriality from the lower intertidal zone to forested habitats. Results: We generated 129 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) that represent key members of these gut microbial communities, establishing a foundational resource for future studies on crab-microbiome interactions. We found that host genus explained most of the variation in bacterial community composition, while degree of terrestrial adaptation (i.e. terrestrial grade) explained a smaller proportion. We also identified multiple bacterial genera that strikingly differed in relative abundance across terrestrial grades, crab genera, and diet type. Broad-scale functional analyses of general carbon metabolism across crabs revealed an absence of complete pathways in crabs from lower terrestrial grades, suggesting a functional divergence in gut communities linked to habitat transition. Fine-scale functional analyses of predicted carbohydrate-active enzyme (CAZyme) domains allowed us to connect specific MAGs to lignocellulose degradation pathway genes, demonstrating that different crab genera harbor distinct microbial taxa that may have similar CAZyme profiles in their guts. Conclusions: This work provides a foundational metagenomic resource for genomic exploration of microbial communities in terrestrial crab guts. These results suggest that the gut microbiomes of terrestrially adapted crabs are structured primarily by host identity and may have convergently acquired microbes with similar functions to help perform lignocellulose degradation. Overall, different degrees of adaptation to terrestrial environments, including resulting dietary shifts, may be responsible for functional divergence in crab gut community assembly.

title: Performance Test of the QNome Nanopore Sequencer for Arthropod DNA Barcoding
authors: Thompson, K. A.; Prosser, S. W.; Floyd, R. M.; Jafarpour, S.; Ozsahin, E.; Hebert, P. D.
abstract: Nanopore sequencers have the potential to liberate DNA sequencing from centralized core facilities to distributed analytical nodes. Until recently, Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) had been the sole manufacturer of a portable nanopore sequencer, but analogous platforms are in production. Nanopore sequencers from Qitan Technology (QT) are widely used in China but have been unavailable outside that nation and have not been subject to rigorous, independent performance testing. Enabled by early access to QT's least expensive sequencer and flow cell, the QNome-3841 and QCell-384, we tested whether they could generate accurate DNA barcodes cost-effectively. In several tests involving amplicon pools from 96 to 9,120 specimens, QT recovered valid DNA barcodes from nearly as many specimens (98.5%) as ONT. QT sequences had slightly lower accuracy than their ONT counterparts (median per-read identity 98.04% vs. 99.39%) and QT frequently failed to resolve the correct length of G/C homopolymers. However, barcode sequences from the two platforms were nearly indistinguishable after bioinformatic treatment with the Barcode Inference Pipeline (BIP). QT's wash kit performed well, enabling a QCell to sequence eight amplicon pools with negligible carryover (four of >800,000 reads) among eight runs, and a gradual degradation of the flow cell. Its ultra-fast protocol allowed library preparation in a single step that could be completed in under 10 minutes, but it led to a significant reduction in read retention. Once widely available, QT devices will be well-suited to support DNA barcode analysis.

title: Evolutionary Design of Membrane-Lytic Antimicrobial Peptides with Mixture of Experts
authors: Dong, R.; Song, C.
abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) hold great promise in combating drug-resistant pathogens, yet current design models do not explicitly account for their primary mode of action, membrane disruption. To address this gap, we propose AMPainterV2, a model that designs membrane-lytic AMPs using generative adversarial imitation learning. AMPainterV2 integrates a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) policy network to support insertion, deletion, and mutation operations, thereby expanding the evolutionary design space. In vitro experiments demonstrate that all ten top-ranked peptides evolved from random sequences are active membrane-lytic AMPs, with the best candidate achieving a mean minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) of 1.5 M and superior membrane-lytic activity compared to polymyxin B. Particularly, a deletion-only version of AMPainterV2 enables membrane-lytic AMP miniaturization, yielding six miniaturized peptides with comparable or improved activity and an average 36% length reduction. Collectively, AMPainterV2 advances mechanism-driven AMP design and offers a valuable tool for cost-effective AMP development.

title: Improved long-read sequencing technology reveals full genome architecture of Malian Plasmodium falciparum field isolates
authors: Diaz-Terenti, B.; Diakite, M.; Ranford-Cartwright, L. C.; Pradhan, S.; Martos-Contreras, M. d. C.; Otto, T. D.; Gomez-Diaz, E.
abstract: Understanding genome plasticity in malaria parasites and the diversity of their repetitive gene families requires high-quality reference genomes derived from parasites recently isolated from patients. However, generating such genomes in Plasmodium falciparum remains challenging owing to the parasite's extreme AT content, extensive repetitive regions, and the frequent occurrence of multiclonal infections in endemic settings. As a result, most available reference genomes are derived from laboratory-adapted strains, that have experienced prolonged in vitro maintenance, and that incompletely represent natural parasite diversity. We developed and optimized a de novo assembly strategy based on PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing and applied it to eight recently-isolated and cloned P. falciparum parasites from Mali. HiFi sequencing enabled highly accurate genome reconstruction, yielding assemblies with a mean of 18 contigs, 301 pseudogenes, and a frameshift rate of 0.04% following Liftoff annotation. Assemblies showed high structural integrity and near-complete chromosomes, including improved recovery of subtelomeric regions and multigene families, without requiring short-read correction. Despite overall conservation of chromosome organization, substantial variation was observed in chromosome-end architecture, subtelomeric structure, and telomeric repeat content among parasite genomes. Our approach simplifies the generation of high-quality P. falciparum genomes and reduces sequencing requirements fourfold. The resulting assemblies enabled characterization of natural variation in telomere plasticity and multicopy gene family diversity in field isolates. These findings establish PacBio HiFi sequencing as an effective and scalable strategy for producing highly contiguous and accurate de novo assemblies of P. falciparum, supporting the development of geographically-diverse, field-relevant malaria parasite reference genomes.

title: DNA methylation assigns sequencing reads to closely related bacterial strains when their sequence cannot
authors: Kakabra, K.; Claesson, M. J.
abstract: Clinical and public-health questions often concern strains rather than species, yet co-resident strains of one species can be so closely related that a single long read carries no sequence difference between them. We measured how often this happens in 639 pairs of isolates of Enterococcus faecium, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Listeria monocytogenes and Staphylococcus aureus sequenced on one nanopore platform. Among the 297 pairs above 99% average nucleotide identity (ANI), 40.37% of read placements (a read counted against one strain's genome) carried no sequence difference between the two strains, and above 99.9% ANI about three quarters did. Strains of one species also differ in the DNA motifs they methylate. Our method, Epilect, assigns single nanopore reads to strains from the basecaller's methylation calls, given a methylation profile for each strain, and declines to call when the evidence is weak. In the pairs above 99% ANI it correctly assigned 21.8% of the read placements that sequence could not place, at a precision of 0.959. In computational mixtures of 65 pairs of distinct strains at or above 99.5% ANI that were predicted to differ in methylation, its per-read F1 score exceeded that of the best of three sequence-based read-phasing tools by 0.25 (95% CI 0.08 to 0.37); where equally related strains were predicted to share a methylome, the comparison reversed. DNA methylation therefore supplies strain evidence on reads whose sequence carries none, and whether it will do so for a given pair of strains can be estimated before sequencing.

title: Systematic benchmarking of small variant calling pipelines for long-read RNA sequencing data
authors: Wang, J.; Robinson, M. D.
abstract: Background: Long-read RNA sequencing (lrRNA-seq) enables transcript-resolved variant detection, but systematic and neutral evaluations of small variants calling pipelines remain limited. The performance of existing tools across sequencing technologies, alignment strategies, variant caller choice, genomic contexts and downstream haplotype phasing is not fully understood. Results: Here, we systematically benchmark six lrRNA-seq variant callers (Clair3-RNA, DeepVariant, NanoTS, isoLASER, longcallR and longcallR-nn), along with a widely used short-read RNA-seq variant caller (GATK HaplotypeCaller) as a baseline, using Genome in a Bottle (GIAB) datasets comprising three cell lines sequenced with four ONT and two PacBio library preparation protocols. We further evaluate the impact of upstream alignment strategies, including aligner choice and alignment transformation, on variant-calling performance. Accuracy is assessed across sequencing depths and genomic contexts. Additionally, we compare haplotype phasing tools (WhatsHap, LongPhase, HapCUT2, HiPhase, isoLASER and longcallR) using variant calls generated by different callers to identify optimal pipeline combinations. Finally, we extend our evaluation of variant-calling performance to more recent LongBench datasets. Conclusions: Our benchmark shows that sequencing characteristics are the strongest determinant of lrRNA-seq variant-calling performance, followed by variant caller and alignment strategies, with additional effects from genomic context. Variant caller strengths differed by platform and variant type: Clair3-RNA showed the broadest and most robust applicability across ONT and PacBio chemistries; NanoTS performed best or near-best for SNVs on newer chemistries; longcallR was competitive for SNV calling; and DeepVariant performed strongly on PacBio, particularly for indels. For downstream haplotype phasing, no single method excelled across all metrics. HiPhase and LongPhase achieved the lowest switch error rates on PacBio and ONT data, respectively; WhatsHap maximized coverage and contiguity; and HapCUT2 balanced accuracy and coverage for SNVs. LongcallR offers a strong alternative for joint variant calling and phasing.

title: DeepCDS: Ab initio coding sequence prediction in prokaryotic metagenomic short reads
authors: Nielsen, L. S.; Nielsen, H.; Winther, O.
abstract: Accurate coding sequence prediction in short prokaryotic metagenomic sequences, such as Illumina reads, remains challenging due to sequence fragmentation, unknown sequence origins, and sequencing errors. Here we introduce DeepCDS, a deep learning-based ab initio coding sequence predictor trained on short prokaryotic sequences with and without simulated Illumina-like sequencing errors. DeepCDS integrates embeddings from the protein language model ESM-2 with nucleotide-level information to predict complete and partial coding sequences. Benchmarking on 215 phylogenetically diverse prokaryotic organisms demonstrates that DeepCDS consistently outperforms well-established and widely used methods in coding sequence detection across sequence lengths from 75 to 1,000 base pairs, including improved identification of both canonical and non-canonical start codons as well as stop codons, and greater robustness to different sequencing error profiles. DeepCDS also recovers more coding sequences from functionally uncharacterized genes and remains operational on sequences shorter than existing tools support. We additionally evaluate DeepCDS on a simulated metagenomic dataset from the Critical Assessment of Metagenome Interpretation initiative, where it likewise achieves the strongest performance among tested tools, and on a real human gut metagenome, where its predictions are more frequently supported by known proteins. These findings suggest that amino acid-level context, here provided by a protein language model, contributes complementary information for nucleotide-level coding sequence detection, especially at very short lengths. Ultimately, DeepCDS may help uncover the functional potential of the vast microbial diversity that remains genomically uncharacterized.

title: Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic analysis of oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid against extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producing Escherichia coli in an in vitro bladder infection model: impact on clinical breakpoints
authors: Anderson, C. R. B.; van Gorp, E.; Won, H.; Roberts, J. A.; Cottingham, H.; Breen, S. K. J.; Landersdorfer, C. B.; Meletiadis, J.; Peleg, A. Y.; Abbott, I.
abstract: Uropathogens with acquired ESBL-genes can limit effective oral treatment options. Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid can be used as targeted therapy (500/125mg, 8-hourly). Despite favorable urinary pharmacokinetics (PK), there is little urine-specific data that quantifies the exposure required for bacterial clearance. A dynamic in vitro bladder model was employed, allowing for the simulated treatment of UTIs with oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid. Sixteen Escherichia coli isolates (12 clinical ceftriaxone-resistant uropathogens, 4 laboratory isolates) were selected. Bacterial response to treatment, emergence of resistance, exposure-response targets and PK/PD indexes were explored. Following simulation of standard-dose oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (500/125mg, 8-hourly; Cmax 935mg/L; AUC0-24 14272mg/L), 14/16 isolates displayed no growth at the end of treatment, with elimination in seven isolates confirmed after a 24h antibiotic-free follow up. As exposure was reduced, greater survival and regrowth were observed. Only two isolates had significant post-exposure rises in MIC (32 to 128mg/L, 64 to 256mg/L). %T>MIC was the best predictor for end of treatment outcome (?log10cfu/mL: stasis 52.7%, 1log10 kill 61.8%, 2log10 kill 71.1%, R2=0.9062). Lower R2 values were found with EUCAST MIC measurements (fixed 2mg/L clavulanic acid) as compared to CLSI MIC measurements (2:1 amoxicillin to clavulanic acid). Monte Carlo simulations indicated that standard-dose 8-hourly would achieve all %T>MIC targets in >95% of virtual patients with MICs ?64 mg/L, regardless of MIC method (CLSI or EUCAST). Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid displays time-dependent killing against ceftriaxone-resistant E. coli. This data supports clinical breakpoints for uncomplicated UTI for isolates with MIC ? 64mg/L, assuming 500/125mg oral dosing 8-hourly.

title: High-resolution 3D genome mapping of late replicative senescence reveals hypomethylation-associated loop expansion, weakened cell identity, and locus-specific L1 derepression
authors: Kelsey, M. M. G.; Dalgarno, A.; Evans, S. A.; Nunez, T. A.; Rocha, A.; Clark, K.; Sedivy, J. M.; Neretti, N.
abstract: Cellular senescence contributes to aging and age-associated diseases through the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), which is fueled in part by derepression of retrotransposable elements. While senescence is driven by transcriptional and epigenetic changes, the contribution of higher-order genome organization remains incompletely defined, particularly at the resolution required to detect chromatin loops. Here we present ~3 kb-resolution Hi-C maps of late-stage replicatively senescent (RS), proliferating, and quiescent human lung fibroblasts, integrated with total RNA-seq and Nanopore long-read DNA sequencing. RS cells exhibit widespread compartment and subcompartment switching toward active states, consistent with a global loss of heterochromatin. We observe a striking expansion of chromatin loops in RS cells, with an approximately sixfold excess of senescence-specific loops over proliferation- or quiescence-specific loops. These senescence-specific loops are enriched in the B compartment relative to other loop classes, are accompanied by DNA hypomethylation at loop anchors, and are enriched for neuronal-lineage gene programs that are concordantly upregulated, suggesting a structural correlate of the loss of cell-type identity recently described in aging chromatin. Compartment and subcompartment reorganization, but not loop status, is associated with retrotransposon derepression. We identify L1HS_14q23.2_3, an intact L1HS element, as a locus where compartment switching, subcompartment activation, novel loop formation, and pronounced promoter demethylation appear to promote locus-specific derepression. Quiescent fibroblasts unexpectedly share inflammatory transcriptional features with RS cells, raising important considerations for experimental design in senescence research.

title: Molecular evolution of Andes virus lineages leading to recent human outbreaks
authors: Sharma, C.; Oversti, S.; Stass, R.; Lucaci, A. G.; Audet, J.; Safronetz, D.; Zhao, L.; Lythgoe, K.; Katzourakis, A.; Bowden, T. A.; Lytras, S.; Ghafari, M.
abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) is exceptional among hantaviruses in its capacity for person-to-person transmission, but whether outbreaks reflect recent viral adaptation or emergence of pre-existing reservoir lineages remains unclear. We generated paired blood- and nasal-derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and ecological opportunity.

title: MB-CasFire™: A Plug-and-Play, Thermostable CRISPR Enzyme for Precise Nucleic Acid Detection
authors: Broughton, J. P.; Alpay, E.; Fantin, N. J.; Ansaloni, S.; Elsener, S.; Jung, J. K.; Zhang, Y.; Madrid, I. Z.; Shiigi, S. A.; Rajan, S.; Jain, I.; Wright, W. D.; Hendriks, C. G.; Tymoshenko, S.; Ratushna, V.; Lee, S.; Warner, M.; Hong, R.; Sui, X.; Panchal, S.; Garske, A. L.; Miao, X.; Chen, J. S.
abstract: CRISPR-based detection technologies have the potential to enable precise, rapid, and cost-effective diagnostic and biosurveillance solutions by pairing sensitive and specific nucleic acid detection with a simple workflow. Combining isothermal amplification and CRISPR detection in a single reaction as a "one-pot" detection method can meet these needs, but only if the CRISPR enzyme remains active at the temperatures and salt concentrations that isothermal amplification requires. Here we describe MB-CasFire, a CRISPR-Cas enzyme engineered from a naturally thermostable Cas12a for improved stability and performance, as a "plug-and-play" DETECTR(R) (DNA Endonuclease-Targeted CRISPR Trans Reporter) enzyme for sensitive and specific nucleic acid detection. MB-CasFire remains active at elevated temperatures in amplification buffers and supports one-pot detection with loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) and nicking enzyme amplification reaction (NEAR), eliminating transfers between amplification and readout, and increasing the signal-to-noise to enable precise nucleic acid detection. This method, called OnePot DETECTR, is also compatible with commercially available isothermal master mixes, including those from New England Biolabs, allowing assays to be assembled from standard reagents. Using MB-CasFire, we detected SARS-CoV-2 in nasal swab samples with a LAMP-based OnePot DETECTR assay and Neisseria gonorrhoeae in urine samples with a NEAR-based OnePot DETECTR assay. MB-CasFire also functioned in multiplex detection and single-nucleotide polymorphism discrimination assays for antibiotic resistance genotyping. These results support MB-CasFire as a versatile detection enzyme that simplifies assay architecture for CRISPR-based detection assays that amplify, recognize, and report the presence of nucleic acid targets in a single reaction without thermocycling.

title: An observational study examining nasopharyngeal resistome evolution among children under the selective pressure of antibiotic exposure and hospitalisation for pneumonia in Malawi: A study protocol
authors: O'Connor, L.; Kalizang'oma, A.; Chimalizeni, Y.; Meehan, C.; Androga, G.; Brown, C.; Henrion, M.; Chaguza, C.; French, N.; Heyderman, R. S.; Kwambana-Adams, B.
abstract:
IntroductionAntimicrobial resistance (AMR) to first line antibiotics for pneumonia is a major global health problem, and AMR-attributable deaths are prevalent in sub-Saharan Africa. Improved data on how AMR develops and influences health outcomes in resource limited settings is crucial. The nasopharynx is a reservoir for pneumonia pathogens and their resistome, the genetic determinants of AMR. No study has explored whether human resistome composition in children with pneumonia is associated with health outcomes. This study will examine whether antibiotic treatment and hospital admission for pneumonia generate a persistent hospital-acquired nasopharyngeal resistome in children, and whether this is associated with re-hospitalisation.

MethodsThis is an observational case-control study, that will recruit 350 children aged 12-36 months from four groups in Blantyre, Malawi: healthy children in the community (healthy community), children with pneumonia treated in the community (community pneumonia), children hospitalised with pneumonia (hospital pneumonia) and children re-hospitalised with pneumonia (re-hospitalised pneumonia). Nasopharyngeal swabs will be taken at recruitment and 3-month follow-up study visits for metagenomic sequencing to characterise the nasopharyngeal microbiome and resistome; urine samples will be taken at recruitment for an antibiotic activity bioassay. Socio-demographic data, co-morbidities, pneumonia severity, antibiotic exposure and health outcomes will be recorded.

AnalysisCross-sectional comparisons between groups at recruitment will examine whether nasopharyngeal resistome (NPR) composition differs by pneumonia severity, antibiotic and healthcare exposure. Longitudinal comparisons within groups will assess the dynamics of NPR composition over time. The study is powered to detect a medium effect size (Cohens D = 0.505) change in the relative abundance of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) between all four groups. Primary outcomes are the difference in beta diversity (Bray-Curtis dissimilarity index), and relative abundance of ARG classes in the NPR. The primary objectives are to estimate the difference in diversity and relative abundance of the NPR between hospitalised pneumonia participants when compared to 1) healthy community and 2) community pneumonia participants, and to investigate whether participants re-hospitalised with pneumonia within a 3-month period have a persistent hospital-acquired NPR pattern.

Ethics and disseminationThe study has been approved by the Kamuzu University of Heath Sciences Research Ethics Committee (KUREC, formerly Malawi College of Medicine Research Ethics Committee; Ref: P.10/24-1200) and Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine Research Ethics Committee (LSTM REC; Ref: 24-076).

Trial registration numberISRCTN64027792

STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDYO_ST_ABSStrengthsC_ST_ABSO_LIStudy design that uses metagenomic deep sequencing to enable direct, concurrent comparison of nasopharyngeal microbiome (NPM) and resistome (NPR) composition between community and hospitalised paediatric populations with pneumonia in a resource-limited setting.
C_LIO_LIData on reported and urinary bioassay-detected antibiotic use prior to, and throughout the study, enabling detailed examination of antibiotic selective pressure on the NPR.
C_LIO_LIInvestigation of the association between NPR composition and adverse clinical outcomes from pneumonia.
C_LI

LimitationsO_LILimitations to this study include few sampling time points (two for community pneumonia and three for hospitalised pneumonia), which may not fully capture the impact of antibiotic exposure; the potential for residual confounding following adjustment for known potential confounders (e.g. age, sex, co-morbidities, household exposure to smoke and breastfeeding) in the association between resistome composition and adverse clinical outcomes, for which the authors have detailed statistical analysis measures; and ability to only determine association between NPR composition and adverse clinical outcomes, rather than causal inference, due to the case-control study design.
C_LI

SUMMARYO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABSThe nasopharynx is a reservoir for pneumonia pathogens and their genetic determinants of antibiotic resistance in children. Studies of nasopharyngeal microbiome composition have shown association with paediatric pneumonia severity and mortality.

What this study addsThis study will describe nasopharyngeal resistome (NPR) evolution under selective pressure of antibiotics and hospitalisation for paediatric pneumonia, and explore whether NPR composition is associated with health outcomes in a resource-limited setting.

How this study might affect research, practice or policyThis exploratory study could inform larger scale observational studies to examine the association between antibiotic resistance and health outcomes, by defining high-risk nasopharyngeal resistome composition, helping to determine the required sample size and contributing open-source bioinformatic pipelines. The study could also inform research for public health interventions, including antibiotic stewardship.

title: No Point Beating Around the Bedpan: Lessons from a Major Intra-Hospital NDM-Producing Escherichia coli Carriage Outbreak : a Mixed-Methods Study.
authors: Le Hir, A.; Vincent, P.; Sardi, F. S.; Giglione, C.; Bouton, N.; Stavris, C.; Maisonobe, L.; Chiche, L.; Fliniaux, C.; Dortet, L.; Castagnier, M.; Brisson, J.; Rebaudet, S.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance constitutes a major threat to global public health. Among emerging extensively drug-resistant bacteria (eXDR), carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (CPE) expose hospitals to outbreaks through rapid dissemination, and to therapeutic limitations. Through a mixed epidemiological qualitative methods study, we report the most extensive CPE carriage outbreak known to date in France, which occurred at Hopital Europeen Marseille (HEM) between January and June2025. By the end of November 2024, the admission of an index patient returning from Senegal carrying an NDM-producing Escherichia coli led to an extensive transmission, despite adherence to national screen and isolate guidelines. Nearly 7,500 rectal screening tests identified 481 CPE carriers (including 343 NDM, 129 OXA-48-like and 9 other CPE), and 14 vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium carriers. This major outbreak prompted an extraordinary response involving clinical, technical and administrative teams within the institution. It highlighted operational limitations in current screening, cohorting and biocleaning strategies in the context of a hospital-wide outbreak. We describe the outbreak trajectory, the control measures implemented and provide a structured synthesis of lessons learned across organisational, scientific and policy domains.

title: Pseudomonas aeruginosa in bronchiectasis: unmasking population diversity and antimicrobial resistance in the Australian context
authors: Strickland, K. R.; Baird, T.; Burr, L. D.; Dunn, E. M.; Littlejohn, M. L.; Davies, J. L.; Bashford, J. J.; Burke, A.; Evans, I.; Christensen, J.; Brock, J.; McIntosh, L.; Price, E. P.; Sarovich, D. S.
abstract: ABSTRACT Background: Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections in bronchiectasis airways result in poorer lung function, advanced lung lobe involvement, worsened life quality, and higher hospitalisation rates. Despite high prevalence, little is known about P. aeruginosa population genomics, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) rates, persistence, and transmission dynamics in Australians with bronchiectasis. Methods: P. aeruginosa (n=137) isolated between 2009 and 2025 from 59 Australians with bronchiectasis underwent antimicrobial susceptibility testing against 11 antipseudomonal drugs, whole-genome sequencing, comparative genomics, and in silico AMR determinant identification. Data were integrated with 4,575 publicly available bronchiectasis-derived P. aeruginosa genomes to determine global phylogenomic and AMR determinant patterns. Results: High AMR rates were identified in the Australian isolates, with 75.9% resistant to at least one antimicrobial, 19.7% multidrug-resistant, and 9.5% extremely drug-resistant. AMR rates were highest (64.2%) for ciprofloxacin and cefepime (44.5%), and lowest for piperacillin/tazobactam (8.8%) and colistin (0.7%). Phylogenomics uncovered several instances of within-host evolution, hypermutation, persistence, and multi-lineage infections. Of the fifty-seven identified multilocus sequence types (STs), seven (12.3%) were novel, five were high-risk international clones (ST274 [6.6%], ST395 [0.7%], ST244 [0.7%], ST277 [0.7%], ST298 [0.7%]) and three were common global clones (ST253 [5.1%], ST155 [3.6%], ST260 [0.7%]). No high-risk AMR-conferring mobile genetic elements were seen, although numerous chromosomal AMR determinants were identified. AMR determinant prevalence was consistent with the global dataset, with no evidence of geographic clustering. Conclusions: Our study provides critical insights into P. aeruginosa diversity in Australians with bronchiectasis. High AMR rates and chronic colonisation highlight the need to improve diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship measures, and infection control practices in this neglected clinical cohort.
